Chapter 3 The Large Language Model Training Pipeline

3.1 Training Models

The training pipeline of a large language model follows a somewhat standard methodology: starting from a model architecture where the parameters are initialized randomly, we train language capabilities through a process that is called pretraining. During pretraining, we feed large text corpora to our models, which they are trained on autoregressively. The result of this stage is a base model, which is generally not yet suited for specific, practical applications. Hence, we need to adapt it to a downstream task or purpose. This stage is called posttraining, where we show specific types of additional data to the model using which we elicit task-specific behavior, such as instruction-following or classification settings.

3.1.1 Encoder versus Decoder Models

As we saw in the previous chapter, there are two dominant styles of models. On the one hand, encoder models are able to create rich contextualized representations based on input data. However, most of the recent successes are based on the decoder models. While encoders are better at understanding tasks (classification, sentiment), decoders excel at generative tasks. Decoder models have grown in size, both in terms of number of trainable parameters, and the available training data. This leads to models that are surprisingly capable of generalization to unseen contexts.

Let us have a look in more detail at the relevant steps in the decoder-only training pipeline.

3.1.2 Pretraining/Finetuning Paradigm

A central feature of the success of current training pipelines is the use of transfer learning. One of the standard applications of modern transformer models is to take a model that has been trained on a large, generic dataset, and then retrain it on a new task. The model is pretrained on the large, generic, corpus, and then finetuned on the new, specific, task, for which a small dataset is present. Finetuning for the new task is quick, since the dataset is small, but also since the pretrained weights have been transferred. The finetuning-training does not have to start from scratch.

This pretraining/finetuning distinction of the transfer learning paradigm is at the heart of large language model training pipelines. Rather than starting the training from scratch, the model can reuse already-learned linguistic knowledge in new scenarios, thus speeding up the training process. Pretraining of large, commercial models may take months. Usually, the new task is specific (such as question answering in a certain domain, or sentiment analysis). For the new task, a dedicated dataset will be used to finetune the model. During finetuning, a subset of the model’s weights are updated carefully to retain the general linguistic capabilities of the pretrained model, while gaining an understanding of the new task. Finetuning a model to a new task takes typically on the order of minutes to hours.

3.1.3 Open and Closed Models

Popular LLMs are OpenAI’s ChatGPT series [Achiam et al., 2023, Ouyang et al., 2022], Meta’s LLaMa family [Touvron et al., 2023], Google’s Gemma [Chowdhery et al., 2023] and Gemini [Anil et al., 2023], Anthropic’s Claude family, Moonshot AI’s Kimi, DeepSeek [Guo et al., 2025], and Qwen [Bai et al., 2025], among others.

There are different degrees of openness between these models. For example, a model’s training data can be made public, the network architecture of a model can be disclosed, and the trained weights can be released. However, the companies behind commercial models seldom publish all elements of their model and training procedure, as they seek to retain some competitive edge.

In response, the scientific community has developed fully open-source models, such as BLOOM [Le Scao et al., 2023], Pythia [Biderman et al., 2023], and OLMo [Groeneveld et al., 2024], to contribute to the collective understanding of how large language models work. Of these models all elements of the training pipeline are public, and they are the focus of this chapter. We also highlight certain aspects of some commercial models.

Although the models are all based on the transformer architecture, there are small differences between individual components and their overall layout, for example to capitalize on hardware differences or specific optimizations developed by their respective creators. For instance, Google optimized Gemini for their TPU-based compute infrastructure [Jouppi et al., 2023]. We discuss further improvements to the architecture extensively in Chapter 4.

3.2 Training Pipeline

We will now describe in more detail the steps of a standard training pipeline. LLMs are constructed using an elaborate pipeline with different training phases [Radford et al., 2019, Minaee et al., 2024]. We will describe the phases, as shown in Figure 3.1. The combinations of individual phases are usually referred to as training recipes, as they denote the order in which the models were trained. At each phase, a new dataset may be used, together with a new loss function. Each phase is designed to imbue the model with a specific capability. This will become clear as we discuss the individual phases.

3.2.1 Acquire Data

The first step in the pipeline is to acquire data. Typically, massive, general-purpose text corpora are used [Brown et al., 2020]. The corpora consist of raw text without the need for manual labeling. This data is typically aggregated from both curated and uncurated online sources, then refined through cleaning heuristics to mitigate the effect of harmful, private, or copyrighted content. The corpora that are used for pretraining are large. Modern LLMs are trained on a web-scale magnitude of data, often reaching the scale of trillions of tokens. Some examples of datasets are:

  • •

    Common Crawl: a massive, non-profit snapshot of the web containing billions of pages; alternative sources include https://archive.org. While the size is unparalleled, the quality of the data is under discussion [Baack, 2024]. Many derivatives, such as C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus) present a filtered subset of English web text [Raffel et al., 2020] to enhance the quality of the data.

  • •

    Dolma 3: a data mixture that is designed to maximize performance across a diverse suite of tasks. It is used in the OLMo open source/open data project [Ettinger et al., 2025, Soldaini et al., 2024].

  • •

    SmolLM3: utilizes a large three-stage training strategy with 11.2 trillion tokens that dynamically mixes web, math, and code data to optimize reasoning and knowledge acquisition [Bakouch et al., 2025].

Recent research emphasizes that data diversity is as critical as size for improving cross-domain knowledge and downstream generalization [Gao et al., 2020]. The corpus called The Pile has been specifically created as a heterogeneous corpus. For example, models trained on The Pile show significant gains in coding efficiency (Bits Per Byte, BPB)11 1 Bits-Per-Byte is a tokenizer-agnostic metric from information theory that measures the average bits needed per symbol, reflecting coding efficiency, see also Section 3.3.2. across disparate domains, such as GitHub repositories, medical papers, and philosophy texts (see Figure 3.2). It is therefore often used as a benchmark, where successful performance on Pile BPB serves as an indicator of a model’s world knowledge and complex reasoning abilities.

Curation of data for pretraining requires defining complex data cleaning pipelines that transform raw data from multiple sources into a single collection of cleaned, plain text documents. Often, this process focuses on quality assurance and safety. The curation process begins with source prioritization, where the mixture is weighted toward high-quality sources such as Wikipedia, books, and other known curated sources. Further, to ensure the integrity of the corpus, researchers apply noise reduction heuristics to strip away boilerplate text, navigation menus, and possibly inappropriate content. Furthermore, de-duplication is performed at both the URL and document levels; this is essential to prevent the model from memorizing redundant information and overfitting on repetitive data.

Beyond accuracy, the pipeline must select data that matches safety and ethical constraints. This too is commonly implemented through heuristic-based filtering. Furthermore, toxicity-detection systems are implemented to remove hate speech, although these methods often yield mixed results. A significant challenge in this phase is bias mitigation, as automated filters can inadvertently flag and suppress legitimate data written in specific dialects, such as African American English, leading to the accidental exclusion of diverse voices from the training set.

3.2.2 Pretrain

The second step in the training pipeline is pretraining the model on the curated corpus, a process that yields a generalist natural language model. This stage uses a self-supervised transformer approach [Vaswani et al., 2017] on the unlabeled text.

In order to acquire internal representations of language, conceptual semantic relationships, and world knowledge, the model is trained using masked-token cloze-like tasks. In such tasks the objective is to predict masked tokens conditioned on a preceding context of large corpora of sequences (i.e., representations of text, image patches). This process is self-supervised (no human-annotated data is required) and is known to yield rich representations of language, relations between concepts, and world knowledge, in various forms.

Formally, the language modeling objective maximizes the probability of the tokens in a sentence 𝒰={u0,…,un}\mathcal{U}=\{u_{0},\dots,u_{n}\}, based on a window kk of existing tokens (Equation 3.1). L⁡(𝒰)L(\mathcal{U}) is the language modeling loss.

L⁡(𝒰)=∑ilog⁡P⁡(ui|ui−k,…,ui−1;Θ)L(\mathcal{U})=\sum_{i}\log P(u_{i}|u_{i-k},\dots,u_{i-1};\Theta) (3.1)

Language models estimate these probabilities through trainable parameters Θ\Theta, optimized via gradient updates. Given that model sizes range from millions to over a trillion parameters, large datasets are required to ensure convergence. During this training phase, teacher forcing is employed: the model makes a prediction, but the ground-truth token—rather than the model’s own output—is provided as the input for the next step. In contrast, during autoregressive generation at inference time, the model must rely on its own predictions as the input for subsequent tokens. Tokens are created by running the appropriate tokenizer, as explained in Section 2.1.4.

In pretraining, a key challenge is to ensure that the model learns efficiently and remains stable throughout the trillions of gradient updates. Over time, different strategies have evolved that aim to keep the training process under control. One such strategy is curriculum learning. In human learning, we start by learning easy concepts (such as addition) before we tackle more difficult concepts (multiplication, logarithms). In language modeling, this idea is used in data mixtures, or data curricula. Rather than training on all data types simultaneously, researchers select a specific mixture of data sources to train on first, see the example in Figure 3.3. Creation of mixtures involves strategically ordering the data according to difficulty. In a training curriculum we start with easy-to-learn general web crawls, and then shift toward harder high-quality reasoning data (math and code) in later stages. The underlying idea is that this helps the model converge quicker on more complex logic [Bengio et al., 2009].

Other mechanisms for stabilizing training are employed, as training at this scale is notoriously unstable and prone to loss spikes [Takase et al., 2025]. Stability is maintained through standard machine learning techniques such as weight decay, layer normalization, and sophisticated learning rate schedulers. The use of specialized optimizers and the monitoring of gradient norms helps to prevent parameters from diverging during the intensive pretraining process. An example of how switching embedding layers can lead to more stable training is shown in Figure 3.4. The left figure shows the training loss for the 336M and 752M BERT model. While the original architecture performs well on the 336M model, the modifications in (b) enable stable training with lower training loss [Shoeybi et al., 2020].

3.2.3 Finetune

After pretraining comes posttraining, of which the first important training step is finetuning. LLMs are rarely used in an autocomplete generic predict-next-word setting, people rather use them to answer questions, give advice and recall information. Finetuning is the process of taking a pretrained model that has already learned general language patterns, and then train it further on a smaller, more specific dataset. In finetuning, we apply a general model to a specific (narrow) task on a labeled dataset, using a supervised learning approach. A popular efficient method is low-rank optimization, which finetunes a small subset of the parameters [Hu et al., 2021, Wei et al., 2022, Minaee et al., 2024].

Supervised Finetuning (SFT)

Finetuning can be applied to many specialized tasks. The most general models use supervised finetuning to be able to follow instructions and perform reasoning steps [Ettinger et al., 2025]. The supervised finetuning step is especially important for smaller models, offering an efficient mechanism for significant improvements in general chat, reasoning, and function-calling capabilities.

Supervised finetuning is also used for more specialized tasks, such as toxicity reduction. WildChat [Zhao et al., 2024] provides over a million real-world user-ChatGPT interactions, capturing how humans prompt the LLM with varying complexity and toxicity.

For learning reasoning capabilities, OpenThoughts [Guha et al., 2025] contains step-by-step reasoning chains, distilled from advanced models to enhance problem-solving capabilities in math, science, and coding. Human-obtained data is supplemented by synthetic data, which involves generating instructions and responses using larger teacher models (such as GPT-5) to fill specific data gaps and scale up training volume [Zhang et al., 2026].

Finetuning does not only pertain to general instruction-following or reasoning. Other tasks can be, for example, translation from one language to another, or question answering in health-care or customer service. Especially for industrial applications, where tasks are narrow and models are smaller, finetuning is a fruitful undertaking.

In Chapter 11 we will discuss the use of tools by LLMs, a central aspect of agentic LLM. The training to use tools also takes place in the supervised finetuning step in the training pipeline [Wei et al., 2022, Minaee et al., 2024].

Furthermore, finetuning is instrumental in establishing a model’s persona and deepening its expertise. For instance, organizations can train models to adopt a specific tone of voice, for example so that a customer service bot maintains a consistent brand identity, be that empathetic and formal or witty and casual. Finally, the injection of deep domain knowledge enables the model to master the intricate terminology and logic of niche fields, such as industry-specific patent information or debugging proprietary legacy code.

Ultimately, finetuning transforms a generalist predictor into a specialized expert, often allowing smaller, more efficient models to outperform larger foundational models on specific tasks.

3.2.4 Preference Tuning

A problem that surfaced in early models is that training tends to amplify extreme socially unacceptable texts in the training data and run wild, crowding out moderate points of view. Since then, an essential step for LLMs to become socially acceptable, is for pipelines to include a phase in which the model is tuned to behave in socially acceptable ways. This phase is called preference tuning.

In this phase we align the finetuned model with user expectations (preference alignment). The goal of this step is to improve the model to give socially acceptable answers, prevent hate speech, reduce hallucinations, and improve instruction adherence.

Standard methods for preference tuning include reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) [Ouyang et al., 2022], which trains a reward model to approximate human values, and direct preference optimization (DPO) [Rafailov et al., 2024], which optimizes the policy directly from preference data. A high-level overview of RLHF is shown in Figure 3.5. To address the bottleneck of human annotation, modern pipelines increasingly utilize reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) [Bai et al., 2022], where a stronger model generates the preference signals.

Achieving alignment with human values is not an easy task, and we usually distinguish between safety alignment, value alignment and preference alignment. In the latter case, a complication is that preferences are subjective preferences (such as writing style) that change per person.

Value alignment

On a higher level, value alignment focuses on ensuring that the model’s underlying principles and worldviews resonate with broad human ethics. Unlike individual preferences, this involves anchoring the model to high-level concepts such as fairness, helpfulness, and honesty. In practice, this means the model is governed by a set of written principles (a constitution) to ensure that it adheres to the policies set out by the developer.

However, this value alignment usually leads to a trade-off, where optimizing a model for safety and helpfulness also degrades its performance on other capabilities, such as factual recall or creativity [Lin et al., 2024]. This trade-off is otherwise known as the alignment tax.

Safety alignment

Safety alignment is the process of setting hard boundaries on model behavior to prevent catastrophic or harmful outputs. While preference alignment might focus on tone, and value alignment on viewpoint, safety alignment focuses on adversarial robustness and the refusal of malicious prompts. Example methodologies for ensuring safety includes red teaming, where models are subjected to rigorous jailbreak attempts to identify vulnerabilities, and guard railing, where specific refusal boundaries for high-risk responses are filtered.

Objective alignment

Finally, for domains where objective truths exist, such as mathematics or coding, methods known as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) [Lambert et al., 2024] are employed. Unlike standard RLHF, RLVR optimizes for objective correctness by leveraging ground-truth signals to robustly improve reasoning capabilities. Examples include code that compiles, or correct mathematical solutions. In the latter case, the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm is often used [Guo et al., 2025], a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) that enhances mathematical reasoning abilities while concurrently optimizing the memory usage of PPO. It does so by sampling multiple answers from the policy model and using their relative quality (as assessed by a verifier) to compute the rewards. Instead of relying on human labels for learning what counts as a good answer, the model gets direct rewards (+1, or -1) from a deterministic verifier [Guo et al., 2025, Shao et al., 2024], see Figure 3.6.

3.2.5 Infer

The final step in the training pipeline is the inference step. This is the step in which the trained model is finally used. Here the user finally gets to interact with the model. Finally, we can use the fruits of our training efforts.

At inference time, we use natural language prompts (instructions and questions) to obtain responses from the model. Prompting is the preferred way of using LLMs to have the model answer our questions. Inference results can be sensitive to the way that a prompt is formulated. The use of certain words, or re-ordering words in the prompt, can influence the answer of the model. This sensitivity has led to prompt engineering and context engineering, skills that have become important for users of LLMs [Sahoo et al., 2024].

Interestingly, as we discussed in the previous chapter, in decoder models whose size is beyond hundreds of billions parameters a new learning method emerges: in-context learning (ICL) [Brown et al., 2020, Wei et al., 2022]. In-context learning is a method where the prompt contains a small number of examples, together with an instruction. These examples point the model in a certain direction and it uses them to learn the answer. ICL is a form of within-prompt few-shot learning. ICL is also a type of learning where no parameters of the model are changed—it is example learning without parameter training [Dong et al., 2022].

In the remainder of this book we will see many examples of the way in which in-context learning is used, such as in agentic harnesses. Inference-time in-context learning is a major driver of agentic LLM.

3.2.6 Concluding Remarks

We have now described the phases of a typical LLM training pipeline. Note that the pipeline that we described is an example of a typical approach, and different models are trained in different ways. Current modern training pipelines are elaborate, and training is costly. Innovations to training pipelines are the topic of current research, see, for example, Guo et al. [2025], Du et al. [2025].

Being able to obtain predictions quickly is key, and multiple techniques have been developed to speed up the process. For instance, is is important to strike a balance between the reasoning effort and response quality. Research into test time scaling studies this trade-off. A higher inference-time effort costs more compute time, but may yield a better answer. We discuss these and other optimization techniques in Chapter 4.

3.3 Benchmarks, and Performance

After the pipeline has been used to train the model, we wish to find out how well the model performs. LLMs are created using a variety of modeling techniques, for different tasks, on different datasets. As a result, they have often obtained remarkable capabilities. For example, LLMs perform well on natural language understanding tasks (GLUE, SQUAD, Xsum) [Wang et al., 2018, Wang et al., 2019, Rajpurkar et al., 2016, Narayan et al., 2018], translation [Kocmi et al., 2022, Papineni et al., 2002, Sennrich et al., 2015], question answering tasks [Roberts et al., 2020], and poetry composition [Zhang and Eger, 2024], to name just a few domains. The broad applicability of LLMs shows their versatility, although the rapid development of the field, as well as ongoing research efforts, raise many open questions related to the capabilities of LLMs in many domains and contexts.

We will now discuss benchmarks that are commonly used to test the performance of our models.

3.3.1 Common tasks

Let us have a closer look at some common LLM tasks. The tasks can largely be grouped under the two language processing categories that we introduced previously: natural language understanding (NLU) and natural language generation (NLG). Depending on the category, the exact task formulation, and the underlying data, the performance metric will differ. We will discuss each separately.

Note that performance is an ambiguous term. In NLP, it is often used in the context of task performance (accuracy), instead of computational performance (speed). While exact evaluation criteria differ depending on the task, modern evaluation practices primarily focus on task performance. However, how many of the calls to the LLM we make, and how quickly we can get responses from the model, is also important to achieve high scores on contemporary benchmarks, as we will see in later chapters.

3.3.2 Metrics

In order to monitor or report the (task) performance of LLMs, different metrics are used, depending on the stage of the training that we are in.

Pretraining Metrics

In pretraining, we are mostly interested in knowing whether the model is able to accurately predict the next word. The standard metric is perplexity, shown in Equation 3.2. Perplexity measures the model’s uncertainty when predicting the next token, and is directly related to the cross-entropy loss function. Low perplexity indicates that the model assigns high probability to the correct next tokens. For perplexity, lower is better.

PPL(X)=exp(−1N∑i=1NlogP(xi∣x<i))\text{PPL}(X)=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log P(x_{i}\mid x_{<i})\right) (3.2)
BPB=−1B∑i=1Nlog2P(xi∣x<i)\text{BPB}=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log_{2}P(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}) (3.3)

Perplexity is computed over tokens; adjusting perplexity to stick to word boundaries needs careful normalization [Pimentel and Meister, 2024]. Moreover, even when adjusted, it is still tokenizer-specific, as other tokenizers can lead to other subwords and hence other probability distributions.

As an alternative, bits-per-byte (BPB), shown in Equation 3.3, normalizes the loss to the byte level, which enables fair comparisons between models that use different tokenization schemes [Borgeaud et al., 2022]. It measures the average number of bits required to encode a single byte of data.

Posttraining Metrics

In posttraining and inference, when the model is used for problem solving, generation, or reasoning, we look at the deterministic success rates, based on ground truth data. Often, tasks are set up in multiple-choice question/answering formats, where there is a single correct answer. For these types of tasks, we commonly report accuracy, the percentage of questions for which a correct response is given. For accuracy, higher is better.

In the regular setup, the model needs to provide an answer in one unique attempt. However, since sampling from a language model is a stochastic process, we may request additional attempts, and see if the answer is among them. This is formalized in the Pass@K metric: the percentage of problems solved correctly on the model’s KKth attempt; higher is better. Common values for KK include 1, 5, 10, 100.

3.3.3 Common Benchmarks

While measuring the performance of LLMs remains an active area of research, many datasets have become commonplace for reporting their general capabilities. These datasets are designed to only be used for evaluating the quality of a model, and are not intended as additional training data. As such, they serve as semi-standardized benchmarks. Ongoing efforts for moving to field standards, such as MLCommons [Thiyagalingam et al., 2022], show an increasing need for objective and sound evaluation setups.

Data Contamination

Modern benchmarks run a risk of data contamination [Balloccu et al., 2024]. As pretraining data increases in size (often a considerable ratio of the total size of the internet), the line between in- and out-of-domain data becomes increasingly blurred, especially given that commercial vendors often do not specify the sources of their training data (either out of commercial interest or for other reasons). Hence, when we wish to measure true generalization to unseen data, we need to ensure that the model has not seen the data before (we wish to prevent data contamination).

It is common for benchmarks to host a public, freely accessible dataset for quick experimentation by developers, but to maintain a private dataset that commercial vendors have restricted access to, to prevent data contamination. Furthermore, in order to maintain the benchmark’s usefulness into the future, developers often actively update the samples in the benchmark.

In Table 3.1, we provide a non-exhaustive list of general-purpose benchmarks that are popular at the time of writing.

3.4 Concluding Remarks

In the field of LLM development, it has become common for commercial LLM developers (such as Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, Mistral) to publish a tech report that informs the expert public on how the model behaves across popular benchmarks. Often, such as tech report is published as a preprint, without going through academic peer-review, and many details that would be necessary for full scientific reproducibility (such as data recipe, model architecture) are left out, for commercial reasons. Nonetheless, these reports provide useful information to derive insights into what LLMs can and cannot do.

First, we find that modern LLMs demonstrate a distinct performance hierarchy across benchmarks, as they have effectively solved broad knowledge tasks, but still struggle to master complex reasoning and autonomous agentic tasks. On static knowledge and professional exam benchmarks (such as MMLU and TruthfulQA), frontier models (such as GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, and Claude 4.5 Opus) have reached, at the time of writing, near-saturation, consistently scoring above 85–90% and surpassing human expert baselines.

The newest generation of reasoning models (such as OpenAI’s o1, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen-3.5) have recently achieved great progress, pushing math and science pass rates from low percentages to expert levels. Despite these advances, the software engineering SWE-bench remains the ultimate stress test for reliability; while scores have risen from negligible (¡2%) to respectable levels (40-50% on verified subsets) for top coding agents, the gap between answering a coding question and autonomously fixing a real-world repository issue remains a significant hurdle for modern AI.

Open Questions

Open questions about the origin of LLMs capabilities still remain. As the pipelines have grown complex, both in terms of training (What data matters? What training steps are most important?) and inference (How to extract high quality reasoning traces?), drawing conclusions is difficult. For example, it is an open question whether pretraining or posttraining is more important, and whether knowledge comes mostly from pretraining, and posttraining only serves for finding a good task interface [Zhou et al., 2023].

The remaining parts of this book will discuss posttraining and inference-time reasoning methods and agent training methods. But first, we will look at scaling laws, in the next chapter.

Chapter 4 Scaling Laws and Efficient Large Language Models

4.1 Scaling Laws: Compute, Data, Parameters

There are three primary factors involved in the training of LLMs: (1) the amount of compute, (2) the size of the dataset, and (3) the size of the model. Studies have shown that these three factors relate to the final performance of a model, measured as its loss on a held-out test set (LL). This relation has been found to be both smooth and predictable. The relationship takes the form of a power law: as any of the three resources is increased, the loss decreases proportionally to a negative power of that resource. For instance, doubling the model size might reduce the loss by a factor of 2−α2^{-\alpha} for some positive exponent α\alpha. Because the behavior is predictable, we can estimate how much a model will improve (for instance, from doubling the training dataset size) before committing to an expensive training run.

We define these three quantities (CC, DD, NN) as follows:

  • •

    Compute (CC): the total amount of arithmetic performed over the entire training run, measured in floating point operations (FLOPs). Note that this is a count of operations in total, not a rate per second. A widely used approximation relates it to the other two quantities as C≈6​N​DC\approx 6ND, since processing a single token touches each of the NN parameters roughly six times across the forward (twice) and backward pass (four times).

  • •

    Dataset size (DD): the total number of tokens the model is trained on. Note that a token is a subword unit defined by the tokenizer, so the same corpus corresponds to different values of DD under different tokenizers. The count of DD is the number of tokens as they are used during the training run. When data is repeated over several epochs, the repeated tokens still add to DD but may yield diminishing returns compared to fresh data.

  • •

    Model size (NN): the number of trainable parameters (weights) in the model architecture. This count usually refers only to the parameters that increase when scaling model depth, and therefore excludes the embedding matrix.

Training large models comes at considerable cost, usually in the realm of tens of millions of dollars, and up to months of compute time. Scaling laws allow us to predict whether a model will train well.

4.1.1 Kaplan Scaling Laws

There are different empirical results for scaling laws that are found by fitting a function to empirical test data. For instance, in Figure 4.1, every point is a trained model on a fixed dataset with a similar experimental setup, while only changing the three primary variables C,D,NC,D,N. In early 2020, Kaplan et al. [2020] found how model performance is related to C,D,NC,D,N. They estimated, following empirical observations, that the loss follows independent power laws rekated to the three main variables: L⁡(N)∝N−αNL(N)\propto N^{-\alpha_{N}} and L⁡(D)∝D−αDL(D)\propto D^{-\alpha_{D}}, with αN≈0.076\alpha_{N}\approx 0.076 and αD≈0.095\alpha_{D}\approx 0.095.

The individual power laws can be combined into a single optimizable equation, shown in Equation 4.1. This relationship was assumed to be generic: it would apply well as models of loss behavior for “other generative modeling tasks” [Kaplan et al., 2020, p. 5]. The authors further showed that, under no other constraints than compute budget, their derivations would point to optimal model size NN, an ideal dataset size DD, defined by optimal step size (SS) and batch size (BB).

L⁡(N,D)=[(NcN)αNαD+DcD]αDL(N,D)=\Big[\Big(\frac{N_{c}}{N}\Big)^{\frac{\alpha_{N}}{\alpha_{D}}}+\frac{D_{c}}{D}\Big]^{\alpha_{D}} (4.1)

Specifically, they concluded that as the compute budget CC increases, model size NN should be increased faster than data size DD (N∝C0.73N\propto C^{0.73} and D∝C0.27D\propto C^{0.27}11 1 B∝C0.24,S∝C0.03,D=B⋅S∝C0.27B\propto C^{0.24},\,S\propto C^{0.03},\,D=B\cdot S\propto C^{0.27}), leading to the development of large models such as GPT-3. The negative exponents reflect diminishing returns: each doubling of model size or dataset size lowers the loss by only a few percent.

At first glance, this recommendation seems to contradict the exponents themselves: since αD>αN\alpha_{D}>\alpha_{N}, data scaling reduces the loss faster than parameter scaling for the same relative increase in compute. The reason is that compute, not the resource itself, is the constraint: because C≈6​N​DC\approx 6ND, increasing DD consumes compute just as increasing NN does. This means that NN is with becoming a bottleneck with increasing likelihood. Hence, once the compute cost for DD is accounted for, allocating additional compute to NN yields a better return than allocating it to DD. This means that the optimal allocation favors larger models.

Sample efficiency

A separate observation of Kaplan et al. [2020] is that larger models are more sample-efficient. For a fixed number of training tokens, a larger model reaches a lower loss, and to reach a given target loss it requires fewer tokens and fewer optimization steps than a smaller one. This effect is visualized in Figure 4.2.

4.1.2 Chinchilla Scaling Laws

In 2022, Hoffmann et al. [2022] reevaluated these findings with a model called Chinchilla, and found, surprisingly, that most large models at the time were severely undertrained. This discrepancy can be traced back to the methodology of Kaplan et al. [2020]: their optimal allocation was extrapolated from the early, non-converged training dynamics of many models rather than from runs trained to convergence, which systematically biased their conclusions toward larger models trained for fewer steps.

The key insight from the Chinchilla study was that for every doubling of the compute budget, both the model size NN and the number of training tokens DD should be increased in roughly equal proportions (N∝C0.5N\propto C^{0.5} and D∝C0.5D\propto C^{0.5}). Their rule of thumb suggests training on approximately 20 tokens for every trainable parameter in the model to achieve compute optimality. This result has since been reproduced [Besiroglu et al., 2024] and has been shown to be robust to sizable perturbations [Schaeffer et al., 2025].

In their scaling laws, the loss is modeled as a function of the parameter count NN and the number of tokens DD that have been trained on, as follows:

L⁡(N,D)=E+ANα+BDβL(N,D)=E+\frac{A}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{B}{D^{\beta}} (4.2)

The first term EE captures the irreducible loss, corresponding to the entropy of natural text. The second term ANα\frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} captures the sub-optimality of a model with finite parameters NN, and the final term BDβ\frac{B}{D^{\beta}} captures the sub-optimality due to training on a finite number of tokens DD. Although α\alpha and β\beta here play the same role as Kaplan’s αN\alpha_{N} and αD\alpha_{D} (the exponents governing how the loss falls off with model size and data) they are a different parameterization: they are fit jointly within this two-term form and therefore take different values. Fitting the Chinchilla scaling function on more than 400 models found the following parameter estimates:

E≈1.69,A≈406.4,B≈410.7,α≈0.34,β≈0.28E\approx 1.69,\quad A\approx 406.4,\quad B\approx 410.7,\quad\alpha\approx 0.34,\quad\beta\approx 0.28 (4.3)

By optimizing this loss function under the constraint of a fixed compute budget CC (recall C≈6​N​DC\approx 6ND), we can derive the compute-optimal model size No​p​tN_{opt} and data size Do​p​tD_{opt} for any budget CC:

No​p​t​(C)=G​(C6)a,Do​p​t​(C)=1G​(C6)bN_{opt}(C)=G\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{a},\quad D_{opt}(C)=\frac{1}{G}\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{b} (4.4)

where G=(α​Aβ​B)1α+βG=\big(\frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}\big)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+\beta}} is a constant, a=βα+β≈0.45a=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\approx 0.45 and b=αα+β≈0.55b=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\approx 0.55.

Note that aa and bb are not independent: by construction a+b=1a+b=1. This follows directly from C≈6​N​DC\approx 6ND, since taking logarithms gives log⁡C=log⁡6+log⁡N+log⁡D\log C=\log 6+\log N+\log D. Writing No​p​t∝CaN_{opt}\propto C^{a} and Do​p​t∝CbD_{opt}\propto C^{b}, this becomes log⁡C=const+a​log⁡C+b​log⁡C\log C=\text{const}+a\log C+b\log C, which can only hold for all CC if a+b=1a+b=1. The same constraint applies to Kaplan’s exponents (0.73+0.27=10.73+0.27=1). The difference for Chinchilla was how the budget is split between NN and DD.

This rule is approximately linear because No​p​tN_{opt} and Do​p​tD_{opt} grow with the compute budget CC at almost the same rate: their exponents a≈0.45a\approx 0.45 and b≈0.55b\approx 0.55 are close, so the ratio Do​p​t/No​p​tD_{opt}/N_{opt} stays near a constant value of roughly 2020 across many orders of magnitude of compute. The value is best understood as an empirical calibration anchored on real compute-optimal runs rather than a number that results cleanly from the fitted coefficients. The Chinchilla model itself (70B parameters trained on 1.4T tokens) sits exactly at D/N=20D/N=20. Table 4.1 shows several well-known models relative to this rule. Models below the ratio are undertrained (too large for their token budget), while models far above it are deliberately overtrained to obtain a small model that is cheap to run at inference time. Earlier flagship models such as GPT-3 and Gopher fall well below the line (D/N≈1D/N\approx 1–22): they were made very large but trained on comparatively too few tokens. It is worth stressing that D≈20​ND\approx 20N is optimal only for minimizing the training loss at a fixed training budget. When a model will later serve many inference requests, it is often deliberately over-trained on far more than 2020 tokens per parameter, trading additional training cost for a smaller model that is cheaper to run at inference time. LLaMA-3 8B, for instance, is trained on roughly 19001900 tokens per parameter. This deliberate extreme over-training is chosen so that a small model still reaches a low loss, and is cheap to run during inference.

The picture so far is fairly clean: test loss falls smoothly, monotonically, and predictably with compute, data, and parameters. However, in practice, various factors influence our results. We discuss four phenomena that each probe a different edge of that picture: (1) compute-optimal curves, (2) emergent abilities, (3) inverse scaling, and (4) grokking.

4.1.3 Compute-Optimal Curve

Computer hardware and energy are finite resources. A practical question is how to split a fixed compute budget CC between model size NN and dataset size DD to obtain the best possible model. Scaling laws answer this through the compute-optimal frontier: the allocation of CC that minimizes the loss.

This frontier is located empirically with the IsoFLOP method [Hoffmann et al., 2022], shown in Figure 4.3. For various model sizes, we choose the number of training tokens such that the final FLOPs is a constant. The learning rate is adjusted using a cosine annealing schedule, with the cosine cycle length is set to match the target FLOP count. We find a clear valley in loss, meaning that for a given FLOP budget there is an optimal model size to train (left). Using the location of these valleys, we project optimal model size and number of tokens for larger models (center and right). In green, we show the estimated number of parameters and tokens for an optimal model trained with the compute budget of Gopher. For a fixed FLOP budget we train several models of different sizes: a model that is too small underfits, while a model that is too large is forced to train on too few tokens, so the resulting curve of loss against model size is U-shaped. Its minimum identifies the compute-optimal model size No​p​tN_{opt}, from which the matching token count Do​p​t=C/6​No​p​tD_{opt}=C/6N_{opt} follows via C≈6​N​DC\approx 6ND. Fitting a parabola to each such curve locates this minimum, and repeating the procedure across budgets finds how No​p​tN_{opt} and Do​p​tD_{opt} grow with compute.

This parabola fitting must be done with care, and the simplification introduces systematic biases in the estimated optimum [Czech et al., 2026]. These biases persist even on noise-free synthetic data and stem from three sources: (1) spacing the sampled model sizes too coarsely, (2) sampling that fails to locate the true minimum symmetrically, and (3) the genuine asymmetry of the loss surface, which a symmetric parabola cannot represent. At the scale of Llama-3, they estimate that such biases waste on the order of $1.4M of compute. As a remedy, they recommend fitting the parametric loss model L⁡(N,D)=E+A/Nα+B/DβL(N,D)=E+A/N^{\alpha}+B/D^{\beta} directly—Chinchilla Approach 3, the same form we used above to derive the D≈20​ND\approx 20N rule—with a numerically robust optimizer, rather than reading the optimum off fitted parabolas.

Complementary views on scaling [Paquette et al., 2024] study analytically solvable models (power-law random features trained with one-pass stochastic gradient descent) instead of fitting curves to trained models. They find that the compute-optimal exponent is not a single universal constant, but that the data-complexity/target-complexity plane instead splits into four primary phases (plus three sub-phases), each with its own exponent governing how NoptN_{\mbox{opt}} grows with compute. The answer to the question which allocation rule to apply, and whether a fixed 20 tokens per parameter is even the right shape, depends on the regime of the problem.

Scaling for finetuning

The preceding works studied how pretraining scales. Do these scaling laws also govern finetuning? Zhang et al. [2024] study this question for both full-model finetuning, which updates all of the model’s weights, and parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT), which freezes the pretrained weights and trains only a small set of added parameters (as in LoRA) [Hu et al., 2021]. The lesson most relevant to compute budgeting is that finetuning performance improves more from scaling the size of the base model than from collecting additional finetuning data, while adding more trainable PEFT parameters helps little. In practice, a task that underperforms is usually better served by starting from a larger pretrained model than by enlarging the adapter or gathering more finetuning examples.

4.1.4 Emergent Abilities

Some of the most interesting phenomena in LLM scaling are emergent abilities: capabilities that are not present in smaller models but that appear suddenly as model size or compute cross a certain threshold [Wei et al., 2022]. Examples include multi-step reasoning, few-shot translation, and specialized coding tasks, as shown in Figure 4.4. The ability to perform a task via few-shot prompting is emergent when a language model achieves random performance until a certain scale, after which performance significantly increases to well-above random.

However, the suddenness of the appearance has been contested. Schaeffer et al. [2023] argue that emergent abilities might be a mirage caused by the choice of evaluation metrics. For instance, in Figure 4.5, we see that while non-smooth discrete metrics (such as accuracy or exact match) show sharp jumps—they are non-smooth, after all—underlying metrics (such as the cross-entropy loss or token-level probability) follow a smooth, predictable power law across scales.

4.1.5 Inverse Scaling

While most tasks improve with scale, some exhibit inverse scaling, where larger models perform worse or develop stronger biases. This may happen in tasks where a distractor answer is more probable according to the language modeling objective than the correct answer, leading larger (and more confident) models to consistently choose the wrong option [McKenzie et al., 2023, Michaelov and Bergen, 2023].

An example of inverse scaling is hindsight neglect, a task that tests whether a bet was worth taking based on its expected value. In case the expected value is positive, the model should respond with yes, and in case of a negative expected value it should respond with no. The situation is as follows. The model is only shown few-shot examples where the actual outcome always matches the expected value (that is, the bettor won money when the expected value was positive and lost money when the expected value was negative). The model is then asked a question about whether it was correct to take a bet where the expected value and the actual outcome do not match. Hindsight neglect tests whether models can correctly generalize from instructions when the few-shot examples are correctly-labeled but misleading. Repetitive algebra tests how models respond to simple algebra questions when given a specific pattern of correctly-labeled few-shot examples. Figure 4.6 shows that models generally start around random performance, but fall below random performance at around 102210^{22} training FLOPs.

4.1.6 Grokking

Grokking is a relatively recent paradox in statistical learning theory. This theory holds that, conventionally, when a large model is presented with a small dataset, it will overfit, due to memorization of the examples. Grokking, then, occurs when we continue to train this too-large model, and, after much more training, the model suddenly finds a generalizing solution [Power et al., 2022].

While originally observed on small algorithmic tasks, such as modular addition, the grokking phenomenon suggests that scaling the number of training steps (over-training) can lead to qualitative shifts from memorization to understanding, even without increasing the dataset size DD, see Figure 4.7.

The figure shows a data wall that initially limits scaling as the data is running out [Villalobos et al., 2024], but later, after much more training, the model groks a generalizing solution.

Grokking is relevant to language modeling since we are rapidly running out of high-quality human text on the internet to satisfy the requirements on data DD of Chinchilla scaling for next-generation models. Because of these inherent limits, researchers are looking beyond simple scaling of DD. As an alternative, we can look at a variety of these new frontiers: (1) better architectural efficiency (such as Mixture of Experts), (2) inference-time scaling (such as giving models more compute during inference to think, as seen in OpenAI’s o-series), or (3) synthetic data generation (Chapter 19).

4.2 Small Language Models

As the requirements for compute and data continue to grow, there is an increasing interest in small language models (SLMs): models that are small enough to run on consumer hardware or even mobile or edge devices while maintaining high performance. These models are often developed using techniques that optimize for efficiency without sacrificing too much performance.

To understand the deployment landscape for these models, it is helpful to categorize common types of compute infrastructure:

  • •

    Datacenters: High-performance GPUs (such as NVIDIA H100s) and TPUs, primarily used for pretraining large models and hosting high-throughput inference APIs.

  • •

    Consumer Hardware: Standard desktop GPUs and high-end CPUs, where SLMs can be affordably finetuned or run locally by individual users.

  • •

    Edge Devices: Mobile phones, Internet-of-Things devices, and laptops, which are increasingly equipped with Neural Processing Units (NPUs) specifically designed for low-power, efficient on-device inference.

To fit models into the latter constrained environments, optimization techniques focus on speeding up throughput, reducing latency, reducing memory usage, and increasing sample efficiency. The techniques for achieving these goals can be grouped into two categories: (1) model-centric optimization, which targets the architecture of the models and their optimization approaches, and (2) data-centric optimization, which targets the data used to train the models. We will discuss both categories.

4.2.1 Model-centric Optimization

First we discuss the model-centric optimization techniques. We introduce the following techniques that allow for efficient training of smaller models, while still maintaining high task performance. Model-centric techniques can focus on pretraining/finetuning or inference.

4.2.1.1 Reducing Pretraining Cost
Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)

Methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [Hu et al., 2021] allow for adapting a large model to a new task by training only a tiny fraction (often <1<1%) of its parameters [Lialin et al., 2023]. The key observation is that the weight update learned during finetuning has a low intrinsic rank: although a pretrained weight matrix W0∈ℝd×kW_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} is full-rank, the change Δ​W\Delta W needed to adapt it to a new task can be approximated well by a low-rank matrix. Instead of updating W0W_{0} directly, LoRA freezes it and represents the update as a product of two small matrices,

W=W0+Δ​W=W0+B​A,B∈ℝd×r,A∈ℝr×kW=W_{0}+\Delta W=W_{0}+BA,\qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\;\;A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k} (4.5)

where the rank r≪min⁡(d,k)r\ll\min(d,k). For an input xx, the modified forward pass becomes

h=W0​x+αr​B​A​x,h=W_{0}x+\frac{\alpha}{r}\,BAx, (4.6)

where α\alpha is a constant scaling factor that controls the magnitude of the update, roughly similar to a learning rate in standard training. This is visualized in Figure 4.8. We compute weight updates only for AA and BB, reducing the number of trainable parameters from d×kd\times k to r⁡(d+k)r(d+k). At initialization AA is drawn from a random Gaussian and BB is set to zero, so Δ​W=0\Delta W=0 and training starts from the pretrained model. Because Δ​W\Delta W can directly be merged back into W0W_{0} after training, LoRA adds no inference latency, and a single base model can be served with many small, swappable task-specific adapters.

Architectural Innovations

A second family of techniques changes the model architecture itself so that it is cheaper to run, rather than compressing a fixed architecture after the fact. Two influential examples are Grouped-Query Attention and Mixture of Experts.

Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) [Ainslie et al., 2023] targets the memory bandwidth bottleneck of autoregressive decoding. In standard multi-head attention (MHA), every query head has its own key and value matrix, which we all need to use for computing attention scores. At the other extreme, multi-query attention (MQA) lets all query heads share a single key/value head, which shrinks the computation but can hurt expressive quality and training stability. GQA interpolates between these two: the query heads are divided into gg groups, and all heads within a group share one key/value head. With g=1g=1 it is equivalent to MQA, and with gg equal to the number of heads it is equivalent to MHA, so gg trades quality against memory usage. Often, GQA is combined with the KV-caching optimizations discussed next in Section 4.2, and it is now the default attention variant in many open-weight models.

Mixture of Experts (MoE) [Shazeer et al., 2017] decouples the total number of parameters from the compute spent per token. Instead of a single dense feed-forward block in each layer, a MoE layer contains many parallel “expert” sub-networks together with a lightweight gating network (router) that activates only a small number of experts (typically the top-11 or 22) for each token. Because only the chosen experts perform computation, the per-token cost stays close to that of a single dense block even as the total parameter count (and hence the model’s overall capacity) grows by an order of magnitude or more [Fedus et al., 2022].

This sparse activation is why models such as Mixtral and many recent frontier systems can have hundreds of billions of total parameters while activating only a fraction of them per token. The trade-offs are (1) that all experts must still be held in memory, (2) that the load must be balanced across experts (often via an auxiliary loss) so that no expert is over- or under-used, and (3) that routing introduces additional engineering complexity. The MoE architecture is visualized in Figure 4.9, which shows a top-kk routing mechanism, configured with k=2k=2, where the gating function selects the two highest-scoring FFN experts for each token based on the router. The selected experts are evaluated in parallel, with their outputs aggregated using weighted summation [Zhang et al., 2025].

Knowledge Distillation

A large teacher model is used to train a smaller student model by encouraging the student to match the teacher’s output distribution [Gu et al., 2023, Xu et al., 2024]. Crucially, the student learns from the teacher’s full soft probabilities (typically softened with a temperature) rather than only the single correct answer. These soft targets carry richer information: for instance, which wrong answers the teacher considers plausible. This lets the student approach the teacher’s quality at a fraction of its size. The same idea underpins the synthetic-data generation discussed below, where a frontier model effectively acts as the teacher, generating high-quality training data for a smaller student model.

4.2.1.2 Reducing Inference Cost

Once a model is trained, it can be further optimized for deployment at inference time. Whereas training-time techniques focus on reducing the cost of producing the model, inference-time techniques target the cost of using it: the throughput (tokens generated per second), the latency (time to the first and each subsequent token), and the memory footprint required to serve a request. We discuss several techniques that are commonly used to reduce inference cost, which can be applied to both large and small models.

Key–Value (KV) Caching

During autoregressive generation, the model produces one token at a time, and each new token attends to all previous tokens. Recomputing the attention keys and values for the entire context at every step is quadratically expensive. However, when we predict a new token, the context remains the same. Instead of recomputing the attention values, we can store the key and value vectors of past tokens in a KV cache and reuse them. This turns per-step attention into a linear-cost lookup. This is the basic optimization that makes decoding practical, but it comes at a cost: the cache grows linearly with both sequence length and batch size and quickly dominates memory usage for long contexts. This problem has motivated both the architectural choices above (GQA and MQA shrink the cache by sharing key/value heads across query heads) and dedicated memory-management schemes such as PagedAttention, which stores the cache in non-contiguous blocks to reduce fragmentation and enable higher serving throughput [Kwon et al., 2023].

Pruning

A more extreme method for reducing model size is to consider removing redundant or less important connections in the neural network [Ma et al., 2023]. Pruning can be unstructured (zeroing out individual weights) or structured (removing entire neurons, attention heads, or layers); the latter yields concrete speedups on standard hardware, whereas the former requires sparsity-aware kernels to realize its benefits.

Quantization

Another method of saving memory during inference is to reduce the size of the matrix that needs to be loaded into memory. Rather than making the matrix dimensions smaller, we can also lower the precision of weights entries (e.g., from 16-bit to 8-bit or 4-bit numbers). This significantly reduces memory usage and speeds up inference. However, in principle, lower precision means lower performance. The same idea can also be applied to the KV cache itself to keep long contexts in memory. Quantization is a frequently used approach [Dettmers et al., 2022, Dettmers and Zettlemoyer, 2023, Xiao et al., 2023].

Alternatively, rather than casting all weights to the same precision, mixed precision modes have been proposed, with different levels of numerical precision for different parts of the computation, to balance speed and stability [Micikevicius et al., 2017]. This approach may suffer from non-deterministic results due to numerical instabilities [Yuan et al., 2025].

Speculative Decoding

A key technique for optimizing inference efficiency is speculative decoding [Leviathan et al., 2023]. This approach uses a small draft model to generate multiple tokens quickly, which are then verified in parallel by a larger target model. This allows for faster inference (up to 2-3 fold speedup) without sacrificing the quality of the larger model, effectively leveraging the different points on the scaling curve.

4.2.2 Data-centric Optimization

In addition to model-centric approaches, the literature emphasizes that data quality and curation are often more important than the size of the dataset when training efficient models [Luo et al., 2025]. Small models can perform well if they are trained on highly curated, high-quality data. Hence, it is important to create a good data recipe, in addition to an efficient model architecture. Data-centric techniques broadly fall into two camps: selecting the most useful parts from a broader pool of data, and generating new synthetic data where good data is scarce.

4.2.2.1 Data Selection and Curation

Rather than training on all available text, a growing body of work shows that carefully choosing which data to train on, and in what proportions, yields better models for the same compute budget. For pretraining, NVIDIA’s CLIMB framework [Diao et al., 2026] embeds a large corpus into a semantic space, clusters it, and then iteratively searches for the data mixture that minimises proxy-model loss. The resulting ClimbMix dataset (400B tokens) lets a sub-billion-parameter model outperform comparable models trained on far larger but unfiltered corpora. The same principle applies at the finetuning stage: LIMA [Zhou et al., 2023] shows that supervised finetuning on only 1,0001{,}000 carefully curated prompt–response pairs is enough to produce a strong instruction-following model, supporting the view that most knowledge is acquired during pretraining and that alignment mainly teaches the model a desired response style.

4.2.2.2 Synthetic Data Gathering

When suitable data does not exist, it can be generated. The Textbooks Are All You Need approach, used for models such as Microsoft’s Phi series [Gunasekar et al., 2023], demonstrates that training on clean, synthetic textbook-quality data can allow a relatively small model of 1.3B parameters to outperform models ten times its size.

Such pipelines typically rely on frontier models to generate the data, combined with LLM-as-a-judge scoring to filter for the most accurate and educational examples, and rigorous decontamination to ensure the synthetic data does not leak benchmark test sets and inflate reported performance. This approach is particularly valuable for reasoning data: by training on step-by-step reasoning trajectories produced by larger models, complex problem-solving skills can be distilled into a smaller architecture (see also Chapter 6) [Muennighoff et al., 2025, Arora and Zanette, 2026].

4.2.2.3 Sample-Efficient Learning

Beyond synthetic data, there is an increased research focus on how models can learn more efficiently from limited, naturalistic data. Initiatives such as the BabyLM Challenge [Warstadt et al., 2023] focus on training models under strict data constraints (e.g., 10M to 100M tokens). This mirrors the volume of language input a human child receives during early development, driving innovation in sample-efficient architectures while providing insights into cognitively plausible language acquisition.

4.2.3 Popular models

Having surveyed improvement techniques, it is useful to look at how popular large and small models apply them in practice. Models are commonly categorized by their openness: closed-weight (proprietary) models expose only an API, open-weight models release their trained parameters, and open-source models additionally share the training data and code. In practice openness is a matter of degree rather than a strict category, and we may subsequently use an openness index to rate the transparency [Artificial Analysis, 2026]. Most open models can be found on repositories such as Hugging Face.

Below, we briefly describe some of the most popular open-weight models that are designed to be efficient enough to run on consumer hardware, and the techniques they use to achieve this. This is not an exhaustive list, but rather a selection of influential models that exemplify the trends in efficiency techniques and their scales, at the time of writing.

Phi series

[Abdin et al., 2024]. The Phi-series are capable SLMs that are efficient enough to run locally on mobile devices. The core innovation behind the Phi models is their data-centric training methodology. Microsoft curates high-quality, heavily filtered web data combined with synthetic data generated by larger models. This allows small models (such as the 3.8 billion parameter Phi-3-mini) to perform well, rivaling the reasoning capabilities of much larger models such as GPT-3.5 and Mixtral.

Gemma series

[Mesnard et al., 2024] Google emphasizes that Gemma models inherit Gemini’s strong generalist capabilities, particularly in text, reasoning, and coding, while advancing the state-of-the-art for their specific size classes, but little is known about their training method or data.

OLMo family

[Ettinger et al., 2025] The OLMo (Open Language Model) family is developed by the Allen Institute for AI to be a completely open-source model. The OLMo project open-sourced the full training pipeline, including code and data: the pre-training dataset (Dolma), the training and evaluation code, training logs, and intermediate checkpoints. This transparency allows researchers to study training dynamics, data influences, and algorithmic biases.

Qwen series

[Bai et al., 2023] The Qwen family represents a high-performing suite of foundational and instruction-tuned models, ranging from sub-billion dense models to large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures. They are notable for their multilingual capabilities and performance on mathematics, coding, and logical reasoning benchmarks.

OpenELM

[Mehta et al., 2024] Apple’s Efficient Language Model family is designed to run efficiently on edge devices. The layer-wise scaling strategy uses smaller latent dimensions in layers closer to the input and widens them closer to the output. This results in high accuracy for low parameter count.

gpt-oss

[Agarwal et al., 2025] OpenAI released two open-weight reasoning models that use an efficient mixture-of-expert architecture, optimized for agentic capabilities.

Mixtral series

[Jiang et al., 2024] These models popularized Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) architectures in the open-weights ecosystem (e.g., Mixtral 8x7B), allowing for large parameter counts with few active parameters during inference, to maximize efficiency.

Llama series

[Grattafiori et al., 2024] Meta’s Llama models have become frequently used. Trained on large datasets (up to 15 trillion tokens for Llama 3) and ranging from small edge-friendly sizes to large 405B parameter frontier models, they established the standard for scaling laws in open models and catalyzed an ecosystem of finetuned models and derivatives.

DeepSeek

[Liu et al., 2025] DeepSeek-V3 is a large Mixture-of-Experts model (671B total parameters with 37B activated per token) notable for the stability of its training. It combines Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for a compressed key-value cache with an auxiliary-loss-free strategy for expert load balancing, and was trained in FP8 mixed precision, achieving frontier-level performance at a small compute cost. The line also includes the DeepSeek-R1 reasoning models.

GLM

[Zeng et al., 2026] Developed by Zhipu AI, the GLM (General Language Model) family is built on strong reasoning capabilities that are developed early in training, and retained throughout the training process. Recent iterations are optimized for agentic workflows and software engineering, targeting tool-use and code-generation performance rather than text completion alone.

Pythia

[Biderman et al., 2023] EleutherAI’s Pythia is a suite of models (ranging from 70M to 12B parameters) designed to support research into training dynamics and scaling. Every model is trained on the same data in the same order, with intermediate checkpoints released per model, enabling controlled studies of how capabilities, memorization, and biases emerge over the course of training.

BLOOM

[Scao et al., 2023] BLOOM is a 176B-parameter open-access model produced by the BigScience collaborative research effort. Trained on the ROOTS corpus, spanning 46 natural languages and 13 programming languages, it was among the first large-scale models to prioritize multilingual coverage and full openness, released under a Responsible AI License.

SmolLM

[Allal et al., 2025] Hugging Face’s SmolLM is a family of compact models (135M, 360M, and 1.7B parameters) aimed at efficient on-device deployment, much like the Phi series. Its performance stems from data curation: it is trained on the SmolLM-Corpus, which combines high-quality web data, Python code examples, and synthetically (Mixtral) generated textbooks and stories.

4.3 Inference-Time Compute

The traditional scaling laws focus on the relationship between compute and performance at training time. More recent studies shift part of this computational burden to inference: inference-time scaling (or test-time compute) [Muennighoff et al., 2025]. Rather than spending all compute during training, a model is allowed to deliberate longer at inference time. This is measured by the number of tokens generated or reasoning paths explored, in order to produce a higher-quality answer. Hence, optimizing throughput (tokens/s) becomes of prime importance: the faster tokens can be produced, the more reasoning a model is able to do during the same amount of time.

Increasing this inference-time budget in terms of tokens can lead to significant improvements in capabilities [Du et al., 2024]; recent work indicates that optimally allocating test-time compute can allow smaller models to outperform larger ones on difficult reasoning tasks [Snell et al., 2024]. These gains are not guaranteed, however, and depend on the task and on the specific search or verification strategy employed [Stechly et al., 2023]. Beyond performance, this shift also reframes a broader question about what kind of systems LLMs are, which we take up in detail in Chapter 6.

4.4 Sustainable Language Models

The large scale of LLM training and deployment has significant environmental and economic implications. The energy consumption of AI training and inference is large, and the subsequent water consumption for cooling comes with a strain on water distribution pipelines [Li et al., 2025, Jegham et al., 2025]. Measuring the energy use and carbon footprint of training has only recently entered standard reporting [Ding and Shi, 2024]. It has been reported that training a single large model can consume as much energy as hundreds of households use in a year. Training a model such as BLOOM emitted over 50 tonnes of CO2 equivalent when accounting for both dynamic power consumption and the embodied carbon of hardware manufacturing [Luccioni et al., 2023].

As the use of LLMs is increasing in science and society, the total carbon footprint is increasingly dominated by inference rather than training, especially for models used by millions of people daily [Özcan et al., 2025, Wu et al., 2022, Samsi et al., 2023]. This creates an opportunity: spending more compute during training to create a smaller, more efficient model (as discussed in Section 4.1) can significantly reduce the long-term environmental cost of deployment.

As global inference demand scales to billions of daily queries, the cumulative energy consumption and associated financial cost overtake the initial training investment [Faiz et al., 2024]. Deploying large models at this scale requires a substantial data center infrastructure, and large electricity and water consumption. Consequently, there is a strong push toward deploying Small Language Models (SLMs) for sustainable, large-scale use. By minimizing the parameter and quantization count, SLMs reduce the memory bandwidth and compute required per generated token, offering a greener and more economically viable solution.

Privacy and Data Leakage

Beyond environmental concerns, the centralization of LLMs through cloud APIs introduces privacy vulnerabilities. When users query cloud-based models, sensitive personal data, corporate intellectual property, or protected health information must be transmitted to third-party servers. This creates risks of data leakage [Aiyappa et al., 2023, Li et al., 2024], either through unauthorized interception, adversarial extraction attacks, or the inadvertent memorization and subsequent regurgitation of private user prompts by the model [Chen et al., 2024, Maini et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2022].

To mitigate these privacy risks and reduce reliance on cloud infrastructure, developers can move from API-based inference toward local, on-device inference [Qu et al., 2025]:

  • •

    API-Based Inference: API-based inference relies on powerful remote servers. While this allows access to frontier models with hundreds of billions of parameters, it suffers from network latency, requires constant internet connectivity, and inherently exposes user data to cloud providers.

  • •

    Local Inference: Local inference runs the model directly on the user’s hardware (e.g., smartphones, laptops, or edge servers). This ensures data privacy because prompts never leave the device while also eliminating network latency and guaranteeing offline availability.

Local inference is constrained by the physical limits of consumer and edge hardware. For instance, memory and bandwidth are limited. LLM inference is a memory-bound process. Storing model weights requires significant RAM capacity, while generating tokens requires a high memory bandwidth. Furthermore, most mobile devices are powered by a battery. Running intensive matrix multiplications on mobile devices or standard laptops can lead to rapid battery drain and thermal throttling.

To make local deployment feasible, developers must rely on the inference-time optimization techniques, such as quantization (e.g., 4-bit) and speculative decoding, alongside the increasing availability of specialized neural processing units (NPUs) designed for low-power edge AI.

4.5 Concluding Remarks

As LLM use becomes more ubiquitous and the demand for quick responses increases, the focus in LLM development is shifting towards more efficient solutions. Hence, the focus on scaling data, compute, and model size purely for raw performance is transitioning into a focus on scaling for efficiency.

While the fundamental power laws still hold, the focus has shifted from simply training the largest possible model toward compute-optimal training, inference-time scaling, and initiatives to develop capable small models that run on consumer and edge hardware.

The directions that have been discussed in this chapter are complementary rather than competing: the model-centric techniques (LoRA, GQA, MoE, quantization, distillation) and the data-centric techniques (careful data selection and synthetic generation) are increasingly combined within a single training recipe.

As we move closer to the data wall, the role of synthetic data and architectural efficiency are likely to grow in importance, and the ability to do more with less is becoming a research focus.
