Chapter 5 Case Study 1: Building LLMs from Scratch

5.1 Building a Chatbot

We will work through a practical case that covers the full lifecycle of a modern ChatGPT-style language model. We use nanochat,11 1 https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat a minimal, single-codebase, full-stack implementation of an instruction-following LLM, released by Andrej Karpathy in April 2025. Unlike his earlier nanoGPT, which covered pre-training only, nanochat implements the complete training pipeline: a Byte Pair Encoding tokenizer, pre-training on web text followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on benchmark datasets, an inference server, and a chat web UI.

The code uses mostly pure Python with minimal dependencies, and therefore is easy to use and extend. The codebase comprises roughly 8,000 lines of Python and a small amount of Rust.22 2 If that number sounds large, it is worth noting that the corresponding proprietary systems run to millions of lines. Nanochat is aimed to be a small self-contained version.

The performance of nanochat is striking: a GPT-2-capable LLM (which cost ∼\sim$43,000 to train in 2019 [Radford et al., 2019]) for only $48 (∼\sim2 hours of 8xH100 GPU node). While this compute is not exactly commonplace for standard student projects at a university, we can scale down the experiment to make it suited to a hands-on course assignment. It is important to realize that every gradient update and every design decision is visible, from raw bytes to a working chat assistant. We will take you trough the nanochat pipeline across four tasks that you should all perform.

Because GPU budgets on a course are limited, you will train a small model (depth 4, depending on availability, see Section 5.3); you will then reflect on what may happen at larger scale using some theory and the published (nanochat) benchmarks.

5.2 Background: Karpathy’s nanochat

The case study will give you direct, hands-on experience with every stage of the modern LLM training pipeline, from input text to a deployed chat assistant. This experience will ground the theoretical concepts from Chapters 2–4 in concrete, debuggable code.

nanochat is configured out of the box to train a compute-optimal model by setting a single complexity dial: --depth, which specifies the number of transformer layers. All other hyperparameters—embedding width, number of attention heads, learning rate schedule, training horizon, weight decay—are derived automatically in a near-optimal way. This keeps the configuration space manageable while preserving the full educational value of understanding what each parameter does.

The training pipeline proceeds with the by now hopefully familiar stages, which are briefly described next.

Pretraining

The model is trained on approximately 6 billion tokens drawn from CLIMBMix [Diao et al., 2026], a clustering-based iteratively bootstrapped data mixture corpus. A depth-24 (∼\sim1.4B-parameter) model trains to a validation loss of 2.41 (0.717 bits-per-byte) in roughly 4 hours on a 4×\timesH100 node compute cluster.

Supervised finetuning (SFT)

Starting from the pretrained checkpoint, the model is finetuned on a mixture of instruction-following and reasoning data: SmolTalk [Ben Allal and others, 2024] (460K general-purpose conversations), MMLU (multiple-choice knowledge questions, 3 epochs), GSM-8K (grade-school mathematics, 4 epochs), identity conversations, and synthetic spelling tasks—approximately 1.1 million training examples in total. Note that the cross-entropy loss is computed only on assistant tokens, not on user prompts, mirroring the InstructGPT training procedure [Ouyang et al., 2022].

Before each training stage, a BPE tokenizer is trained on 2 billion characters using a Rust implementation, producing a vocabulary of 32,768 tokens in under one minute.

A web inference server and a lightweight JavaScript chat UI are included out of the box, allowing immediate interaction with your trained model.

Supplementary resources

Two freely available courses provide complementary perspectives on the material in this case study. The Hugging Face LLM Course [Hugging Face, 2022] introduces the transformers, datasets, tokenizers, and accelerate libraries, and the Hugging Face Hub through which most open-weight models are distributed and evaluated today. Mathieu Labonne’s LLM Course [Labonne, 2023] provides a practitioner roadmap covering pre-training data curation, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA), preference alignment (DPO, PPO, GRPO), quantization (GGUF, GPTQ), and production inference serving (vLLM, TGI). Together these resources situate nanochat within the broader open-source LLM ecosystem and are referenced explicitly in Tasks 3 and 4. You are also free to browse around for additional resources. It is strongly recommended to link and reference sources in your report where needed.

5.3 Experiment Preparation

Repository

Clone the course repository and read the README carefully before writing any code.

Compute

No dedicated compute is necessary. You may use your own laptop (with a GPU), or a larger computer. The experiments are planned so that each run completes a maximum of approximately 8 hours. For pretraining, use a --depth 4 configuration; --depth 2 is acceptable only if your hardware does not permit the larger model. Do not attempt depth ≥\geq12 unless you have some serious hardware.

Logging

nanochat logs training loss, validation loss, and bits-per-byte at configurable intervals to your terminal, and additional functionality for reporting and saving information during the run is available. It is therefore wise to enable structured logging to a .jsonl file from the start. Retrofitting logging after a run is painful. You may want to experiment with the logging file formats. We recommend using a service such as wandb.ai before training full models.

5.4 Task 0: Model Hub warm-up.

Description

Before starting the tasks, it is a good idea to get a feel for common parameter settings and common training settings for different models. For this purpose, practice navigating the Hugging Face Hub.33 3 https://huggingface.co/models For each of the three model IDs in Table 5.1, locate and record:

    the number of training tokens or steps,

  2. 2.

    the model architecture (number of layers, hidden dimension, attention heads, number of trainable parameters), and

  3. 3.

Pay attention to where you look for each piece of information: some fields appear directly on the model card, others require inspecting config.json under the Files tab, and some are only available in the accompanying paper. Include a short table with your findings in your report, noting the source for each field.

5.5 Task 1: Tokenization

5.5.1 What to Do

Train a BPE tokenizer using nanochat’s Rust tokenizer trainer on a 500 million character sample of the CLIMBMix dataset. Run two experiments: one with a vocabulary size of 8,192 tokens and one with 32,768 tokens.

5.5.2 Deliverables
  • •

    A short script that reproduces your tokenizer training run.

  • •

    A report section (at most 1 page) answering the following questions with evidence from your own tokenizer outputs:

    1. 1.

      What is BPE, and how does it differ from word-level and character-level tokenization? Draw a merge tree for a concrete example (you can look for one in the data, or make your own. Do not reuse an existing example!). Make sure to also include the counts for your merges.

    2. 2.

      How does vocabulary size affect compression ratio (tokens per character) and sequence length for a fixed text sample? Show measurements from both of your tokenizers on English text.

    3. 3.

      Why does vocabulary size matter for the downstream language model? In your answer, consider the embedding matrix size, the softmax denominator, and the challenge of learning reliable representations for rare tokens.

    4. 4.

      What artifacts or failure cases do you observe? How does your tokenizer handle numbers, source code, or non-English text?

Pay attention to: correctness of the BPE explanation; quality of empirical evidence; depth of analysis on vocabulary trade-offs; perceptiveness of failure-case discussion.

5.6 Task 2: Pretraining

5.6.1 What to Do

Pretrain a transformer using nanochat with --depth 4 (or, in case your computer is not fast enough, --depth 2) on the CLIMBMix dataset. Log training loss, validation loss, and bits-per-byte at regular checkpoints.

5.6.2 Deliverables
  • •

    Bits-per-byte curves for training and validation set (plots, to be included in the report). Use bpb instead of the raw loss.

  • •

    A saved model checkpoint.

  • •

    A report section (approximately 2 pages) covering:

    1. 1.

      The Depth Parameter: Explain what the --depth argument controls in nanochat and how the codebase derives all other hyperparameters automatically from it: embedding width, number of attention heads, learning rate schedule, training horizon. For the chosen depth, state the number of layers, attention heads, embedding dimension, the total trainable parameter count, and the number of total tokens the model will be trained on. Why is a single-dial design useful for such a codebase? What are its limitations compared to tuning each hyperparameter independently?

    2. 2.

      Scaling Laws: Using the Chinchilla framework [Hoffmann et al., 2022], compute the compute-optimal number of training tokens for your model’s parameter count. How does nanochat’s default training horizon compare? What does it mean to be under-trained or over-trained?

    3. 3.

      Loss Analysis: Plot the progress of bits-per-byte (bpb) during training as your training curve and explain its shape. At what point does the curve flatten? What does the gap between training and validation tell you?

    4. 4.

      Qualitative Inspection: Sample five completions from your pretrained model with no system prompt (raw next-token prediction). What is the model able to do at this stage, and why do you think that is the case?

Pay attention to: correctness of the depth-parameter explanation and auto-configuration description; accuracy of architecture description; correct application of scaling law calculations; quality of loss analysis; insightfulness of qualitative assessment.

5.7 Task 3: Mid-Training and Supervised Finetuning

5.7.1 What to Do

Recall that nanochat only performs two training stages: pretraining and SFT. However, in the book, we discussed that additional stages in the form of mid-training can help the model perform better. In this task, you will implement a new mid-training stage by modifying scripts/chat_sft.py. The goal is to separate reasoning adaptation (mid-training) from instruction following (SFT) and measure the effect empirically.

Stage 1 — Mid-training

Modify the train_tasks list in chat_sft.py so that it contains only reasoning and knowledge tasks: MMLU and GSM-8K. Remove all other conversational and spelling data. Run chat_sft.py from your pre-trained base checkpoint and save the resulting checkpoint.

Stage 2 — SFT

Modify chat_sft.py again so that train_tasks contains only SmolTalk. You will also need to make a small change so the script loads your Stage 1 checkpoint rather than the base pre-trained model. Inspect the load_model call in chat_sft.py as a starting point.44 4 Hint: read nanochat/checkpoint_manager.py to understand how checkpoints are located. Run chat_sft.py from your Stage 1 checkpoint to proceed with SFT after mid-training.

After each stage, evaluate with scripts/chat_eval.py on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and GSM-8K.

Sanity check: Before running Stage 1, inspect the data: print the first few rows of the MMLU and SmolTalk datasets to understand their format and content. Make sure you are able to answer: how many training examples does each dataset contribute, and what does a single training example look like?

5.7.2 Deliverables
  • •

    Two checkpoints, one for each stage (mid-training and SFT).

  • •

    Evaluation scores on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and GSM-8K after each stage, reported as a table. This should be part of the report (see below).

  • •

    A report section (approximately 3 pages) covering:

    1. 1.

      Implementation: Describe the changes you made to the codebase such that you can do training in stages. List the hyperparameters that you are using for the training experiments. You are free to experiment with them!

    2. 2.

      Loss Masking: Why is the SFT loss computed only on assistant tokens? Construct a concrete token-level example illustrating what the loss would look like with and without masking.

    3. 3.

      Dataset Analysis: For each stage, describe the dataset used, its approximate size, and why it was chosen for that stage specifically. What values or potential biases might be embedded in dataset training splits? How might these shape model behavior?

    4. 4.

      Benchmark Scores: Report your evaluation scores after each stage in a table. What changed between Stage 1 and Stage 2, and why? Also compare to the pretrained results such that your analysis covers all three stages. Note any results that surprised you.

    5. 5.

      Parameter-efficient Finetuning: nanochat performs full fine-tuning: every parameter is updated during SFT. Describe how LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) and its quantized variant QLoRA differ from full fine-tuning. What are the trade-offs in compute, memory, and final model quality? Would you recommend using PEFT techniques for the depths we have used in training so far?

Pay attention to: correctness and clarity of the implementation description; correctness of the loss-masking explanation; critical quality of dataset analysis; accuracy and completeness of reported benchmark scores and their interpretation; conceptual accuracy of the LoRA/QLoRA comparison.

5.8.1 Part A: Inference and Deployment

Launch nanochat’s inference server and web UI. Interact with your trained model. Then address the following in your report (approximately 1 page):

  1. 1.

    The Inference Loop: Describe how autoregressive sampling works, including the role of the key–value (KV) cache in avoiding redundant computation across decoding steps. Then address the following two questions. Where does your model fall relative to models of similar parameter count? 5.8.2 Part B: Critical Reflection

Write a short discussion (approximately 0.5-1 page) responding to one of the following three prompts.

Prompt 1 — Access and Democratization nanochat’s headline claim is that “the best ChatGPT that $100 can buy” brings LLM training within reach of individuals. Critically evaluate this claim. Who still cannot access this pipeline, and why?

Prompt 2 — Data and Values nanochat pretrains on CLIMBMix, a clustering-based iteratively bootstrapped data mixture corpus. What decisions were made in constructing this dataset, and whose values do they embed? How might a different pre-training corpus lead to a qualitatively different model?

Estimate the carbon cost of your own training run using an established methodology (e.g. the ML CO2 Impact calculator).55 5 https://mlco2.impact.compute.org Situate this in the broader context of LLM environmental impact. Is cheap the same as low-impact?

5.10 Concluding Remarks

In this chapter we have used nanochat as a window into the complete LLM training pipeline. You have trained a BPE tokenizer, observed a transformer learn from web text, adapted that model to follow instructions, evaluated it on standard benchmarks, and deployed it as a chat assistant.

The gap between your depth-4 model and the frontier will be obvious, because we don’t expect you to have access to datacenter-grade compute capabilities. However, the experiments are, in theory, scalable: rerunning at higher depths and with additional data resources should lead to more capable models, as predicted by the scaling laws. After completion of Assignment 1, you have essentially trained a full LLM by yourself, and you will be better equipped for future experiments where an increased scale is necessary.

Part II Reasoning

This part is about the brains of our agents, and how they use them to learn. The previous part showed us how a basic next-token LLM is trained. In agentic models typically more advanced reasoning and multi-modal models are used (which we continue to call LLM). In this part we will discuss these more advanced models, why they are needed, and how they are trained and used.

The first chapter of this part introduces reasoning models. Originally LLMs could not solve simple reasoning problems, and the chain of thought concept caused a major leap forward in this field. We will discuss math word problems, chain of thought prompting, and in-context learning. We will see models that use self-reflection to try to improve their own behavior. Self-reflection loops led to the development of agentic harnesses for LLMs.

In the following chapter we go beyond language: we will see that the transformer architecture also works for vision and action domains. We will discuss various kinds of World Models, models that allow agents to act more intelligently in their interaction with the world.

In the last chapter of this part, we introduce the concept of metalearning, a paradigm that is present in many of the types of learning that we see in agentic LLMs. We will discuss what metalearning is, and why it is a challenging form of machine learning.

Chapter 6 Multi-step Reasoning in LLMs

6.1 In-Context Reasoning

As we noted Chapter 3, in large models, beyond hundreds of billions of parameters, a new kind of learning has emerged in LLMs. It is called in-context learning (ICL) or prompt-learning [Brown et al., 2020]. It is an important learning method, which we will discuss in more detail in this section. Then, we will discuss common benchmarks, and the chain of thought method for multi-step reasoning.

6.1.1 In-Context Learning

In-context learning [Dong et al., 2022] occurs not at training time, but at inference time, from examples that are provided in the LLM prompt, when the model is used to answer questions. These examples cause the decoder model to access relevant knowledge stored in the LLM. Because of this rich knowledge, in-context learning finds accurate results with few examples, which is why it is a so-called few-shot learning method. The few-shot learning is made possible by the large size of the model, containing rich and varied knowledge on many topics.

Learning, not Training

A main difference between in-context learning and finetuning or pretraining is that in-context learning does not change the parameters of the transformer. Since no model-parameters are changed at inference time, it is not a parameter training method; however, since it does learn an answer from provided examples, it is a learning method. A consequence is that ICL has the disadvantage of forgetfulness: since model parameters remain unchanged, all learned information is lost between LLM calls. To share information between LLM calls, previous results must be added to the prompt of the next call, in the context window, as extra learning examples.

Context Window

How does in-context learning work? The part of an LLM in which the prompt is written is called its context window. The decoder model learns inside this context window, from the examples that are provided in the prompt. A point to note is that all examples that the answer is learned from must be provided together in the context window—they should fit in the prompt. Typically, the size of the context window is limited to a few thousand tokens, and only few examples can be provided: all ICL is able to perform is few-shot learning. This becomes problematic when the amount of information that we wish to learn from grows, since the context window is typically limited in size. We might say that in-context learning suffers from long-term memory loss.

Example

In in-context learning, a prompt, consisting of a few pieces of demonstration context, is concatenated with a query question, which is given to the context window of the language model [Liu et al., 2023]. The model will then generate the answer by performing a forward pass through the model. For example, when the task is emotion recognition in a social media post, I missed the bus today, can be followed by I felt so [___], and the model could answer with bad. Alternatively, for translation, we could follow I missed the bus today, by French: [___] to request a translation. The prompt contains background information that is recognized by the model, selecting the desired model context.

Few-shot Learning and the Holy Grail of Machine Learning

In-context learning works when language models contain enough knowledge, allowing them to generalize on the (few) examples provided in the prompt. The user provides a few relevant examples in the prompt, in order to prime the LLM to select the right background knowledge for answering the prompted instruction. Contexts that contain a few examples are said to perform few-shot learning. Contexts that contain only instructions, with zero examples, are said to perform zero-shot learning.

ICL is a form of few-shot learning that caused much excitement among researchers. In traditional machine learning, a model ff is trained on dataset. To achieve high accuracy on complex problems, the datasets must contain many examples. Traditional machine learning is a form of many-shot learning, requiring many (expensive) training epochs to train the parameters of the model. In-context learning, on the other hand, is cheap, requiring just a few examples followed by a single forward pass through the decoder model (since the expensive training has been done in the pretraining phase). Few-shot learning is something of the holy grail of machine learning: a model that generalizes, cheaply.

Practical Considerations and Prompt Engineering

In-context learning further has the practical advantage of convenience: we can perform ICL on an LLM that runs commercially in the cloud, from our smartphone, without going through the difficulty of finding a computer to train a large model on.

Although prompts provide a user-friendly interface to LLMs, the success of in-context learning tends to be quite sensitive to the way a prompt is formulated or when different examples are provided. Prompt-learning is brittle, and a new field called prompt engineering has emerged to help human users to learn how to make LLMs do what we want them to do [Radford et al., 2019, Wei et al., 2022a, Giray, 2023, Sahoo et al., 2024].

In most LLMs the context window is provided with hidden prompts, the system prompts, to specify a particular role for the model, to prevent the use of swear words, and, in chatbots, to have a short history of previous search results, to allow for more naturally flowing conversations.

In-context learning has spawned much further research. One of the areas is multi-step reasoning, which is the topic of this chapter. Reasoning used to be an area where LLMs performed poorly. For example, LLMs failed at simple math exercises. To better understand this application domain we will introduce a few reasoning benchmarks. Then we will discuss an in-context learning method that greatly improved the performance of reasoning by LLMs.

6.1.2 Multi-step Reasoning Benchmarks

Progress in artificial intelligence is measured by benchmarks. The research on multi-step reasoning with LLMs started with easy (grade school) math word problems. Specifically for the study of such easy reasoning the GSM8K benchmark was composed [Cobbe et al., 2021]. GSM8K was created with the aim of providing high quality problems, of high diversity and moderate difficulty, in natural language. It consists of 8500 human-written math problems and solutions. Language models struggled to achieve good performance on this dataset before chain of thought was introduced (see the next section). Here is an example of a typical math word problem:

Problem: Romeo bakes 4 trays with two dozen batches of cookies in a week. If these cookies are shared amongst 16 people equally, how many cookies does each person consume?
Answer: 4×2×12/16=64\times 2\times 12/16=6.

The GSM8K benchmark, although it may look easy to us, turned out to be difficult for LLMs. When it was introduced, the state of the art LLM GPT-3-175B achieved a rather low accuracy of around 15% [Wei et al., 2022b]. Other benchmarks of similar math word problems are the SVAMP varying structures benchmark [Patel et al., 2021], the ASDiv dataset of diverse math problems [Miao et al., 2021], the AQuA dataset of algebraic word problems [Ling et al., 2017], and the MAWPS benchmark [Koncel-Kedziorski et al., 2016].

Later, benchmarks for other tasks were introduced, to assess LLM reasoning abilities in other fields of reasoning. For example, benchmarks have been developed on advanced mathematical questions (AIME [Codeforces, 2024]), computer code comprehension (Spider [Yu et al., 2018], transcoding (translating a program in one computer language to another) [Roziere et al., 2020]), robotic movement (Alfworld [Shridhar et al., 2020], kitchen tasks [Ahn et al., 2022]), puzzle solving (Game24 [Yao et al., 2024]), creative writing [Yao et al., 2024]), board games (Checkmate problems [Yang et al., 2024], MineCraft [Fan et al., 2022]), and webpage navigation (WebShop [Yao et al., 2022a]). Further relevant benchmark studies also focus on games and planning problems [Ruoss et al., 2024, Paglieri et al., 2025, Wen et al., 2025a].

The goal of benchmarks is to be able to clearly compare the performance of different approaches. However, it can be difficult to directly compare different benchmarking results, since there may be differences in the way the experiments were conducted. See Kamoi et al. [2024], Shojaee et al. [2025] for a critical discussion of challenges in benchmarking LLM reasoning.

6.1.3 Chain of Thought Prompting

Around 2022, regular LLMs of the time performed poorly on simple math word problems. Interestingly, the standard Chapter 4 approach to improve performance of LLMs by scaling up the size of the LLM, did not solve the problem [Rae et al., 2021]. The problem appeared to be somehow fundamental in nature, and researchers went looking for a different approach.

The LLM architecture is a transformer-based decoder. Given a certain input, it is designed to produce a single token. LLMs are next-token predictors. When we prompt such a decoder to produce an answer, it does as it is instructed to: it provides an answer quickly—any answer. But that is not how humans work towards an answer in a mathematical reasoning problem, we divide the question into a sequence of steps to solve (4×2×12/16=64\times 2\times 12/16=6). Thus, for the LLM, what we should do instead is to prompt it to follow a well-chosen sequence of intermediate steps, answer those, and thus work towards the final answer, just as a student is taught to break down a complex problem into smaller steps, and to also provide the reasoning steps when answering a problem in school—Don’t just tell me the answer, but tell me how you arrived at the answer. Children are taught in school to break down a big problem into a sequence of small steps, when solving a mathematical problem. Similarly, we should guide the language model to explicitly produce such intermediate steps, and then to combine the results. The LLM should then provide an answer that includes the intermediate steps, arriving at a correct result.

Thus, our few-shot prompt should contain examples of intermediate reasoning steps, instead of only examples of the final answer. This question was studied by Wei et al. [2022b], amongst others, who introduced the chain of thought approach. Figure 6.1 illustrates how the approach works, in addition to related approaches, that it inspired.

The way to instruct an LLM to generate intermediate steps is to manually write a prompt consisting of specific reasoning steps to answer the task (for example, calculate how many balls are in the container, or in how many pieces the pie was cut). Indeed, when Wei et al. [2022b] tried this approach, and the LLM was prompted to rephrase information from the question as intermediate reasoning steps in its answer, the LLM performed much better than when it was prompted to produce a single answer. The example from the chain of thought paper is shown in Figure 6.1. When shown the longer example prompt, the LLM follows the longer example when answering the question (Few-Shot CoT). On GSM8K, the chain of thought approach showed a large increase in accuracy, from 16% to 47%.

The idea that, when prompted, an LLM can be made to follow step-by-step instructions, has caused much excitement and has opened up further research on multi-step reasoning with LLMs. Chain of thought (CoT) has become a standard prompting approach in LLMs since.

In the original paper the prompts were hand-written by the researchers for the individual types of problems. Kojima et al. [2022] go a step further. They show that the addition of a single task-independent sentence (Let’s think step by step) also significantly improves performance for many problems. Since this text does not contain problem-related elements, it is as a form of zero-shot learning. Figure 6.1 compares the approaches (second and third column). Experiments further show that with this addition significant performance gains are also achieved on other reasoning benchmarks, including arithmetic, symbolic, and logical reasoning (achieving 70% accuracy on GSM8K when self consistency (see next section) is also included, using the newer PaLM LLM [Wang et al., 2022]).

The chain of thought idea itself is inspired by Scratchpad [Nye et al., 2021], by other earlier work where natural language steps are generated for arithmetic reasoning [Ling et al., 2017, Cobbe et al., 2021], and by the use of formal languages for reasoning [Roy and Roth, 2016, Chiang and Chen, 2018, Amini et al., 2019, Chen et al., 2019].

6.1.3.1 Self Evaluation

LLMs are not perfect, and errors in results occur. When multiple reasoning steps are generated, errors accumulate. To prevent the errors from getting out of hand we should pay extra attention to the evaluation of results. We will now review approaches to reduce error accumulation, either by examining the model, or by evaluating intermediate reasoning steps.

When LLMs are prompted to perform CoT reasoning, they perform a sequence of steps. Performing multiple steps makes them sensitive to mistakes and vulnerable to error accumulation [Weng et al., 2022, Xiao et al., 2023]. Several methods have been developed to prevent error accumulation. One approach is to create a new model to separately evaluate the results. Weng et al. [2022] propose an automated approach using evaluation by the same LLM, called self verification. The LLM is prompted to use the conclusion of the chain of thought reasoning chain as a condition for solving the original problem and then compare the answer, going back to the original question. The LLM is given variations of its own conclusion and is instructed to choose the one with the highest similarity to the original question.

A popular related approach is self consistency [Wang et al., 2022]. Self consistency is an ensemble approach (a well-known machine learning technique to make a strong learner by running multiple weaker learners [Sagi and Rokach, 2018, Breiman, 2001]). Conventionally, the answer of an LLM query is extracted from the decoder network by greedily following the path with the highest logit values. In self consistency, greedy single-path decoding is replaced by majority voting over a wider sample of paths. By sampling diverse reasoning paths, evaluating them, and selecting the most consistent answer among them, self consistency effectively asks the LLM to perform the same query multiple times, and takes the majority-vote of the internal decoding paths of the transformer model. Self consistency works because complex reasoning problems typically have different reasoning paths that lead to the correct answer. Figure 6.2 provides an example of the approach.

Self consistency has been evaluated on arithmetic reasoning, on commonsense reasoning and on symbolic reasoning, with a variety of LLMs, including GPT-3. Self consistency typically improves the performance of chain of thought by a further 10-20 percentage points. Self consistency is often used in combination with chain of thought in modern LLMs.

6.1.3.2 Code Generation for Validation

Another approach to improve the accuracy of a sequence of reasoning steps is to switch from a natural to a formal language. The advantage of a formal language is that it is less ambiguous than a natural language. Examples are computer languages, such as Python, or mathematical logic.

LLMs have been quite successful in generating computer code from natural language prompts. Chen et al. [2021] introduced Codex, a GPT model that was trained on publicly available code in the repository GitHub. Codex is able to generate correct programs from descriptions in natural language, such as commentary strings. Subsequently, the use of a formal language for reasoning has become a popular approach. Many approaches generate the reasoning steps in Python, so that the code can be evaluated by a compiler, debugger, or interpreter. Human programmers, when writing code, typically follow a cycle of writing some code, compiling and executing it to look for errors, and then using the feedback to improve the code. This approach is followed, for example, in self debugging [Chen et al., 2023]. It follows the same steps of code generation, code execution, and code explanation. Self debugging is able to identify mistakes in its own code by investigating the execution results, and can also provide an explanation of the generated code, in natural language.

Another approach, program aided language [Gao et al., 2023], uses the LLM to generate Python and then use an interpreter to evaluate the result. In this approach the problem is translated into small pieces of Python code, that can then be executed by an interpreter to solve the problem. Figure 6.1 (fourth column) illustrates the program aided language approach. When the evaluation of the reasoning steps is offloaded to the Python interpreter, decomposing the natural language problem into executable code-steps remains the only task for the LLM. Gao et al. [2023] provide extensive experimental evidence showing the synergy between the neural LLM and the symbolic interpreter. Experiments were performed on 13 mathematical, symbolic, and algorithmic reasoning tasks, achieving more accurate results than much larger models of the time (for example, program aided language reported 72% on GSM8K and 93% on Penguins).

6.1.3.3 Evolving code generation prompts

The work on verification with formal languages has lead to several works that generate working code tuned for solving specific problems automatically, without human feedback. Romera-Paredes et al. [2024] introduced FunSearch, an approach that integrates formal methods and LLMs to enhance mathematical reasoning and code generation. FunSearch uses a genetic approach with multiple populations of candidate solutions (programs), which are evaluated using a function depending on the problem specification. After evaluating the generated programs from the starting prompt, a new prompt is created, in an iterative fashion, combining a selection of sampled programs sorted according to their evaluation score, and the LLM is requested to generate a new program. Another work leverages evolutionary computation methods to generate and optimize evolutionary algorithms [van Stein and Bäck, 2024]. This approach, LLaMEA (Large Language Model Evolutionary Algorithm), utilizes LLMs to design and optimize evolutionary algorithms. The approach uses LLMs to generate initial algorithmic structures, which are then refined through mutation and selection. Accuracy improvements on the Black-Box Optimization Benchmark (BBOB) [Hansen and Ros, 2010] are reported of 11 percentage points.

6.2 Self-Reflection and State

In-context learning has emerged as a powerful new few-shot learning method. When our few-shot examples specify reasoning steps, we can improve the capabilities of LLMs even more.

In this section we will look at some of the limits of in-context learning, and we will look at ways to extend the limits. We will first discuss the question of state and memory. We will look at how state can be passed between separate invocations of LLMs, at long context windows, and at the question if LLMs are good at solving problems for which they have to manipulate state.

6.2.1 LLMs are Memory-less Functions

In-context few-shot learning exploits the capabilities of LLMs to retrieve knowledge, conditioned by the prompt. The instructions and examples are provided, and the transformer architecture finds the answer (next token) in its vast model of (K,V)(K,V)-parameters. With chain of thought prompts, the LLM is conditioned on few-shot reasoning steps that are specified in the prompt.

In-context learning uses the LLM in a functional way, where all input to the LLM is provided in the prompt. The model ff finds the answer aa for the input prompt pp:

f⁡(p)→a.f(p)\rightarrow a.

In principle, LLMs do not retain information between LLM calls (model parameters remain unchanged, and there are no global variables with history). If we wish to refine our request, and we wish to carry state information from the previous call to the next, then all such state must be specified by the user in the new prompt p′p^{\prime}. The model itself has forgotten all about the previous answer.

For a chatbot, repeating the entire conversational history in each new question would be a cumbersome and unnatural way of conversing. In human conversation our conversation partners do remember what was last said, without us having to explicitly repeat their last sentence (although, when interviewing politicians, journalists sometimes use this method to try to keep them on message). Commercial chatbots overcome this problem in part using system prompts, by invisibly providing the output of the previous LLM call to the prompt for a new LLM query. However, the principle remains that LLMs are good at finding associative next-token answers for a prompt, but not at all at remembering answers and manipulating the state of variables as we know them from general computer programming languages. As no parameters are changed, LLMs do not remember in-context state between calls.

6.2.2 Retrieval Augmentation and Long Context Windows

The LLM-memory problem goes deeper. All information for the query must be specified in a context window. The size of this context window is limited, which fundamentally limits the amount of information that can be communicated to the LLM for a query. This limitation is a problem when a large text (such as a book) is to be summarized. Furthermore, in Section 20.2.1 we will discuss in-context reinforcement learning methods, that work by storing full episode histories in the context window. In short, methods are needed to pass more information to the LLM.

One of the earliest methods to extend the amount of information at inference time is retrieval augmentation for generative AI (RAG). RAG lets the LLM place a call to external data, such as a corporate database, or to Wikipedia [Lewis et al., 2020]. RAG’s use is also in reducing factual hallucinations and providing access to time-sensitive information, such as financial or logistics data. RAG will be discussed in Chapter 12.

For passing longer texts to the model, LLMs have been developed with longer context windows. With the standard transformer architecture, the compute requirements scale quadratically with the size of the context window, and linear architectures are being developed [Ren et al., 2024]. Another solution is to compress the information in the context window, for example using semantic compression [Fei et al., 2024], by chunking the information [Wang et al., 2023, Zhou et al., 2025], or by recursive methods [Zhang et al., 2025]. Devising novel memory architectures for LLMs is an active area of research [Yan et al., 2025].

6.2.3 LLMs and Stateful Problems

LLMs perform poorly at solving problems in which state must be managed [Wong et al., 2025]. This occurs for example in planning problems in which the current state has to be remembered accurately, even in simple board games such as the one shown in Figure 6.3. LLMs tend to mix up the states, and to provide plausible sounding answers that may be correct for games that it has seen in its training corpus, but that are wrong for the actual board state at hand [Paglieri et al., 2025, Ruoss et al., 2024].

Many approaches have been tried to improve reasoning with state, often inspired by reinforcement learning and planning algorithms [Wong et al., 2026]. To see how LLMs can be used to solve these stateful problems, we discuss how the memory-less nature of LLMs makes them suffer from a problem known as the knowing-doing gap. Other, advanced, methods have been developed to allow LLMs to deal better with stateful problems. Chapter 20 will discuss these advanced approaches.

Knowing-Doing Gap

In addition to the lack of state between LLM calls, there is another memory-related problem, in the internal execution by the LLM of certain tasks.

This problem has been named the knowing-doing gap. This gap describes the curious phenomenon where an LLM is able to generate a correct textual description to solve a problem, even the correct algorithm, but is not able to execute this algorithm correctly [Paglieri et al., 2025]. When you ask an LLM how to solve a certain problem, it can promptly provide the right algorithm in executable Python code. When one subsequently asks it to actually solve this problem, the LLM does not correctly follow the algorithm that it just generated. More often than not, errors start appearing between state changes of the variables in the algorithm that it generated [Paglieri et al., 2025, Ruoss et al., 2024]. Note that faithfully executing algorithmic code step by step, tracking values in registers, is not what the attention-based transformers in LLMs were designed for at all—they were designed to simulate natural language processing through a form of associative memory [La Malfa et al., 2024].11 1 Note further that the human mind sometimes has the same problem: we can easily describe an algorithm for long division, but when asked to compute 12345/4212345/42, we may make mistakes—computers are good at this, but not humans, and also not LLMs.

In addition to the knowing-doing gap, there is another state-management problem. Prompting an LLM to play the first few moves of a board game against itself may show a game in which pieces on the board magically (dis)appear between moves. The model does not recognize that the moves that it plays that may have been good in certain situations, do not fit the current board position, and even decorates these wrong moves with a plausibly sounding reason in a chatty conversational style. LLMs have difficulty reliably managing the state transition of a variable that goes from one value to another value. Individual values tend to be forgotten or mixed up. Additional text can be inserted into the prompt to instruct the model to carefully track values of variables before making a next step [La Malfa et al., 2024], but this is a cumbersome and error-prone solution.

Both the knowing-doing gap and the disappearing-pieces problem can be circumvented by calling an external interpreter to execute an LLM-generated algorithm. This strategy is sometimes taken by commercial chatbots. It is a smart, practical, solution, since, in addition to being able to correctly execute Python code, the Python interpreter will do so more efficiently than an LLM.

Chapter 20 will discuss other approaches that address state and memory in the transformer architecture.

6.2.4 Agentic Harness for Prompt Improvement

In addition to resorting to externally executing generated code, other methods have been developed to deal with memory and state. In this section, we will go agentic, and introduce small external algorithms to explicitly manage state and prompts. Such an algorithm is called a harness. The harness may also call the same LLM in different roles, with different prompts for each role, for example, for generation or for evaluation of states. We start with prompt management based on search algorithms.

When the LLM is called in different roles, for example to critique (evaluate) its own performance (that it just generated), the LLM can be said to perform self-reflection. This somewhat anthropomorphic term is often used in the literature for these approaches. Exactly what (not who) is doing the self-reflecting, the LLM, or the agentic harness, is a matter for debate.

6.2.4.1 Search-based Prompt Optimization

We will now discuss search-based inference-time decision methods. These are in-context learning methods that go beyond chain of thought. Chain of thought explores a single line of reasoning steps, where each step has a single successor step. Search-based methods explore multiple options at each step, creating a tree of possibilities.

When we wish to examine a tree of possible reasoning steps, then we need a method to keep track of the state of which step we have seen, what the best answer so far was, and which steps should still be further examined. As we have seen, LLMs are not terribly good at keeping track of state, whereas conventional computer algorithms, such as small pieces of Python code, are. Such an algorithm will decompose the problem into a search tree, where multiple alternative steps are generated that can be searched multiple steps into the future (see Figure 6.6 on page 6.6). The algorithms call the LLM as a subroutine prompting it to perform requested tasks, such as action selection and reward evaluation. Then, backtracking can be performed by the algorithm, allowing alternative steps to be tried. This control algorithm is external to the LLM. It wraps around the LLM, keeping track of state, managing the prompts, shielding it from the outside world (and shielding the outside world from LLMs that mess up state). The control algorithm is called a harness.

We start our discussion of control strategies with depth-first and breadth-first search [Cormen et al., 2022]. Tree of thoughts [Yao et al., 2024] uses breadth-first or depth-first search to dynamically follow different reasoning steps.22 2 Tree of thoughts is a popular approach. The Huggingface link is here: https://huggingface.co/blog/sadhaklal/tree-of-thoughts Both the generation (red) and the evaluation (green) part in tree of thoughts are performed by prompting the LLM, see Figure 6.4.

Together, the two LLM prompts with the external control, allow systematic exploration of the space of reasoning steps, performing look-ahead and backtracking.

Tree of thoughts (ToT) has been used on planning-based puzzles, such as the Game of 24. In this game, 4 numbers are give, and the task is to reach the number 24 by using the arithmetic operators (+−∗/)(+-*/) in between the numbers. For example, for the numbers 44 99 1010 1313, a solution would be (10−4)∗(13−9)=24(10-4)*(13-9)=24. Tree of thoughts first generates a position with the propose prompt: Input 4 9 10 13; Possible next steps: to which the model answers by generating possible next step thoughts. These are then evaluated by the model with an evaluation prompt including chain of thought examples. Figure 6.5 shows a possible prompting sequence from the original paper.

The authors compare their approach to traditional linear chain of thought with self consistency on the Game of 24, Creative writing, and Mini crossword, achieving an accuracy of 74% on a Game of 24 task. The other tasks are evaluated qualitatively. Figure 6.6 illustrates the different reasoning structures.33 3 A similarly named approach is graph of thoughts [Besta et al., 2024]. Graph of thoughts allows more general reasoning graphs, providing a formal framework, where the different elements can then be specified manually.

Tree of thoughts is an elegant approach, adding two of the simplest possible search structures on top of an LLM. The sequence of prompts is easy to follow, and finding and correcting mistakes is also easy.

The two search methods of tree of thoughts follow a fixed expansion policy. Next, we will discuss more advanced learning-based approaches, that may perform better, at the cost of higher algorithmic complexity.

6.2.4.2 Self-Reflection

Many approaches have been devised that use the LLM in more than one role. Such approaches are generally called self-reflective approaches. The LLM is used not just to evaluate a prompt, but also to generate new reasoning steps, and often to refine them.

The field of self-reflection is young and new approaches are being developed regularly. We will present four such approaches: self refine, ReAct, reflexion, and buffer of thoughts. These approaches use the LLMs in different ways, using schemes inspired by reinforcement learning to let the LLMs improve themselves.

Self Refine

The first approach is self refine [Madaan et al., 2023]. This approach aims to improve answers from feedback. The LLM generates an initial output and provides feedback for its answer, using the LLM to refine itself, iteratively. The LLM is thus used to improve its own answers, see Figure 6.7.

Self refine prompts the LLM in three ways: (1) for initial generation, (2) for feedback, and (3) for refinement, following a greedy reasoning chain. Self refine reportedly improves significantly over regular chain of thought, on benchmarks such as dialogue response generation, code optimization, and constrained generation. This approach does follow a linear, greedy, reasoning chain, where a single successor is tried in a state (it does not explore a tree, as in ToT).

ReAct

Generalizing the greedy approach, we can use LLMs to examine multiple options per state. A notable approach that combines reinforcement learning and LLMs is ReAct [Yao et al., 2022b].44 4 https://github.com/ysymyth/ReAct ReAct uses chain of thought prompt-learning as part of a reinforcement learning framework that also uses external knowledge sources (Wikipedia) and finetuning; for error reduction, grounding, and for reducing hallucination. The framework allows hand-written prompts. On two interactive decision making benchmarks (Alfworld and WebShop), ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learning methods by an absolute success rate of 34% and 10% respectively.

Reflexion

The ReAct work has been developed further. Reflexion [Shinn et al., 2024] creates AI agents that learn by reflecting on failures and enhance their results, inspired by the way that humans do this.55 5 https://github.com/noahshinn/reflexion Reflexion uses three prompts for the LLM: actor, evaluator, and reflector. The reflexion harness incorporates explicit memory between LLM calls. For trajectory generation it has a short-term memory, and for storing experience information it has a long term memory. This approach addresses the state management problem of regular LLMs using memory in the external algorithm. Reflexion works as follows: (1) an actor model generates text and actions, (2) an evaluator model scores the outputs produced by the actor, and (3) a self-reflection model generates verbal reinforcement cues to assist the actor to self-improve (see Figure 6.8). For the actor, chain of thought and ReAct can be used. Reflexion has been evaluated on decision-making, reasoning, and coding tasks. Improvements of 10-20 percentage points are reported [Shinn et al., 2024].

Buffer of Thoughts

Another approach is buffer of thoughts [Yang et al., 2024], which goes a step towards metareasoning [Gao et al., 2024]. It introduces a meta-buffer that stores high-level thought-templates. Thought-templates are derived from a variety of tasks. Buffer of thoughts uses a problem distiller that stores high-level thoughts distilled from different problems in a meta-buffer, which is actively managed for capacity. Figure 6.9 compares the buffer of thoughts approach to other approaches such as chain of thought and tree of thoughts. Buffer of thoughts outperforms other methods in puzzles such as Game of 24 (by 11%) and checkmating (by 51%). Thought templates are related to metacognition (thinking about thinking) [Didolkar et al., 2024].

Critique and Prompt Sensitivity

The concept of self-reflection is not without pitfalls and criticism. To start, the basic idea of asking a model to refine its results begs the question why the model did not give the better answer in the first place. Next, studies by Huang et al. [2023], Shojaee et al. [2025] find methodological issues with some of the studies, such as the use of data labels that reveal the answer, second refinement prompts that unintentionally reveal more information than the initial prompts, and the use of the same LLM for agent and environment. In one reproducibility study performance did not exceed that of chain of thought with self consistency [Huang et al., 2023]. LLMs are sensitive to how a question is formulated in the prompt. Self-reflection is still a young and active field of research, with an appealing premise, but many open questions.

The approaches that we have presented potentially make many LLM calls, which can become expensive and slow. Finding the optimum approach for your problem may require quite some experimentation. In Chapter 10 we will discuss a practical case study where we will get hands-on experience with self-reflection methods. Please keep the preceding critique in mind.

6.2.4.3 Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

The focus of this chapter is on in-context learning. In-context learning occurs at inference time, and no parameters are trained or changed. Finetuning occurs at training time, and does change the parameters of the model. In this section we will, however, briefly talk about a mix of finetuning and in-context learning, we will be mixing training and inference.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards refers to an algorithmic approach for training language models on tasks with verifiable outcomes such as mathematical problem-solving and instruction following. Especially for reasoning problems, such as math word problems and coding, inference-time chain of thought results have been found to significantly improve models when they are used for finetuning.

RLVR is an improvement over reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), dispensing with the need for human feedback. In many domains, such as mathematics, a simple function exists to check if an answer is correct, without the need for human feedback. RLVR leverages the existing RLHF objective but replaces the reward model with a verification function. RLVR samples completions from a policy model given a set of prompts, and verifies their correctness using a deterministic function. If correct, the reward is positive, otherwise it is 0. This reward is then used to train against using PPO [Schulman et al., 2017] (a standard reinforcement learning algorithm), as in RLHF.

An influential approach of this type was proposed in the development of DeepSeek-R1 Guo et al. [2025]. This method distinguishes itself from external reasoning approaches by emphasizing the model’s self-generated reasoning steps. It learns the steps through reinforcement learning, integrating data generation and training in a single loop. Lowering the supervised data requirements to train LLMs, DeepSeek’s methodology leverages reinforcement learning to enable models to evolve reasoning skills autonomously. By starting with a base model and applying reinforcement learning, the system identifies and reinforces effective reasoning patterns. DeepSeek uses group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), which calculates advantages with group-based scoring [Shao et al., 2024].

One of the key features of DeepSeek’s approach is the emergence of sophisticated reasoning behaviors during finetuning, such as reflection and exploration of alternative problem-solving methods [Mercer et al., 2025]. These behaviors arise spontaneously as a result of the model’s interaction with the reinforcement learning environment, rather than being pre-programmed, and without external self-reflection loops. For example, DeepSeek-R1-Zero learns to allocate more thinking time to problems by reevaluating its initial approach. This autonomous approach of learning to reason may lead to more stable and adaptive reasoning LLMs.

One of the successes behind GRPO is its focus on applications for which verifiable rewards exist, allowing reinforcement learning methods to be used. The focus on verifiable rewards has been quite successful, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods are often used in finetuning LLMs [Lambert et al., 2024].

RLVR methods such as GRPO are typically used dynamically, where an inference time chain of thought query is used to answer a query from the training set to finetune the model. Thus, test time inference is used for finetuning. The impressive results of DeepSeek [Guo et al., 2025] have made GRPO [Shao et al., 2024] and RLVR [Lambert et al., 2024, Guo et al., 2025, Wen et al., 2025b, Yue et al., 2025] highly popular finetuning methods.

6.3 Concluding Remarks

In the preceding pages we have seen how the reasoning capabilities of language models can be improved. The best-known approach is chain of thought, which is a prompt-engineering method that shows an LLM to provide a multi-step reasoning when it is answering a question, just like we are taught in school when we are shown how to solve math exercises. More elaborate prompt improvement algorithms have been introduced, from depth-first search, via self-reflection, to inference-time reinforcement learning methods. Advanced training methods such as RLVR combine inference-results with finetuning, achieving strong training results.

6.3.1 Brittleness

We have discussed many different algorithmic approaches to create an agentic harness. There are multiple reasons why there are so many. First, the field of agentic LLM is still young, many challenges exist, leading to many new solutions.

Second, the methods are quite brittle. Small changes in prompts, a comma here or there, sometimes make the difference whether an approach works or not. Small changes in hyperparameters, such as the temperature of your model, or even using a different seed of a random number generator, may have large effects. Changes to the memory management method of the agentic harness, or using a different LLM, may all have a large effect on performance.

This may feel like a unsatisfactory state of affairs. Indeed, the field is young, and it will take some years before methods have stabilized. In your experiments, you should keep in mind to always do multiple runs, with different seeds, different models, and different hyperparameter settings. This will help you better understand how your solution works in different circumstances.

6.3.2 Thinking, Fast and Slow

To conclude this chapter we will discuss reasoning in LLMs in a broader perspective. In the history of AI, two approaches, or schools of thought, can be seen: symbolic AI and connectionist AI. Symbolic AI roughly corresponds to the idea that intelligence is best modeled as the manipulation of symbols via the rules of logic. Connectionist AI studies whether intelligence emerges spontaneously out of interactions between connected elements (be they neurons, cells, ants, humans, or robots). Symbolic AI draws on mathematics, connectionist AI on biology. As we already saw in Section 2.3, both schools have developed useful methods, and both schools have seen important successes (such as search algorithms and reasoning, or deep learning and LLMs).

In 2011 Daniel Kahneman published the book Thinking, Fast and Slow in which the terms System 1 and System 2 were used to distinguish human thought into intuitive, fast, thinking, and deliberative, slow, thinking [Kahneman, 2011]. These terms have become popular in artificial intelligence, where fast thinking is linked to associative lookup and slow thinking to multi-step reasoning. At inference time, zero-shot LLMs think fast (System 1 thinking). Inference-time step-by-step methods (either through longer prompts or with an agentic harness) perform deliberative slow thinking (System 2 thinking).

LLMs are based on the connectionist AI tradition (System 1). The use of tools at inference time enhances the LLM part with knowledge retrieval or processing tools from the symbolic AI tradition (System 2).

We should note that whereas researchers sometimes humanize LLMs and their capabilities, LLMs only perform next-token prediction. LLMs are not even close to being human. By generating more tokens to form an answer (reasoning step-by-step), the token-path from the prompt to the final answer becomes longer. The reason that this leads more often to correct answers, might be because it takes smaller steps into the direction of the answer, making the correct answer more plausible with every step in between—not that it is similar to the way humans are taught to solve the problem. Reasoning is narrowing down probabilities such that the correct answer becomes more probable to generate, independent of interpretations related to human cognition [Guo et al., 2025].

6.3.3 Conclusion

In this chapter we have discussed how LLMs can solve language tasks by next-token prediction, and solve tasks that require multi-step reasoning. We have discussed ways to manage complex reasoning structures.

Most methods are in-context methods, efficient and easy to use since the prompts that guide the reasoning are readable by the user. We have introduced the rule of an agentic harness for prompt improvement and memory management. We have also touched upon methods that use pretraining and finetuning, not just for the language part, but also for integrating multi-step reasoning. These methods thus train models for decision making, beyond pure next-token prediction in language models.

There has been much activity in the creation of such richer models, adding visual reasoning, decision making, and actions to become an integral part of the LLMs. In the next chapter we will look deeper into these pretrained and finetuned multi-modal models.
