Chapter 7 Vision, Action and World Models

7.1 Multi-modal Vision Language Models

Many decisions involve vision. As we will see in this section, the transformer architecture is also able to learn tokenized visual patterns. Models that are pretrained on both language and visual data are called vision-language models, or VLMs. VLMs typically consist of (1) a language part, (2) a vision part, and (3) a part that combines both embeddings.

We will discuss various architectures of these vision-language models. For each type of model we will describe the task, the architecture of the model, and the algorithm with which it is trained. We will see impressive results.

Computer vision has a long and successful history in AI. Deep learning has been successful in image recognition tasks, long before the breakthroughs in natural language processing [Krizhevsky et al., 2012]. Can these two successful fields be combined? This is not a trivial question, since the two fields are based on deep learning architectures that re quite different: image processing is based on convolutional neural networks that work well on two-dimensional rectangular grids of pixels, and language processing on transformers that work well on one-dimensional sequences of tokens.

As we will see, architectures have indeed been developed for combining the two fields, to the extent that most frontier models are now VLMs.

7.1.1 Tasks

Let us first discuss the types of tasks that vision-language models must solve, and list some of the popular benchmark suites. For understanding, the models can be tested on visual question answering tasks (VQA), to see if the models have acquired some textual understanding of visual images. A related, but generative, task is that of captioning problems, where models have to generate a textual descriptions of images. Additionally, models may be tasked to do image generation.

Let us have a look at some example tasks. For Figure 7.1, a VQA question could be: What is the mustache made of? and the system should answer: Bananas. Other typical VQA questions are to count the number of certain shapes of a certain color in a certain part of an image (to answer questions such as: Is there a red block in the upper corner of the table in this scene?). The tasks can be quite diverse, and there is a range of popular benchmarks such as MOSAIC [Burda-Lassen et al., 2025], GLOBAL-RG [Bhatia et al., 2024], CultureVQA [Nayak et al., 2024], FoodieQA [Li et al., 2024], and MaRVL [Liu et al., 2021].

In captioning problems, a model could be prompted to provide a caption for the scene in Figure 7.2, which shows a happy dog standing in the ocean. Note that variations may be equally valid, such as a wet dog, a cold dog, or a dog with a red collar standing in the ocean. Popular benchmarks are MS-COCO [Lin et al., 2014], nocaps,11 1 https://nocaps.org and, for video, MSR-VTT [Xu et al., 2016], and VATEX for traditional, short-caption evaluation [Wang et al., 2019]. Newer benchmarks have been developed that focus on detailed, multi-faceted descriptions: DetailCaps [Dong et al., 2024], VDC [Chai et al., 2024], and CapArena [Cheng et al., 2025].

Typical applications of VLMs are summarization, image generation, search and retrieval, image segmentation, and object detection. The Massive Multi-discipline Multi-modal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark (MMMU) for Expert AGI is a comprehensive benchmark for vision-language models [Yue et al., 2024].

7.1.2 Architecture

Now that we have seen the types of tasks that VLMs are tested on, how could we design a model to perform these tasks?

Language, when modeled as a sequence of tokens, is a sequential (1 dimensional) problem domain. Vision, when modeled as a grid of pixels, is a rectangular (2 dimensional) problem domain. Correspondingly, the deep learning architectures for the two applications are different. For language, the transformer architecture is used, finding sequential patterns, and for imaging, the convolutional neural network is used, finding 2-dimensional patterns. It is therefore not obvious what architecture a multi-modal vision-language model should have. Indeed, it was unclear if a VLM would work at all.

Research first focused on the question if the transformer architecture would also be able to work on image processing (in addition to the conventional convolutional neural networks, CNN). Special vision transformers and tokenization schemes were developed that worked well in image processing [Dosovitskiy et al., 2020].

Then, an architecture was needed to combine the language and image embeddings, and to generate language. In general, the architecture of a VLM consists of an image encoder (either a CNN or a specially tokenized vision-transformer) and a text encoder that are connected to an embedding projector to align image and text representations (often a dense neural network), connecting to, finally, a text decoder (a transformer). Figure 7.3 illustrates this architecture, using LLaVa as an example [Liu et al., 2023]. The connection between the visual embedding and the textual embedding is made by a network that projects the visual embedding to another embedding, to allow unified reasoning by the model. The projector network is often a dense neural network (multi-layer perceptron, MLP).

More elaborate architectures have been developed, and the architecture of state of the art VLMs can become quite complex, consisting of multiple transformer modules. As an example, Figure 7.4 shows the generative Stable Diffusion architecture [Esser et al., 2024, Weng, 2021, Yang et al., 2023].

7.1.3 Learning Algorithm

Now that we have seen the tasks and the architecture of VLMs, it is time to look at the type of learning algorithm that is used by the models. The different encoders and projectors allow the VLM to be trained. The training algorithms should align and fuse the knowledge from both the visual and the language encoders. The VLM can then correlate the image and text information so that the model can analyze the query and provide an answer based on the two modalities. The literature reports a variety of approaches for training the VLM.

OpenAI’s CLIP [Radford et al., 2021], which stands for contrastive language-image pretraining, uses contrastive learning. Contrastive learning is a form of self-supervised learning, creating supervisory signals when there are no such labels in the dataset. The idea is to push dissimilar data points apart and pull similar data points together in an embedding space. Contrastive learning maximizes the similarity of representations for positive pairs (such as similar forms of the same image) and minimize the similarity for negative pairs (images of different objects).

Another approach is to use masking. Here the VLM learns to predict randomly obscured parts of an input text or image, just as it is used in language model training. The model learns to reconstruct the hidden pixels in an image given an (unmasked) caption. An example is FLAVA, or foundational language and vision alignment, which uses a vision transformer as image encoder and a transformer for its language encoder and multi-modal projector [Singh et al., 2022].

VLM’s are also used in a generative style, to generate an image based on a text prompt. Popular text-to-image models often use diffusion models [Ho et al., 2022, Yang et al., 2023]. Well-known examples are Google’s Imagen [Baldridge et al., 2024], Midjourney, OpenAI’s DALL-E [Betker et al., 2023] and Stability AI’s stable diffusion [Esser et al., 2024]. DALL-E 2 uses a diffusion model conditioned on CLIP image embeddings. Figure 7.5 shows DALL-E’s well-known surrealistic avocado armchairs.

Pretraining vision language models from scratch is expensive, and since a VLM consists of a language model and a vision model, we could try to see if it is possible to build a VLM out of one or two existing models, that have already been pretrained before. Both a pretrained LLM and a pretrained vision encoder can be used, to which a mapping network can be added that projects the visual embedding to the textual input space of the language model. An example is LLaVA, which stands for large language and vision assistant. LLaVa uses the Vicuna language decoder and the CLIP ViT visual encoder, and their outputs are merged into a shared dimensional space using a linear projector [Liu et al., 2023].

Many vision language models have been developed. VLMs tend to perform well on benchmark tasks and they are often used for decision making in agents. VLMs have become so popular that many current open and commercial LLMs are VLMs: DeepSeek-VL2, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o, Llama 3.2, NVLM, Qwen 2.5-VL.

7.1.4 Results

Let us take a look at how well VLMs perform at captioning and image generation by looking at some of the examples that are reported in the literature.

Vision language models have produced imaginative and inspiring results ranging from visual question answering, object detection, image captioning to text-to-image generation. An example of the test dataset that is used in Flava is shown in Figure 7.6. The successor of DALL-E 2, DALL-E 3, focused on training on highly descriptive generated image captions, yielding even more impressive results [Betker et al., 2023]. Some of the prompt following image generation capabilities of DALL-E 3 are shown in Figure 7.7. Figure 7.8 shows examples from stable diffusion (based on the rectified-flow diffusion models).

7.2 Decisions & Vision Language Action Models

To act, agents must make decisions, and to make decisions, different options must be weighed. As we will see in this section, we can train transformers on episodes of states, actions and rewards {(s,a,r)}\{(s,a,r)\} (see also Section 20.1.2). These models are trained on sequences of language, vision, and robotic actions. Vision-language-action models, VLAs, (Figure 7.9) are trained to output robot API commands, which are a special type of language: the language of commands to steer robotic movement.

The task of a VLA is to understand a visual scene, and, when given a textual command, instruct a robot arm to perform an appropriate action, depending on what the model sees through the camera. These models have shown impressive results of robots generalizing to unseen situations, successfully performing tasks.

7.2.1 Tasks

The main task of VLAs is to perform instructions in the real world, and to do so in a general way, in a changing environment. When a robotic manipulation model has been trained to pick up a set of red pencils, and the task changes to pick up blue pencils, then it would be nice if the model generalizes, and we do not have to assemble a new training set involving blue pencils and re-train the model again from scratch. We also want our model to recognize objects, and recognize when an object is oriented differently, has moved, or the lighting changes. The model should know how to use a robot arm to manipulate objects, and how to perform different actions. See Figure 7.10 for an example, taken from the CLIPort paper [Shridhar et al., 2022].

The hardest task for VLAs is to combine these scenes, objects and actions to manipulations that are complicated combinations of what the model has seen during training, and to generalize to unseen combinations. Especially long-horizon navigation through complex, changing, environments (perhaps even outdoors) is a complex challenge [Shridhar et al., 2022].

In realistic human-robot interaction settings, collecting additional demonstrations is often infeasible. To perform high-level tasks, such as in Figure 7.11, the VLA must be able to recognize objects, their poses, and segmentations of instances. The model must also be able to understand language, and relate the meaning of language to the meaning of visual objects and to the meaning of robotic actions.

As we will see, language provides an intuitive interface for specifying goals and for transferring semantic concepts across tasks. Furthermore, the work on VLMs has shown how to semantically connect different kinds of embeddings.

7.2.2 Architecture

Now that we have seen the task and the challenges, let us look at possible model architectures. Again, they can become quite complex. The transformer architecture is well suited to learn patterns in sequential data, as the results on natural language show. Intuitively, this suggests that transformers may also work well to model sequential decision problems, the type of problems that are often solved in reinforcement learning for robotic action, as we discussed in Section 2.2.3 (and further in depth in Section 20.2.1). These problems consist of a state, from which actions cause the system to enter a new state, which has actions, etc. The transformer architecture is well suited to model these problems.

Early work on decision transformer (DT) [Chen et al., 2021, Janner et al., 2021] showed that on offline (static) reinforcement learning problems, the GPT architecture was indeed able to learn optimal policies. The decision-pretrained transformer (DPT) Lee et al. [2023], Wang et al. [2024a] showed that the basic transformer architectures can be pretrained and finetuned on decision traces. Section 20.1.2 discusses decision traces further.

Following pioneering work on CLIPort [Shridhar et al., 2022, Shridhar et al., 2020], VLAs are often built on VLMs, where the robotic commands are used as regular language tokens. Let us have a closer look at some representative models.

The goal of Mobility VLA [Chiang et al., 2024] is navigation. This VLA is created by combining a long context VLM with topological maps, as illustrated in Figure 7.12.

Mobility VLA is used on a problem category of navigation tasks called multi-modal instruction navigation with demonstration tours (MINT). In this dataset, an environment prior is provided through a previously recorded demonstration video. The model consists of a two-level VLA that combines the environment understanding and common sense reasoning of long-context VLMs with a low-level navigation policy based on topological graphs. The high-level policy is created by combining user instructions from a long-context VLM that finds the goal frame in a demonstration video. Then, a low-level policy starts at this goal frame to traverse a topological graph to generate the robot action instructions at every timestep.

LM-Nav [Shah et al., 2023] uses a different architecture, based on existing models. It takes as input a set of raw observations from the target environment and from free-form textual instructions. From this, it derives an action plan using three pretrained models: a language model (LLM) for extracting landmarks, a vision-language model (VLM) for grounding, and a visual-navigation model (VNM) for execution (not unlike the topological map previously discussed). Together, these models enable LM-Nav to follow textual instructions from visual observations without any finetuning. Figure 7.13 shows an illustration of the approach.

Google’s RT-2 [Brohan et al., 2023] uses a different approach. The idea of RT-2 is to leverage knowledge from the web to inform robotic control: the robot should learn how to act from watching videos. A standard vision language model is finetuned both on textual robotic trajectory data and on Internet-scale vision-language tasks, such as visual question answering. Robotic actions are expressed as regular text tokens and are incorporated directly into the training set in the same way as natural language tokens, as shown in Figure 7.14.

A similar approach is taken by Magma [Yang et al., 2025]. Magma is pretrained on heterogeneous datasets spanning from images and videos to robotics data. However, in Magma the actionable visual objects in images are labeled by special tokens (Set-of-Mark) for action grounding. Similarly, object movements (such as the trace of human hands or robotic arms) are labeled by Trace-of-Mark to ease action planning. Figure 7.15 provides an illustration.

Finally, a VLA called π0\pi_{0} [Black et al., 2024] stresses the reinforcement learning approach by using a pretrained late-fusion vision-language model, as well as a diverse cross-embodiment dataset with a variety of manipulation tasks. The model is inspired by the Transfusion approach [Zhou et al., 2024]. This model is adapted to robot control by adding a separate action expert that produces actions via flow matching, for fluent manipulation skills. The resulting model can either be used directly to perform tasks based on a prompt, or be further finetuned on higher-quality data to enable complex multi-stage tasks, such as folding multiple articles of laundry or assembling a box (see Figure 7.16).

7.2.3 Learning Algorithm

The model architecture of most VLAs is based on VLMs, in some cases augmented with navigation map data. The robotic action commands are typically encoded as regular text commands. Likewise, for pretraining and finetuning typical LLM self-supervised learning algorithms are used, similar to VLMs and decision transformers. Sometimes existing pretrained models are used, to reduce the training expense.

7.2.4 Results

Various VLA models have been created that achieve impressive zero-shot results, generalizing behavior to unseen situations. Chiang et al. [2024], Brohan et al. [2023], Yang et al. [2025] are examples of VLA models for robotic action, achieving complex tasks such as navigation, table top manipulation, or even folding laundry [Black et al., 2024].

VLAs have shown impressive and imaginative results, where robots were able to generalize at inference time without the need for retraining. A survey of VLAs can be found in [Ma et al., 2024].

The results are best appreciated from seeing a video. For π0\pi_{0}, a video is available.22 2 https://www.physicalintelligence.company/blog/pi0 For RT-2, a video is also available.33 3 https://robotics-transformer2.github.io

7.3 World Models, Physics, and Planning

To a VLM, an image consists of pixels without a deeper intrinsic meaning. However, agents that interact with the world need knowledge about physical aspects of that world. The models need an understanding of what is physically possible, so that agents do not walk through walls, as they still sometimes do in video games.

World models help agents understand the world, allowing them to act effectively in the physical world, taking actions that make sense. Originally, LLMs are language models. We can converse with them in natural language, and they necessarily contain some knowledge of the world, but they were not specifically trained to have a wide and deep understanding of worldly affairs. Some researchers argue that in order for agentic LLMs to be truly successful, and for LLMs to reach a high level of general intelligence, research into world models should be strengthened [Sutton et al., 2022, Matsuo et al., 2022, LeCun and others, 2022, Klindt et al., 2026].

Agents and robots that act in the world need a rudimentary understanding of the physics of the world. One of the challenges for training an LLM is to ground its understanding of the physical world and of the possible robotic actions into reality. One way to do this is to learn an agentic model of the world (environment) from feedback on actions.

The term world model has been used in AI in other contexts. Most notably, it refers to the model in model-based reinforcement learning [Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018, Moerland et al., 2023, Sutton, 1991] (see next section). This model contains a local copy of some knowledge of the environment, based on the interactions it has had with the environment, to be used to improve the action policy. The world model contains an efficient, compressed, learned representation of the world [Hafner et al., 2019, Plaat et al., 2020]. The representation of a world model is often called an abstract or latent representation, to contrast it with the regular representation of the real world in the environment. World models are often trained to contain knowledge about physics and certain spatial properties, that puts restrictions on the agent’s actions. The precise contents of the world model depends on the domain in which the agent operates.

Note that in a just few chapters we have progressed from understanding language to understanding the world. The goal of a large language model is to understand some semantics of natural language from statistical patterns in text, to be used for question answering and translation. The goal of a world model is to understand causal relations in the laws of physics, to be used to simulate future world states for our agent. Quite some new technology is necessary to go from LLM to agentic LLM.

We start with a look at how world models are currently used in agentic LLM.

7.3.1 Tasks

World models should encapsulate knowledge of the world, so that an agent can perform meaningful actions. The actions should be grounded in the physical world. For example, the model should understand the limitations of the joints of a robot arm that it is commanding; a navigational agent should understand some physics, such as the concept of gravity, of distance, and that walls are solid objects; a financial agent should understand the consequences of a negative bank balance. Often this is the type of information that humans take for granted, and we are surprised when an agent fails to understand such basic things about the world in which it operates. VLMs that are only trained on pixels may miss the semantic meaning of a specific texture, whether it is a garment, smoke, or a wall.

Standard pretrained LLMs already contain some useful world knowledge. They learn acceptable textual behavior using reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), and acceptable mathematical and coding behavior using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Some early approaches use LLMs as pretrained world model without any finetuning. A natural way to learn about the physics of the world is through interaction: agents can learn acceptable physical behavior through a reinforcement learning-style reward function.

The goal of world models in model-based reinforcement learning is to improve the sample efficiency of learning from interaction, by planning with the world model instead of sampling from the real world. This is especially useful when interacting with the world is more expensive than performing a simulation, as will often be the case in agentic LLM. In the approaches that we will discuss, LLM world models use methods from model-based reinforcement learning (see Section 7.3.5). Currently, world model approaches in LLM are quite diverse. To show which tasks world models are used for in LLMs, we will discuss three examples: WorldGPT, WebDreamer, and WorldCoder.

WorldGPT

The goal of WorldGPT [Ge et al., 2024] is to solve visual question answering and embodied planning tasks, including audio-video question answering. WorldGPT learns a world-VLM from videos. It uses a latent space VLM with external knowledge bases and long-term memory.

WebDreamer

The goal of WebDreamer [Gu et al., 2024] is to improve efficient learning of Web-interaction tasks, such as e-commerce. WebDreamer enables web-agents to simulate actions before execution, and thus be faster and more sample efficient (by not having to act in the real web to gather experience). WebDreamer is a model-based reinforcement learning approach in a web-world. (The name is derived from Dreamer, a series of influential model-based reinforcement learning latent dynamics models [Hafner et al., 2019, Hafner et al., 2020a, Hafner et al., 2023].) Typical tasks are to find products on e-commerce sites. It does so by training a small model from a large model, allowing efficient simulation.

WorldCoder

The goal of WorldCoder [Tang et al., 2024] is also to improve sample efficiency, but the approach is different. WorldCoder improves efficiency by generating the dynamics model (transition function and reward function) in interpretable Python code, which is then used in a standard model-based reinforcement learning design. The generated Python code executes more efficiently than LLM inference does. WorldCoder is used in grid-tasks (Sokoban, see Figure 7.17) and domestic task planning (AlfWorld, see Figure 7.18).

7.3.2 Architecture

The purpose of a world model is to add semantic meaning to observations—actions having consequences—something that LLMs and VLMs may struggle with. When does a pixel belong to a floor to walk on (restrict yy movement) and when is it part of a wall to stop you (restrict xx movement)? A reward function provides feedback information on which actions are good, and which are not. Thus, world model architectures often use a reinforcement learning setting, in which an action policy is trained from feedback rewards. We can think of a world model as a VLM with a policy learner inside.

WorldGPT, WebDreamer, and WorldCoder use different architectures for their world model, which we will now discuss in more detail.

WorldGPT

WorldGPT is based on a standard LLM, Vicuna-7B-v0.44 4 https://huggingface.co/lmsys/vicuna-7b-v1.3, https://lmsys.org It performs reasoning in latent space, following the model-based reinforcement learning approach. The goal of WorldGPT is to be a simulator of realistic dynamics of the world—the transition and the reward function in reinforcement learning. To do so, the architecture helps synthesize multi-modal instruction instances, using a special architecture. At the core WorldGPT follows the common VLM architecture with a central LLM, and a multi-modal encoder and a decoder. To help the model synthesize multi-modal instructions, a cognitive architecture is added to help with specialized or long-term tasks. The architecture adds memory, knowledge retrieval, and context reflection. The context reflection is built on Q-former [Li et al., 2023]. See Figure 7.19 for a diagram of the architecture.

WebDreamer

WebDreamer is aimed at web-interaction. It distills a large model, Qwen-70B [Bai et al., 2025], into a small 7B model. The small model is then used for simulating actions with the world model, before acting in the “real” web-world. It uses model predictive control (MPC) as planning approach [Garcia et al., 1989, Schwenzer et al., 2021] for decision making about website actions, re-planning at each interaction step. WebDreamer leverages LLMs as world model and as value function. The LLM implements both the simulation function (sim) and the scoring function (score), see Figure 7.20. Furthermore, following [Koh et al., 2024], the LLM is used for candidate action generation (in addition to sim and score). The authors employ a two-stage approach: first sampling top-kk actions, and then using the LLM to self-refine unnecessary actions for simulation.

WorldCoder

WorldCoder is a model-based agent that builds a Python program to represent its knowledge of the world. WorldCoder creates a transition function of the world in executable Python code, see Figure 7.21. WorldCoder uses program synthesis. In reinforcement learning, problems are formalized as MDPs, consisting of a state representation SS, action function AA, transition function TT, and reward function RR (see Section 7.3.5). WorldCoder uses an LLM to generate Python code for action, transition and reward functions for a task, as well as for the state representation, which is then used in a model-based reinforcement learning approach. This code is checked and improved, in an iterative self debug refinement process [Chen et al., 2023], see Section 6.1.3.2. This process repeats until the program produces the correct output.

Note that in WorldCoder the learned model is symbolic (the transition function is represented as computer code), where in regular deep reinforcement learning the model is a neural network. At inference time, WorldCoder is efficient, since no LLM calls occur that require forward passes through a large network, only interpretation of the transition and reward function Python code.

In regular model-based LLM approaches, the LLM simulates the world, in WorldCoder the LLM builds a simulation of the world, for later execution. At inference time, the Python interpreter executes the transition function, where in ReAct, an LLM reasons about the world state. For planning problems, the symbolic approach is better suited, since LLMs struggle with planning during inference (see Section 6.2.3).

7.3.3 Learning Algorithm

We will now discuss the pretraining and finetuning algorithms that the different approaches use.

WorldGPT

WorldGPT acquires an understanding of world dynamics by pretraining and finetuning on millions of videos across various domains. Vicuna-7B-v0 is used as the base LLM. Pretraining then uses a language-centric encoder to obtain a unified representation of the multi-modal state. For multi-modal decoding, special tokens are inserted into the LLM’s vocabulary. Training starts uni-modal, and progresses to cross-modal. For finetuning, a special cognitive reinforcement architecture is used with a dataset with fine-grain sequential state-transition sample annotations from more than 10 million videos. As mentioned before, the cognitive architecture consists of memory, knowledge retrieval, and context reflection. Through finetuning, agents acquire specialized knowledge by finetuning on synthetic multi-modal instruction data.

WebDreamer

The WebDreamer approach aims to learn dynamics suitable for model-based reinforcement learning. First the pretrained Qwen-2-VL vision language model [Wang et al., 2024b] is used to initialize the Dreamer-7B model, which is then further finetuned on 3.1 million interaction examples. The data synthesis pipeline consists of (1) random walks over the web, where the model autonomously interacts with web pages through actions such as typing for search and clicking, and (2) synthesis, where Qwen2-VL-72B generates textual descriptions of state changes based on visual snapshots before and after the actions. WebDreamer simulates possible future states for each action over a finite horizon (replanning and retraining according to the model predictive control (MPC) approach, a reinforcement learning approach for adaptive retraining that is used in engineering and control problems).

WorldCoder

WorldCoder uses program synthesis to learn to make a transition function, the function that computes the next state of the world. WorldCoder then performs planning-actions using that coded world model. It initially performs random exploration to initialize a dataset of environmental interactions; it updates its world model using a program synthesis algorithm, generates the code, and then performs planning. Different planners are possible, from depth-limited value iteration (in simple domains) to MCTS (for more complex domains) [Browne et al., 2012].

7.3.4 Results

We will now look at the results of the three approaches.

WorldGPT

The WorldGPT model is evaluated with a multi-modal state transition prediction benchmark. WorldGPT is effective, and understands and predicts the dynamics of complex real-world kitchen and cooking scenarios accurately.

The system is also evaluated as a world simulator, showing that it can generalize to unfamiliar domains. In one experiment, WorldGPT is 30 times faster then traditional diffusion-based methods on audio-video question answering tasks [Ge et al., 2024].

WebDreamer

WebDreamer also performs well. It is reported to surpass GPT-4o performance on web interaction tasks. Substantial performance improvements are reported over reactive baselines, on which it is 4-5 times more efficient than tree search. WebDreamer performs well on the sandbox environment VisualWebArena, and also on real-world websites (Online-Mind2Web and Mind2Web-Live), where tree search methods are difficult to implement and deploy. Moreover, on online benchmarks, using Dreamer-7B, the approach achieves performance comparable to GPT-4o. On real-world websites, WebDreamer outperforms the reactive baseline with a relative gain of 42% and 24%, respectively.

WorldCoder

For WorldCoder results are reported on grid worlds and on task planning (AlfWorld). WorldCoder is more sample-efficient than model-free reinforcement learning, and more compute-efficient compared to ReAct-style agents that try to perform in-context planning by the LLM.

Generating world knowledge as computer code by LLMs brings advantages. It allows prior world knowledge embedded in the LLM to improve code generation, as existing solutions to published problems may well have been seen during pretraining. The code can also be transferred across tasks by reusing pieces of old programs. Furthermore, the results are human readable, allowing the world knowledge to be inspected by humans by reading the generated code.

Though promising for planning problems, a limitation of the WorldCoder approach is inherent to the computational difficulty of planning problems. Problem instances that are difficult to solve with dedicated solvers are also difficult to solve for WorldCoder solvers. The transition function that is generated by the LLM is unlikely to be better than those designed by expert human researchers.

So far, the synthesized code aims to reproduce the transition and reward functions. For future work, self reflection and metalearning approaches may be able to improve performance further.

7.3.5 *Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

World models are being used successfully in agentic LLM. An extensive literature exists on world models in model-based reinforcement learning. At the end of this chapter, we will now provide a brief overview of world models in model-based reinforcement learning, in order to provide more context for the use of world models in LLM.

An influential early model-based approach is Dyna [Sutton, 1991]. Influential recent works are [Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018, Hafner et al., 2020b]. Two modern surveys are Moerland et al. [2023], Plaat et al. [2023].

In reinforcement learning, agents learn how to act in an environment by sampling rewards from actions that are executed in the environment.

7.3.5.1 Model-free Reinforcement Learning

In regular reinforcement learning an optimal agent policy is learned model-free: the best actions for all states are learned directly from interaction with the environment (see Figure 7.22), without the help of an extra model of the environment. Regular reinforcement learning is formally described as a Markov decision process, with four functions {S,T,A,R}\{S,T,A,R\}: a function S⁡(o)→sS(o)\rightarrow s to represent the state of the system for observation oo, a function T⁡(s,a)→s′T(s,a)\rightarrow s^{\prime} that transitions from one state to the next state using an action, a function A⁡(s)→aA(s)\rightarrow a that returns an action for a state, and a function R⁡(s)→rR(s)\rightarrow r that assign a reward value (positive or negative) to a state. The goal of reinforcement learning is to use the MDP to learn an optimal policy π∗​(s)→a∗\pi^{*}(s)\rightarrow a^{*}, the function that returns the best action for each state that the MDP can be in. Thus, a reinforcement learning problem consists of four functions SS, TT, AA, and RR, and the goal of the agent is to find the optimal policy π∗​(s)\pi^{*}(s) with the highest expected cumulative reward. The agent does not have access to TT and RR, functions that reside in the environment. Regular, model-free, reinforcement learning is also called direct reinforcement learning. The direct method naturally has high sample complexity: policy improvement requires sampling, and large MDPs require many samples for the policy improvement process to converge (Figure 7.22).

7.3.5.2 Model-based Reinforcement Learning

In direct reinforcement learning, sampled information is not retained by the agent, but forgotten, and each policy improvement requires a new sample. Interaction by the agent with the outside environment is often expensive, for example for a robot acting in the real world, whose joints wear out. In this case it would be beneficial to find ways to reduce the sample complexity. We should try to improve the policy without having to sample as much from the environment.

A straightforward idea is not to throw away the samples, but to store them in a buffer, and also sample from that buffer of older interaction results, or, slightly more advanced, to train a local surrogate model M=(T^,R^)M=(\hat{T},\hat{R}) of the environment dynamics. When we have trained this local dynamics model, we can also sample from the model, cheaply, in addition to sampling the environment, expensively (see Figure 7.23).

These methods are indirect methods, since, in the last methods, where a local dynamics model is built up by the agent, the policy is learned indirectly (through a local model) from the environment.

Using a local dynamics model is called model-based reinforcement learning. The dynamics model consist of local estimations T^\hat{T} and R^\hat{R} by the agent, estimates of the real TT and RR that are known only to the environment. Model-based reinforcement learning has been successful in some applications, such as Go [Silver et al., 2016], Diplomacy [Bakhtin et al., 2022], StarCraft [Vinyals et al., 2019], and showing learning across domains [Hafner et al., 2020b].

Model-based reinforcement learning also connects to planning, a classic field in symbolic artificial intelligence, that looks ahead into the future, simulating different possible worlds using the efficient latent representation, without having to act in the real world.

7.3.5.3 Dimension Reduction

In deep model-based reinforcement learning, the local dynamics models are also called world models [Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018]. In this context world models reduce high dimensional observation spaces to lower dimensional state and reward spaces, that can then be used in model-based reinforcement learning methods to efficiently improve policy functions. The idea behind world models is that in most high-dimensional environments there are elements that are less important, such as, in a video game, trees in the background that never move, that have little or no relation to the value of the agent’s actions. The goal is to abstract away these unimportant elements of the input space, reducing the effective dimensionality of the state space.

7.3.5.4 Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture

The joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) is proposed by LeCun and others [2022] and further refined in Assran et al. [2023]. The goal of JEPA is to predict future states in an abstract, compressed representation (latent space) rather than trying to recreate raw sensory details or pixels. This goal is similar to the dimension-reduction goal of a world model in model-based reinforcement learning. Where model-based reinforcement learning uses learns a local transition model supervised by rewards, JEPA is a self-supervised representation learning framework. JEPA is trained via self-supervised observation (watching videos or images) to map context embeddings to target embeddings without rewards or explicit actions. Model-based reinforcement learning explicitly incorporates actions, rewards, and control optimization to maximize the return [Lim et al., 2026]. JEPA and reinforcement learning are close, JEPA can be used as a perception engine (world model) for reinforcement learning or planning algorithms, for example to guide robotic control [Destrade et al., 2025].

7.3.5.5 Agentic World Models

In the context of model-based reinforcement learning, LLMs can be used in two different ways. We can use a pre-trained (static) LLM as world model (T^,R^)(\hat{T},\hat{R}) in model-based reinforcement learning (LLM4MBRL). Often this approach uses a tree search or MCTS planning. In this approach, the LLM is used to help reinforcement learning.

Alternatively (model-based) reinforcement learning settings can be used to train LLM world models (MBRL4LLM) with feedback from world-interaction. Now, the LLM has become adaptive, either through an adaptive harness, or by posttraining the model itself, as in a VLA. This approach is also known as agentic world models, and holds much promise for agents to better understand their environment, to act in more realistic ways. In this approach, reinforcement learning is used to help agentic language modeling. This is an active area of research, see, for example, Zuo et al. [2026], including their references.55 5 There is a third connection between reinforcement learning and language modeling. Model-free reinforcement learning is also used inside the LLM training pipeline, for finetuning, as in RLHF and RLVR.

7.4 Concluding Remarks

Transformers can be trained on tokenized language data, but also on other tokenized data. In this chapter we have seen different model architectures for different modalities. Architecturally, the models were quite different. However, most models are transformer based, and tokenization approaches have been devised for a surprising difference in modalities. Let us review the different types of models to see what they have in common:

  • •

    Large language models (LLM) are transformers that are pretrained on tokenized natural language.

  • •

    Vision language models (VLM) are models that consist of a transformer that is trained on tokenized vision data (or a diffusion model, or a convolutional network) and a transformer trained on tokenized natural language, whose embeddings come together in a joint decoder.

  • •

    Decision transformers (DT) are transformers that are trained on tokenized (s,a,r)(s,a,r)-episodes of decision paths (see Section 20.1.2).

  • •

    Vision language action models (VLA) are models that consist of a vision-language architecture that are also trained on tokenized (s,a,r)(s,a,r) episodes of robotic actions.

  • •

    World models are models that consist of a vision-language architecture that are also trained on tokenized (s,a,r)(s,a,r) episodes of real world actions or decisions.

There are other types of models that we have not discussed in this chapter. For example, a large music model (LMM) is a transformer that is pretrained on tokenized musical sequences (which can be either symbolic music (score sheets) or a soundtrack) [Yuan et al., 2025].

This chapter was devoted to advanced models for agents. We discussed language models that were pretrained and finetuned on vision and action. These models understand more of the world, allowing agents to achieve impressive generalization results. We have seen how the LLM, originally a language model, is becoming a world model, a term that is borrowed from the field of model-based reinforcement learning.

At this point it might be good to look back on what we have seen so far. The first part of the book explained how to pretrain models self-referentially for language. Then, Chapter 6 explained how in-context learning emerged, and how it can be used for inference time multi-step reasoning and self-reflection. This chapter discussed pretraining and finetuning methods to yield multi-modal world models of the environment. Together, pretrained language, inference time reasoning, and finetuned world models enable agents more and more to act intelligently and achieve tasks in the world for their users.

We have now discussed many different modalities and training methods. In the next chapter we will take a step back and reflect on how agents can learn in a stable manner, while they are also acting in the world that they learn from.

Chapter 8 Metalearning

8.1 Why Metalearning?

As we have seen, the self-reflecting LLM approaches are powerful, but getting the training processes to converge can be a challenge. In agentic LLM, learning occurs at multiple levels, and sometimes at the same time. In machine learning, algorithms that learn at multiple levels are said to perform metalearning. Metalearning is often described as learning to learn, for example, learning which prompt works better for a certain task. Metalearning can be a powerful concept, but sometimes the different learning levels interfere, and learning stops.

To help us understand why our LLM multi-level learning algorithms sometimes do not work, we will look deeper into metalearning. In this chapter we will discuss how we can improve the stability of dynamic, feedback-rich, metalearning approaches.

The term metalearning is used for multi-level learning algorithms. Metalearning algorithms learn to learn, to quickly solve examples of new, unseen, tasks, that the model has not trained for.

8.1.1 Deep Learning is Slow

Metalearning has a long history in machine learning (see, for example, Schmidhuber [1987], Hospedales et al. [2021], Huisman et al. [2021]). It is inspired by human learning, since humans are said to be able to learn how to learn. Another reason for its development, is speed.

The problem is that regular deep learning is slow. Neural networks for typical deep learning tasks are large, with millions or billions of parameters, and training them requires large datasets, often with millions of examples. Training times for training a network from scratch are long, from hours to months, and only when special parallel parallel hardware (GPU) was employed, did deep learning become successful [Krizhevsky et al., 2012].

At this point, researchers started dreaming about few-shot learning, methods that would achieve high accuracy by training on just a few examples.

8.1.2 Achieving Few-shot Learning

In machine learning, some algorithms are better suited for certain types of problems than others. Furthermore, most training algorithms have elements that can be tuned for performance, such as the learning rate, momentum, the initialization scheme of the parameters, or, for a multi-level algorithm, even the choice of the underlying training algorithm. These elements are called hyperparameters, and they govern how the algorithm learns. Would we be able to learn them?

Different types of problems require different hyperparameter settings. For example, for a smooth dataset, a high learning rate may work well, or a local search algorithm, but for a peaky dataset a lower learning rate works better, or a global search algorithm. The point is that the best hyperparameter configuration in machine learning depends on the task to be solved, and that, crucially, this configuration can be learned. Learning such hyperparameters of the algorithm for different tasks is called metalearning. (In contrast, the learning of the regular parameters of the model is now called base learning.)

The aim of metalearning is to create algorithms that learn certain tasks faster. Instead of using a generic algorithm that is not adapted to the task, starting from scratch, we should use a learning algorithm whose hyperparameters are first matched to the type of task to be solved. The metalearning approach is to first learn from a set of related tasks how to configure the learning algorithm, learning to learn a certain set of tasks faster.

When we have learned the hyperparameter configuration for such an adapted algorithm, we may hope to be able to achieve few-shot training: being able to train on just a few examples, while still achieving high accuracy on examples from a new test task. Metalearning achieves few-shot learning by starting the training not from scratch, but from related knowledge.

Metalearning consists of a (hyper) training loop around a (base) training loop. In classical (non-neural network) machine learning, common hyperparameters are the learning rate, or algorithm selection, where different learning algorithms are tested on training tasks [Brazdil et al., 2022]. In deep learning, the initialization of the neural network weights is often used [Finn et al., 2017].

In agentic LLM, we have also encountered learning at different levels (and we will continue to discuss multi-level learning in the next chapter). It is useful for us to study the theory and insights of the metalearning literature.

8.2 Inner/Outer Loop

As any supervised learning approach, metalearning consists of (1) a meta-train phase, training on a variety of related tasks, and (2) a meta-test phase, testing on a new, unseen, task, to see how well it generalizes to this new task. The goal is to improve generalization by learning a hyperparameter setting of the training algorithm that work well on a wide variety of training tasks.

The process of training the parameters of a model is implemented as an optimization loop, in which a loss-function is used to compute a difference between training examples and current model-estimates. The training algorithm loops over the dataset, each time adjusting the parameters of the model, with the goal to minimize the sum of the loss.

The learning-to-learn concept consists of two loops: an inner training loop to optimize the model’s parameters, and an outer training loop to optimize the algorithm’s hyperparameters. The inner loop optimizes parameters over the examples of one task, the outer loop optimizes hyperparameters over the set of tasks of an application domain.

Each base-learning task 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} has a dataset DiD_{i} and a learning objective, the loss function ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i}. Thus 𝒯i=(Di,ℒi)\mathcal{T}_{i}=(D_{i},\mathcal{L}_{i}). Each dataset consists of pairs of input-examples and labels Di={(xj,yj)}D_{i}=\{(x_{j},y_{j})\}, and is split into a training and a testset Di={Di,t​r​a​i​n,Di,t​e​s​t}D_{i}=\{D_{i,train},D_{i,test}\}. On each training dataset a parameterized model f^θi​(Di,t​r​a​i​n)\hat{f}_{\theta_{i}}(D_{i,{train}}) is estimated, with a loss function ℒi​(θi,Di,t​r​a​i​n)\mathcal{L}_{i}(\theta_{i},D_{i,{train}}). The model f^\hat{f} is approximated with an algorithm that is governed by a set of hyperparameters ω\omega. The particular hyperparameters vary from algorithm to algorithm, but frequently encountered hyperparameters are the learning rate α\alpha, the initial parameters θ0\theta_{0}, and algorithm constants.

The inner loop optimizes the base-parameters θ\theta, and the outer loop optimizes the hyperparameters ω\omega to find the best performance on the set of base tasks with the appropriate test data:

ω⋆=arg​minω⁡ℒ⏟outer loop​(arg​minθi⁡ℒω​(θi,Di,train)⏟inner loop).\omega^{\star}=\underbrace{\argmin_{\omega}\mathcal{L}}_{\textrm{outer loop}}(\underbrace{\argmin_{\theta_{i}}\mathcal{L}_{\omega}(\theta_{i},D_{i,train})}_{\textrm{inner loop}}).

The inner loop optimizes θi\theta_{i} within the datasets DiD_{i} of the tasks 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} , and the outer loop optimizes ω\omega across the tasks and datasets. The outcome of the meta optimization is a set of optimal hyperparameters ω⋆\omega^{\star}.

After metalearning has finished, we have a hyperparameter set (tuned algorithm) that works well for a set of tasks in an application domain, and we can assume that it will generalize well, after training on just a few examples of a new task, scoring high accuracy on testing an unseen example.

Transfer Learning

There is an important connection between metalearning and transfer learning. Transfer learning pretrains the neural network on a single task, and then performs a transfer of the weights to a quick finetuning phase. Transfer learning can thus be regarded as a single iteration of a network-initialization-based metalearning approach: transfer learning is metalearning with just one base learning task.

8.3 LLM and Metalearning

In the field of LLM, we encounter metalearning in many places. A common metalearning approach is to initialize the model parameters to earlier learned knowledge, so that they may train faster on a related task. This is transfer learning, that we find in every standard LLM training pipeline, in the pretrain/finetune phases, where we take the pretrained parameters and finetune them further for a specific task. Metalearning is repeated finetuning, and large language models are a prime example of a metalearning training pipeline that achieves that major goal of machine learning: few-shot learning. In-context learning was one of the major breakthroughs of machine learning [Brown et al., 2020].

When we go to agentic LLM, few-shot learning occurs in many other places as well. We will discuss both static and dynamic forms of metalearning. In static metalearning, weights in inner loops are not influenced by other loops. In dynamic metalearning, they are.

8.3.1 Static LLM Metalearning

We start by reviewing some examples of static LLM metalearning.

8.3.1.1 Pretraining Pipeline

The regular LLM training pipeline is a good example of an elaborate, multi-phase, transfer learning scheme. It achieves good zero-shot performance, in the sense that it can answer many regular queries accurately—where was Mozart born?—based on the pretrained and finetuned knowledge.

The different phases in the pipeline are the inner optimization loops, and the choices of which weights to transfer, and the manual choices of how to finetune in the subsequent phases, can be considered as the outer loop hyperparameter choices.

This is a static form of metalearning, since the weights, once trained in a phase, are not influenced by training results of later phases. Weights are stable between phases of the pipeline. The pipeline is a purely sequential training process.

8.3.1.2 In-Context Learning

Going beyond zero-shot learning, in-context learning is a form of few-shot learning where a few training examples are provided by the user, prompting the LLM to infer a better answer. The pretrained model is the inner loop, the examples in the prompt guide the outer loop.

This is a static form of metalearning, since the values of the weights of the model are not influenced by the examples in the prompt.

8.3.1.3 Chain of Thought

Regular in-context learning provides facts as few-shot examples; it is content-focused. Chain of thought provides process-steps as few-shot examples, it is process-focused.

Again, the pretrained model is the inner loop, the examples in the prompt guide the outer loop, and the weights of the model are static.

8.3.1.4 Static Metalearning is Stable

The regular LLM pipeline consists of transfer learning phases (inner loops), that run in sequence. Once an inner training loop has converged, that phase is not run again. The pipeline is a form of static metalearning. (The results of finetuning are not fed back into the pretrainer again, nor is the pretrainer ran with adjusted hyperparameters based on the finetuning results. The different training phases can not interfere.)

In contrast to static metalearning, there is also dynamic metalearning, where different iterations do interfere.

8.3.2 Dynamic LLM Metalearning

In agentic LLMs different forms of dynamic metalearning are used. In dynamic metalearning the iterations are run concurrently, and can have destabilizing effects on each other’s convergence process.

In previous chapters, we have discussed self-reflection, and RLVR. These are approaches where an inner loop can be changed by an outer loop, and results of one inner loop may affect another inner loop. We have created a moving training target. This may cause unstable divergence of the training process. Training results may also appear brittle: they react greatly to small changes in input values or hyperparameters, such as different random seeds, different prompt reformulations, or even changes in the length of the metalearning process itself. Furthermore, hallucinating tendencies of the base LLM may be amplified when the same model is used in different roles, such as for correction and for generation.

Let us discuss the examples of dynamic metalearning in agentic LLM.

8.3.2.1 Self-Reflection

In self-reflection (Section 6.2.4.2) an agentic harness performs prompt management, calling the LLM in different roles, such as, to evaluate a state, and to refine an answer.

In metalearning terms, the model is the inner training loop, and the harness the outer loop. Although the model itself is static, it is called with different prompts, and the answers of the model are used by the harness to produce new prompts. Therefore, the prompt results (outer loops) start interfering, and may interact in non-linear and non-intuitive ways.

Furthermore, when the same model is used for different roles, imperfections (biases, hallucinations) may be amplified.

8.3.2.2 RLVR

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR, Section 6.2.4.3) is a popular training scheme for code and math applications, where inference-time reasoning results are used for finetuning at training-time.

In metalearning terms, finetuning is the inner loop, and inference-time reasoning is the outer loop. RLVR uses outer loop results in the inner loop, feeding inference results into the training phase, mixing two learning processes. Care should be taken to prevent that inference time errors, which are used as truths, are amplified in the finetuning/inference loop.

8.4 Stabilizing Dynamic Metalearning

Unstable training occurs when inner/outer interference is under-damped. When this happens, oscillation between inner loops and outer loops may grow larger, instead of dying out.

This problem can be mitigated by increased damping, or by decoupling the time by which different inner loops move. For example, the learning rates of one of the loops may be reduced, or the parameters of some of the inner loops may be kept stable for a longer time than the other loops. Another idea is to use a mixture of model types or sizes, such as in Mixture-of-Experts [Jiang et al., 2024]. A student/teacher setup deliberately uses a stronger and a weaker model for the different roles. By using different models, we may hope to dampen hallucinations and interference between inner loops.

In general, when metalearning misbehaves, we should aim to create more diversity, to stimulate exploration, and to prevent greedy behavior that leads to local optima or divergent training. These solutions often require much experimentation to build up intuition about the problem. Debugging agentic LLMs can be challenging.

8.5 Concluding Remarks

As we have seen, we can understand LLM-training as a form of metalearning. Regular LLM training is a form of transfer learning, and inference-time reasoning and training, as is used in agentic LLM, use even more metalearning ideas. Although dynamic metalearning approaches (such as self-reflection) are a powerful concept, care should be taken since interference between inner and outer loops may destabilize the training process. This may happen unexpectedly, in agents that were previously behaving.

When we use a trained model in our agent that interacts with the world, and that agent is also trained using feedback from this interaction, then the model can be regarded as the base learner (inner loop) and the interaction with the world can be regarded as the metalearner (outer loop). All the preceding caveats for in-pipeline metalearning also apply for out-of-pipeline metalearning. Only now, when interacting with the real world, the consequence of errors may be more severe.

Related fields of online machine learning, such as deep reinforcement learning, also suffer from the unstable training and the moving target problem. The field of deep reinforcement learning has introduced many stabilization techniques, such as replay buffers and target networks [Mnih et al., 2015, Hessel et al., 2018]. These methods typically try to decouple the periodicity of the two learning processes, often by slowing down one of them. A similar approach is introduced in Hierarchical Reasoning Models (HRM) [Wang et al., 2025]. HRM consists of a two-layer metalearning approach. Here, too, the learning is stabilized by learning at two different speeds.

Knowledge of such stabilization methods is useful when designing agentic LLM solutions. In the next part we will provide an overview of the different interaction styles by which agentic LLM interact with the world. The styles go from static to dynamic.
