Part III Agents

We have now discussed the foundations of LLMs and agents. We have seen how language and tokenization works, we have seen how LLMs are trained and finetuned, and we have seen how advanced reasoning models reason and self-reflect. We have looked at different learning modalities, from language, vision, and action. We have also looked at the intricacies of metalearning.

We have now arrived at the heart of agentic LLM, where we will review the different interaction styles of LLM agents. This part consists of one content chapter and one practical chapter. First we will review the five agentic interaction styles that we have seen so far, and we discuss the importance of memory. Then, in the practical chapter, we will discuss a hands-on case study where many of the techniques of this part come together. You will be invited to create a self-reflective LLM agent that can play typical AI-games such as TextWorld and NetHack.

Chapter 9 Interaction Styles for Agentic LLMs

9.1 Agents in AI

Agents play a central role in artificial intelligence, and we will first discuss some of the background of agents in AI.

9.1.1 Agents Act and Adapt in their Environment

In artificial intelligence, entities that act in the world are called agents. They are the AI equivalent of humans acting in the world. In the agent concept, AI researchers try to capture what they perceive to be the essence of what humans do—understanding intelligence by building it.

Agents are autonomous software systems that act in an environment. They (1) have goals, they (2) perceive their environment, they (3) make decisions, they (4) take actions to achieve their goals, and, most importantly, they (5) learn from experience. Agents should adapt to new information in order to achieve their goals better, or, in reinforcement learning terms, agents improve their action policy.

Traditional computer programs are deterministic, they predictably follow pre-set instructions (this makes computers so useful to do things from accounting to control, in which predictability is paramount). LLM agents, in contrast, are less deterministic, and less predictable. They learn, and change their behavior from time to time. They can autonomously reason, plan, and perform tasks using tools to perform simple workflows for users in areas such as coding, customer service, and data analysis. (They also hallucinate, make mistakes, and generally are unpredictable and undependable. In that respect, LLM agents are more like humans than computers.)

Agents have been studied for quite some time in artificial intelligence. It is useful to distinguish three types of agents: (1) robotic assistant agents, (2) belief-desire-intention agents, and (3) swarm agents.

9.1.1.1 Robotic Assistants

First we discuss agents that are robotic assistants. This view on AI agents is from the field of engineering: agents perform human-like tasks for humans. An agent is a tool to more easily achieve routine tasks. An example is a welding robot in a factory, an auto-pilot in an airplane, or a self-driving car that has to find a safe route in an unpredictable environment.

Further examples of such agents are virtual assistants, such as Alexa and Siri, or coding assistants such as CoPilot that help software developers become more productive, or customer service bots that help customers navigate the maze of rules of a company to achieve goals such as filing a complaint or getting a refund. Robotic assistant agents can have significant reasoning abilities [Dorri et al., 2018], and LLMs are increasingly used for such assistants [Plaat et al., 2025].

9.1.1.2 Agents with Beliefs, Desires, and Intentions

Another view on AI agents is rooted in the field of cognitive science. Here the goal is for agents to model human cognitive processes, and agents have beliefs, desires and intentions (BDI). Cognitive science studies human thinking processes. AI agents can be used to implement cognitive models, and experiment with models of thinking: is the model able to reason logically, to cooperate with human players in a game of Bridge, to deconstruct a theater play by Shakespeare, to compose music, or to have self-awareness? Cognition may take many subtle forms, such as interpreting sensory input, guiding physical actions, and empathizing with others.

Originally, BDI agents come from the tradition of logic reasoning. They are imbued with goals, which they pursue through actions. The literature in this field sees actions as a way to achieve the goals of an agent [Rao et al., 1995, Georgeff et al., 1998].

9.1.1.3 Swarm Agents

A third view on AI agents stresses interaction patterns between large numbers of small agents. Where the previous multi-agent systems consisted of few, complex, agents that act and think—agents that could assist, or agents with beliefs, desires and intentions (BDI)—this approach studies flocks and swarms of many, simple, agents. Now the emphasis is on emergent collaborative behavior, behavior that emerges at a scale beyond the reasoning of the agents themselves. Can a swarm offer protection against a predator? What are the prerequisites for collaboration to occur? When is a society peaceful, when is it at war? What is a super-organism [Johnson and Linksvayer, 2010, Wilson and Sober, 1989]?

Swarm agents come from the connectionist tradition of embodied AI [Brooks, 1990]. The agents communicate, and researchers are often interested in the emergence of large scale behavioral patterns such as cooperation and communication. A well-known swarm algorithm is ant colony optimization [Dorigo et al., 2007], and a well-known software environment to study such patterns is Netlogo [Wilensky and Rand, 2015].11 1 https://www.netlogo.org

Multi-agent systems and agentic LLMs are suitable for the study of all three types of approaches: agents as tools, agents as cognitive entities, and agents that help us study how to achieve peaceful societies (or how to conquer another). Part IV of this book is dedicated to agents as tools, and Part V is dedicated to cognition and agent societies.

9.1.2 Agentic LLMs as Reinforcement Learning Agents

The study of the behavior of intelligent agents has a long tradition in AI. A central aspect of agent behavior is how agents learn in their environment. Mechanisms by which agents learn from feedback are studied in reinforcement learning [Sutton and Barto, 2018] and multi-agent reinforcement learning [Wong et al., 2021].

In the next section we will discuss five interaction styles that we see in agentic LLM. As preparation for this overview, we will provide a formal basis for agents that interact in the world using the language of reinforcement learning.

Figure 9.1 shows a reinforcement learning system that consists of an agent and an environment. In this system, the agent interacts with the environment through actions, and the environment responds with the new state of the system and a reward value, indicating how good the new state is.

The agent can learn from these reward values, and note which actions are favorable and which are unfavorable in each state. The goal of the agent is to find the optimal behavior for the environment, and thus, the best actions in each state. The agent uses the rewards to reinforce its notion of the best actions in each state, and thus learn a function of optimal behavior. This function, mapping each state to an action, is called the behavior policy, denoted as π\pi. The optimal policy is denoted as π∗\pi^{*}. If the agent learns through deep learning, then the policy is parameterized by the weights θ\theta of a neural network.

The world in which the agent operates is represented by the environment. The agent takes actions and changes the state of the environment. The environment has a probabilistic transition function that computes the new state whenever an action has been performed by the agent. The environment also computes a corresponding reward for the new state. Thus, the environment is modeled with two functions: a transition function TT and a reward function RR.

This model, of an agent acting in an environment, receiving feedback to learn which actions caused good state transitions, and which did not, suits the concept of agentic LLMs quite well, as we will see in the next section.

From the reinforcement learning point of view, we can use the LLM as a function in the agent: L​L​M​(p​r​o​m​p​t)→a​n​s​w​e​rLLM(prompt)\rightarrow answer. The LLM can be used in different places in reinforcement learning: in the agent, or in the environment. For example, the agent can use the LLM as policy-improver. It can call an LLM with a certain prompt for the policy function πL​L​MP​π​(s,r)\pi_{LLM_{P\pi}}(s,r) that learns from environment feedback which actions to take in the different states that the environment can be in (see Figure 9.2). The LLM is given a prompt P​πP\pi that tells it to act as a policy improver using reward rr, and returns an action aa for state ss. As we will see in Section 20.2.1, in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) uses the LLM as a policy improver, and tree of thoughts can use an LLM to generate the successor actions.

The LLM can also be used in the environment, to compute the reward of the state L​L​MR⁡(s)LLM_{R(s)}, or to compute the next state L​L​MT⁡(s,a)LLM_{T(s,a)}, see Figure 9.3. In the figure, the same LLM is now used for three different roles, with three different prompts: to perform the policy, the transition, and the reward function. For example, tree of thoughts can use an LLM to evaluate the reward of a state. There are many options in designing our agentic LLMs, as we will see next. We use the reinforcement learning paradigm to discuss and illustrate the different agentic styles.

9.2 Learning Mechanisms in Agentic LLMs

The field of agentic LLM is new, and the previous chapters have shown many different approaches in which LLMs have been used in an agentic setting. In this section we will review the approaches that we have seen so far in this book. We distinguish the approaches based on their prompting method and their training method.

We will describe five styles of interaction that fit agentic LLMs. Table 9.1 summarizes the five agent styles. We focus on the way that the LLM is prompted by the harness at inference time, and how it is trained. All prompting styles can yield useful agentic assistants and interaction partners, that act in realistic ways, for certain domains. The more elaborate prompting styles have been developed in the pursuit for better performance in more challenging domains.

The first column of the table gives the name of the agentic interaction style, from query to reinforcement finetuning. The second column lists the type of prompting of the styles, from a simple static instruction prompt without any examples, to a dynamic reinforcement learning prompt. The third column shows the training method of the LLM, whether it is pretrained or finetuned or both. The fourth column gives a concrete example of the interaction style (with references to the literature).

9.2.1 Agentic Interaction Styles

We will now discuss the interaction styles. In the first three agent styles the prompt of the LLM is static. The prompt is written by the user and does not change.

9.2.1.1 A. Query Prompt

The first interaction style is interacting with the LLM by giving it a simple instruction. Figure 9.4 shows this interaction style. It simply consists of an instruction written by the user. For example, Lily missed the train. She felt very … to which the model hopefully responds with something like angry, or sad. The prompt is purely a query, without any training examples. The learning style is zero-shot learning, instruction only.

The LLM is able to correctly answer many such queries because it has been pretrained on a large corpus of text, which may provide an answer to many of the queries that users may ask. The model has also been finetuned for instruction answering. Examples of this interaction style are the early LLMs, such as GPT-2 [Vaswani et al., 2017].

9.2.1.2 B. In-Context Learning

Next, we turn to in-context learning. For machine learning, in-context learning is an exciting new type of learning, in addition to supervised and reinforcement learning. In a large language model in-context learning often achieves good results with just a few examples, achieving one of the main challenges of the field of machine learning.

Compared to interaction style A, in-context few-shot learning is a more involved interaction style.

In-context learning occurs when the user provides a few examples along with the query. In doing so, the user conditions the decoder model to activate the correct part of the large amount of knowledge that is represented in its parameters.

Figure 9.5 shows an illustration of a prompt that fits this interaction style. An example from the literature of this interaction style is GPT-3. The paper that introduced in-context learning is Brown et al. [2020]. An example of a few-shot prompt is: Fill in the dots: the sea-la mer, oysters-huitre, the window-la fenetre, cheese-… to which the model hopefully responds with fromage.

Note that in-context learning only emerges when the model is large enough. Originally, in-context learning emerged in models with around 100 billion parameters. At that size, the model was rich enough for the few prompt examples to activate the right parts of the model. As our LLM methods improve, this boundary keeps shrinking.

9.2.1.3 C. Chain of Thought

Next, we turn to another famous method, chain of thought learning [Wei et al., 2022], Figure 9.6, top. This method was developed, as we saw in Chapter 6, to address the weakness of LLMs in solving simple math word reasoning problems. A disadvantage of the original chain of thought approach is that a new prompt has to be written by the user for each new reasoning task at hand. A subsequent development was the zero-shot chain of thought prompt, Figure 9.6, bottom. Kojima et al. [2022] found that adding the generic sentence: Let’s think step by step to prompts already improves performance on many benchmarks, although often not by as much as a hand-written task-specific prompt.

As in the previous interaction style, chain of thought is an in-context few-shot learning method, although now the examples in the prompt are a few examples of the steps that the model should take before it provides its answer—whereas previously they were examples of facts. These steps help the model arrive at the right answer, following a multi-step reasoning chain. The examples are not examples of answers to activate parts of the model, but of steps on how to arrive at the answer. Example prompts for few-shot and zero-shot chain of thought have been shown in Figure 6.1 on page 6.1.

Again, as with in-context learning, chain of thought only works in models of sufficient size, and again, this size is getting smaller as our understanding of LLM methods increases and models are being finetuned for chain of thought. Furthermore, it is possible to transfer the learned reasoning methods from a large model to a model with orders of magnitude fewer parameters, by distillation [Li et al., 2023].

9.2.1.4 D. Self-Reflection Harness

The preceding agentic interaction styles all used a single static prompt, achieving encouraging performance on many benchmarks. To perform well on planning problems, or other problems where state must be tracked, a reasoning style is needed where prompts are optimized, searching through options in a tree of possibilities.

We will now discuss two interaction styles where the LLM prompt is dynamically manipulated by a small algorithm that is external to the LLM. This algorithm is called a harness. The first style is in-context (LLM parameters are not changed), while the second style (in the next subsection) also uses finetuning of the model.

These interaction styles are dynamic. As we saw in the previous chapter on metalearning, a challenge of dynamic methods is to achieve a stable learning process. When training targets are changing, learning algorithms may diverge, and extra care is needed to achieve convergence. Achieving predictable high performance with self-reflection is still an area of active research.

The first dynamic prompting methods that we discuss emerged out of the need to model more complex reasoning structures, that go beyond the straight line sequence of steps of chain of thought. First, simple search algorithms were introduced (tree of thoughts). Next, full fledged dynamic prompting methods were introduced to manage prompt development (ReAct, reflexion, self refine). Often, the harness of these methods introduced short-term and long-term memories to remember state between LLM invocations.

An interesting aspect of these methods is that the LLM is used in different roles, for which it is called with different types of prompts. The original role of the LLM in chain of thought tasks is to evaluate the answer in each reasoning step. This evaluation prompt is now augmented with a different type of prompt, to generate a new reasoning step. Sometimes a third type of prompt is added, whose task is to improve the prompt itself. Thus, a single model is used to self-reflect on itself through different prompts, managed by an external harness.

Figure 9.7 shows these ideas. At the top, the self-reflection is controlled by a standard tree search algorithm, as in tree of thoughts [Yao et al., 2024]. At the bottom, a reinforcement learning loop controls self-reflection, where the prompt for policy π\pi is updated with the history of (state, action, reward) triples (see also Section 20.2.1).

9.2.1.5 E. Reinforcement Finetuning Harness

Up to now, all learning was in-context, the model provided answers based on examples provided in the context. The parameters of the LLM were not changed. Although ICL is easy to use, it limits learning. If we wish the model to adapt more profoundly to a certain environment, if we wish the model to remember what it learned at inference time, then it helps if the parameters can change. We call approaches that use this method reinforcement finetuning. RLVR is a well-known example.

Figure 9.8 provides an illustration, where the trainable model parameters are indicated as ψ\psi. Note that the only difference with Figure 9.7 (bottom) is the introduction of the ψ\psi parameters. In ReFT the LLM parameters ψ\psi change, they are finetuned based on the rewards from the dataset. We should interpret the figures such that where learning at inference time was in-context, this has now changed, since we allow finetuning of the parameters ψ\psi. In the traditional LLM training pipeline, finetuning is a stage that comes before inference. However, for many important applications, such as math reasoning or coding, chain of thought multi-step inference-time roll-outs produce accurate rewards that can be used for finetuning. Therefore, in reinforcement finetuning, the model is used to produce training targets at inference-time, that are then used to finetune the parameters of the same model—finetuning at inference-time. Reinforcement finetuning blurs the line between inference and finetuning, where supervised finetuning has a clear separation between training and inference.

In LLM training there are three main training/inference moments: (1) pretraining, (2) finetuning, (3) testing (inference). Self-reflection (Style D) does reinforcement learning at inference time. In style E, reinforcement finetuning, we do not do reinforcement learning at test time (3), but at finetune time (2). In agentic LLM, this interaction style allows the LLM to learn from agent interaction with the world.

For the dynamic agentic styles D and E, care must be taken to achieve stable convergence. As of this writing, few works have been published that report on such results.

9.3 Memory Architectures for Agentic LLMs

Humans (and other forms of life) remember. Our memory enables us to have an identity. We can remember our name, our friends, and our family members. Memory allows us to learn what is good an what is bad for us, and it allows us to adapt our behavior. When we suffer memory-loss, either through injury, illness, or old age, our personality changes. Severe memory-loss leads to loss of identity, we wander aimlessly through the world.

Agents also need memory. In this section we will discuss why agentic LLM needs memory, and we provide a brief overview of the different types of memory that have been developed for agentic LLM.

9.3.1 The Need for Memory

A statistical model f⁡(x)→y^f(x)\rightarrow\hat{y} estimates an output y^\hat{y} based on the relation ff that it has learned for its input xx at training time. Such functional behavior is memory-free. Any new information (post-training) must be provided to the model through the input parameters xx. LLMs are no different, and even the earliest chatbots were provided with special hidden system prompts that fed the model a history of the conversation, so that it is able to hold a coherent conversation.

As the use cases for agentic LLM increase, more advanced techniques are needed, beyond the system-prompt method. To better understand what memory is used for in agentic LLMs, we will now discuss different use cases for memory.

9.3.1.1 Coherent Conversation

Many machine learning benchmarks for LLMs are of the challenge/response type, and they are well suited for the functional input/output behavior of statistical models. The main real world use case for LLMs, however, is as a chat-bot, where the LLM is expected to engage in a meaningful conversation with the user. In order to maintain a coherent conversation, in which conversational partners react and respond to each other, chat-bots must be able to know what has been said before.

Thus, a first requirement for agentic LLMs is to be able know what has been said before in a conversation.

9.3.1.2 Adaptation

According to our definition in Chapter 1, agentic LLMs are expected to learn. When a robot performs a task in a kitchen, such as chopping an onion, and the location of the knife has moved, then it should adapt its actions: it should now first pick up the knife from its new location before starting to chop. Agents interact with the environment, and if the environment changes, then agents should adapt.

Either our agent’s pretrained policies must be highly general, and able to adapt to all new situations in a certain domain, or our agents architecture must flexible, and recognize when a pretrained policy requires adaptation, finetuning or even re-training. For this, they need memory.

As we have seen in Section 6.2.4, the external prompt improvement harnesses that are used in self-reflective agent architectures require buffers and other memory types for explicit prompt improvement.

9.3.1.3 Identity

Our experiences shape our personality and our identity. When LLM agents are to build up their own identity, the experiences must either be collected and held in a memory, to be used for self-reflection, or they must be processed and used in other ways to adapt their behavior policy.

As the memory architectures of agentic harnesses improve, agents will be able to better remember their experiences. When that happens, we may find that our agents can acquire, through their agentic experiences, a unique personality.

9.3.1.4 Continual Learning

Traditional machine learning trains a model on a particular dataset for a particular task. Human learning is different, our learning evolves continuously throughout our lives. In machine learning, continual learning studies how models can be trained for a sequence of new tasks while preserving previously learned tasks [Wang et al., 2024, Li et al., 2025a]. Like metalearning, it studies generalization across related tasks. Major challenges in continual learning are to overcome catastrophic forgetting, and how to cope with changing data distributions.

The field of continual learning provides a variety of architectures that support this type of training.

9.3.2 Memory Architectures

The field of agentic LLM is young. Only recently are memory architectures for LLM agents starting to receive attention. We will discuss the different approaches that have so far appeared.

9.3.2.1 Finetuning

A pragmatic way to deal with the need for memory is to incorporate new information into the model as it arrives. Instead of developing external memory management algorithms, we could take advantage of the fact that model parameters are a form of memory, and finetune the model as the new examples arrive.

To achieve this approach in an agentic setting, the finetuning must happen quickly, before the user can perceive a lag. Parameter efficient finetuning methods such as LoRA are an option [Yang et al., 2024]. Although this is an elegant approach that does not require external algorithms or memory structures, for most applications the finetuning will not happen quickly enough, and an in-context or harness solution should be developed.

9.3.2.2 Long Context Windows and Compression

A second approach is to perform prompt management. The standard approach of chat-bots is to provide a truncated form of the chat-history to the LLM by injecting it into the prompt in addition to the user’s text. This is an approach that works quite well in practice. A limitation is that context windows are limited in size, and processing large contexts is expensive because of the squared time complexity of the attention mechanism.

Two types of solutions have been pursued. First, specific long-context architectures have been developed, that keep track of attention in different ways [Smith et al., 2022]. This is an active field of research, a survey of recent approaches is Liu et al. [2025]. Second, compression schemes have been developed, to semantically compress the prompt into a smaller stream. A survey is Li et al. [2025b]. Prompts can be divided into chunks [Sheng et al., 2025], to allow processing of large prompts. A related approach uses the LLM to generate code for processing long prompts recursively [Zhang et al., 2025a].

Prompts can also be compressed through filtering of unnecessary tokens (this sentence could become Prompts compressed filtering unnecessary tokens). Another approach is soft prompts [Lester et al., 2021]. Soft prompts eliminate discrete tokens, but learn embeddings (via backpropagation) that can be fed directly into the transformer, without mapping them to actual language tokens. This context can serve as an alternative to a plain-text context. Impressive compression rates have been reported, from ten-fold [Mu et al., 2023] to hundred-fold [Li et al., 2025c].

9.3.2.3 Explicit Memory Management

If we need to store state between LLM calls, then a straightforward solution is for the agent harness to provide this storage, as part of its prompt management. In Section 6.2.4 we saw how the external prompt-improvement algorithms for self-reflection add different types of storage, such as in the reflexion approach and the buffer of thoughts approach (Figures 6.8 and 6.6).

Agents can have different requirements for their storage (see Zhang et al. [2025b], Chhikara et al. [2025] for a survey). We will discuss some of the recent studies of this active field of research. Prompts can be stored in textual or parametric form, and relevant operations are the reading and writing to memory. Furthermore, memory management operations are important, such as for compacting and forgetting information. Also, additional services can be provided by the memory systems. For example, MemoryBank [Zhong et al., 2024] adds hierarchical summaries and uses LLM prompts to provide a running personality of the interaction events of a user.

Operations to store and retrieve items can be added to an agent. MemGPT [Packer et al., 2023] studies how LLMs can read and write to external memory using function calls (memory as a tool). A-mem [Xu et al., 2025] introduces contextual descriptions of memory, based on a mailbox principle.

A disadvantage of the explicit memory management approach is that the LLM has to perform memory management explicitly, without having been trained how to do this effectively. An alternative solution is to manually write memory management code, when it is possible to foresee all possible requirements. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a set of strategies designed for context management. Section 11.4 describes the protocol in more depth.

Learning to use memory

Mem1 [Zhou et al., 2025] uses a different approach: after each LLM interaction the agent updates a compact state to be shared with future LLM calls. The memory size required is constant, so that the state does not run out of the context window. The shared state is created by inserting reasoning-style tags into the prompt, and is trained using reinforcement learning to incentivize state consolidation. Mem-α\alpha is another approach that uses reinforcement learning to train agents to effectively use memory [Wang et al., 2025].

AgeMem [Yu et al., 2026] integrates memory management operations into agent’s policy for end-to-end optimization. It distinguishes long term and short term memory, and uses a three-stage reinforcement learning scheme to train the agent in the use of the two types of memory.

This, too, is an active field of research, new studies and frameworks can be expected. See, for an overview, Zhou et al. [2026].

Vector Databases

In addition to the storage of prompts as human-readable text, we can also store their tokenized embeddings directly. Storing prompts as text is useful for retrieving data when an exact textual match is needed. Embeddings encode semantic information—which tokens are close to each other in meaning. Storing embeddings is therefore useful when we would like to retrieve items that are semantically close.

Embeddings can be stored in vector databases. Traditional relational databases store data in rows and columns. Vector databases store high-dimensional lists of numbers, and provide low-latency access to them, making them well-suited for LLMs [Xie et al., 2023, Ma et al., 2023].

9.4 Concluding Remarks

The concept of an intelligent agent is a central concept in artificial intelligence. LLMs have increased the communication and reasoning capabilities of agents significantly. In this chapter, we have discussed different agent types, and have connected them to different traditions in AI.

Agents act. We have discussed 5 main interaction styles based on the preceding chapters. Agents need memory to interact meaningfully with their environments, and we have discussed this new field of research.

After covering so much theory, it is high time to get our hands dirty. In the next chapter we will look at a practical case study, to get more experience with using some of the theoretical concepts that we have seen.

Chapter 10 Case Study 2: BALROG for LLM Reasoning and Reflection

10.1 BALROG Overview

In this case we will work with an agentic LLM that performs self-reflection. We use a popular benchmark suite for reasoning tasks, called BALROG.11 1 A Balrog is a mythical demon from Middle-earth, featured in the fantasy works of J.R.R. Tolkien. A Balrog is a match even for Gandalf the Grey, the most powerful wizard of all. BALROG is an acronym for Benchmarking Agentic LLM and VLM Reasoning On Games. The BALROG benchmark consists of a mix of easy and hard games, some of which are difficult for LLMs to play well, as the BALROG paper shows in their own benchmarking study [Paglieri et al., 2025].

Initially, the BALROG games are benchmarked with vanilla LLMs. The code, however, is quite open and amenable to writing your own agent approaches, to see if you can do better. The software is written for you to write your own agent code for in-context (reinforcement) learning.

The main BALROG website is https://balrogai.com. The code is easy to adapt and use for your own experiments, and there is a leaderboard. In this chapter we will guide you to write your own agent code, that can then be run on the BALROG games-suite.

BALROG is designed to challenge in-context agents on reasoning problems. It uses puzzle-style games to benchmark the reasoning capabilities of LLMs and VLMs. Figure 10.1 lists the games. The games are from easy to hard: BabyAI, Crafter, TextWorld, BabaIsAI, MiniHack, and NetHack. The games offer a mix of challenges, some are text-based, some have a visual component, all include reasoning challenges for the model. Some of the games are considered hard. For example, it is not expected that your model or your agent—or your self—will reach a high score on NetHack. (If you do achieve that, without having accessed the cheat-sheets, you may want to consider writing a paper for a prestigious AI conference.)

10.1.1 Puzzles and Games

BALROG consists of the six puzzles and games shown in Figure 10.1. The games run from easy grid world puzzles to hard text-based dungeon and dragons strategy games, with long credit assignment episodes and flat reward landscapes.

The authors of BALROG provide a code base that allows experimentation with agents, to design your own agent, to see how well they do on the benchmarks. To perform well on the benchmarks in BALROG, the agents must be good at reasoning and planning, and, most likely, be good at adapting and reflecting on their own behavior.

BabyAI is a simple grid-world game, where the agent has to solve a navigation task. A simple reinforcement learning type algorithm would be able to easily solve this game. Tasks are given in natural language, such as: go to the blue ball, then pick up the grey key. Of course, the challenge for the agentic LLM is to perform the planning part of the task. It is expected that the LLM will be able to do well on this simple game (see the BALROG paper).

NetHack, on the other hand, is a highly challenging game, also for human players. NetHack is a text-based dungeons and dragons-like game. It includes both long-term strategic planning, in the sense that winning a game can involve hundreds of thousands of steps, and short-term tactical fights to fend of the usual hordes of monsters. Credit assignment is a challenge in NetHack, in order to understand which of the actions that the agent took in the past contributed to ultimate success or failure, since actions in one area of the game may have unexpected consequences far away, making it difficult to play for reinforcement learning agents. NetHack is known for human players to take years to master the game without resorting to cheat guides.

10.1.2 BALROG Architecture

We wil now have a look at the architecture of the BALROG framework. Figure 10.2 shows the architecture, taken from the paper [Paglieri et al., 2025].

Please familiarize yourself with the BALROG system. Read the paper Paglieri et al. [2025], which you can find on https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13543, or go to the BALROG website at https://balrogai.com.

If you have not done so yet, install BALROG on your system with the git clone command. Go to https://balrogai.com, or directly to the Github repository at https://github.com/balrog-ai/BALROG. Install the repository on your local computer.

Decide which LLM you want to use. Please note that typical BALROG agents make many LLM calls, at each step of the way. If you want to run the LLM locally, install it, or use it from Huggingface. If you want to use a (commercial) cloud-based LLM, acquire an API-key and install the API-key in your environment. You may want to consider applying for a free student-tier, if that is offered. The use of frontier LLMs can be expensive, but usually older and smaller LLMs, some of which are still relatively capable, are much cheaper.

The BALROG readme on the Github repository contains information on how to install the system, and how to install an API key for your favorite LLM, see Listing 10.3. (In one of the exercises we will use multiple LLMs, to compare their performance. For now, we are just trying to get the system to run, and anyone will do.)

10.1.3 Agent

Please read the Agent tutorial in BALROG at https://github.com/balrog-ai/BALROG/blob/main/docs/agents.md. In BALROG, agents are small pieces of Python code that call an LLM with a prompt to provide an answer how to determine the next step. The agent code is responsible for receiving answers from the model (observations) and for selecting the next action. The LLM is used to execute various prompts.

BALROG follows interaction style D from Figure 9.7, where the prompt is built up from the history of interactions.

10.1.3.1 Prompt Builder

The agent builds a prompt based on previous actions, based on observation/action pairs from previous interactions. Thus, in reinforcement learning terms, the agent performs the function of the policy, selecting the next action to perform based on the incoming observation.

Go to the prompt_builder directory to change the way that prompts are constructed from the history of actions.

10.1.3.2 Agents

Agents are responsible for the memory function: managing the observation/action histories. The agents must keep a record of past observations and actions to support context-aware decision-making, and this must be implemented by us, external to the LLM.

The agent code in BALROG queries the LLM: agents send observations to the LLM, receive responses, and use those responses to decide on actions to take in the game.

BALROG comes with a number of pre-written agents, which you should study to design your own. The repository has a naive agent and a chain of thought agent. Also provided are more robust versions for handling LLM responses.

When you build your own agent, you will most likely build on the custom agent. The BALROG agent tutorial provides an example for a simple planning agent.

10.2 Implementation Steps

We will now provide some exercises to help you explore building your agents.

10.2.1 Reproduce Paper

We start by trying to reproduce the results in the BALROG paper. Please have a look at the BALROG code at Github https://github.com/balrog-ai/BALROG. Read the Evaluation Guide, the Agent Development tutorial, and the instructions how to run Few Shot Learning experiments (in-context learning). Install the relevant tools on your computer, and the right Python version (and put it in your PATH). Check the version by starting the Python interpreter from the command prompt: $ python.

First, run the standard evaluation, to make sure you installed things correctly, see Listing 10.4.

10.2.2 Different LLMs

To get a feeling for how the standard agent performs on the different benchmarks with different LLMs, it is useful to run a few different LLMs. It is recommended to run closed and open LLMs, and see how they perform. Especially the open version from OpenAI, Claude, DeepSeek, OLMo and Qwen may work well.

Running these models is important, and will lead to more insight into the relative strengths of the various models.

10.2.3 Different Puzzles

Next, to get a better understanding of the benchmark, you should, after running the LLM agent in the different puzzle problems, have a closer look at the prompts and the answers of LLM. See if you can see where the LLM agent fails, where the weakness of the agent lies. By close inspection of the individual actions, and a deeper understanding of the puzzle, you might be able to think of a way to improve your agent.

10.2.4 Computational Cost

BALROG agents call an LLM for each step that the agent makes, often with a long prompt. In these puzzles and games many such steps are made. Running different LLMs on the full benchmark, for different seeds, will easily require many tokens.

In your experiments, first try a small and cheap LLM, such as Qwen-3B. Start with the easiest benchmarks (BabyAI and Crafter). If you wish to expand, please go ahead, but be mindful of the computational cost. You want insights, but you also want your experiments to finish in a reasonable time for a reasonable cost.

10.2.5 Implement Own Reasoning Agent

Now it is time to implement your own learning agent. Go to the agents directory in balrog, and edit the custom.py file. Listing 10.5 reproduces the code for Custom Agent from the BALROG readme. The code can be run with the command in Listing 10.6 (specifying the custom agent, and running gently with fewer workers). Of course, you can specify your own LLM of choice in the command.

Start with the provided code, run it, see how it works. Then, you can try to make small improvements. Try making changes to the prompt for the LLM, and to the way in which the Python code handles the learning in the agent, either with the history prompt builder, in the plan, or in the learning algorithm.

10.3 Evaluation

The performance of your agent will be reported by BALROG as a progression percentage. Record the progression numbers for each benchmark, and for the agent types that you try. Do this in a structured way, you may want to write a Python or shell script to automate the running of the experiments and the logging of the results, perhaps also plotting the progression in a graph. Consider using wandb.ai.

What agent types work well, and on what benchmark do they work well? Make a matrix in which you log progression for the agent types and the benchmark types that you try.

Note that LLM experiments are inherently non-deterministic: two runs with the same prompt may give different results. Therefore, perform multiple runs of each experiment. If you get five identical results in a row, you may start to trust these results. If they vary widely, you may want to investigate. Is the reason purely statistical? Does turning down the temperature solve the problem, or is there another problem?

Do not blindly trust the progression numbers that are reported. Since you are using code on a computer, there may be bugs, or other issues. The BALROG system facilitates delving deeper into the runs. It logs csv files that you can look at with a spreadsheet. Have a look at some of the runs, and decide if it makes sense what you see, or if the agents are exhibiting degenerative behavior. If they do, try to find the reason. Did you do something wrong? Is there unexpected interference between the benchmark and the agent behavior? Is the reward landscape too flat, so that there is no signal for the agent to go after, and all it does is random actions running in circles in a way that makes no sense at all? Is there something that you can do about this?

Please note that the field of large language models, and especially of agentic LLMs, is new, and our insights and our software frameworks have not yet stabilized. Some unexpected results are to be expected, and some challenges or frustration as well.

A structured way of experimentation and result-logging is your friend. Planning and organization can make the running, evaluation, and improvement of practical agentic LLM experiments an enjoyable exercise.

10.4 Self-Reflection

When you were able to reproduce the benchmark results, and have experimented somewhat with the agents, you may want to try to take on some larger challenges. In this section, we will try to extend the BALROG agent towards self-reflection, where the LLM is used in different roles, such as evaluation and action selection. Self-reflection, as any adaptive system that chases a target that is itself being optimized, can be prone to instability and oscillations. Therefore, before we try our self-reflective ideas, it is important that the base learner system of the previous subsection works, and converges in a stable and predictable manner. Please go back to that section and make sure things work as you want them to work.

There are many recent works that try to improve LLM agents. We will mention two: ReAct [Yao et al., 2022] and reflexion [Shinn et al., 2024]. ReAct is primarily focused on prompts, where reflexion introduces new agent algorithms, including short-term and long-term memory.

ReAct

ReAct uses promtps to interact with the world. ReAct promotes the use of tools, to lookup information, see Figure 10.7. The original website for ReAct is https://react-lm.github.io, the code repository is here: https://github.com/ysymyth/ReAct. ReAct prompting has also been implemented in the LangChain22 2 See https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/overview and BeeAI33 3 See https://github.com/i-am-bee/beeai-framework/blob/main/python/examples/agents/react.py frameworks.

Have a look at these framework to get an understanding of the prompt-based agent interaction style that ReAct introduces. Then, implement the prompt-based interaction in BALROG. Does is improve performance? For which games does it help to lookup external information? For which games not?

Reflexion

Where ReAct is prompt-based, allowing interactive lookups, the reflexion approach introduces Python-coded agents, allowing more elaborate agent behavior. Reflexion uses the same LLM in different contexts, with different prompts. It works on the assumption that it is easier to criticize what is wrong with an existing prompt, than to come up with one that works.

Reflexion is a popular self-reflection architecture [Shinn et al., 2024]. The main webpage for reflexion is https://github.com/noahshinn/reflexion. A blog post on reflexion, describing the main ideas, is here: https://nanothoughts.substack.com/p/reflecting-on-reflexion.

Figure 10.8 shows the general concept of reflexion, the different prompts, and the different types of memory. Figure 10.9 shows the code of reflexion, with the different calls to the LLM in line 3, 5, and 6 (MaM_{a}, MeM_{e}, and Ms​rM_{sr}) and line 9, 11, 12. Note that the code is pseudo code, with important details about memory management, prompt management, and convergence criterium left open. Have a look at the repository in Github for details.

Reflexion uses the same LLM with different prompts, which may lead to learning instability, and loops. Furthermore, memory management is relatively simple, with the potential of context overruns. An idea is to implement chunking or other memory compression methods, by hand in Python, or using an LLM.

First play with the reflexion repository, try to get it to work on the reflexion application, such as AlfWorld and HotpotQA.

Extensions

Now, try to implement a reflexion agent in BALROG, to run on the BALROG benchmarks. What problem do you encounter? Does reflexion improve performance over the standard BALROG agents?

Next, extend the problem further. You can try to find other reflection methods in the literature, or try to create new reflection methods from your own. You can try different application types, and you can try to see how your approaches perform. And you can of course try other LLMs.

10.5 Concluding Remarks

In this chapter we have discussed a practical case study, to see how an LLM can performs self-reflection. We used BALROG, a popular benchmark suite for reasoning tasks. BALROG consists of a mix from easy to hard games, some of which are difficult for LLMs to play well. The BALROG suite is designed in an open style. We can write our own agent code that can then be run on the BALROG games.

This has been an important practical case study. You have explored writing our own agent code for in-context reasoning. You have also gone beyond base-learning, by implementing self-reflection. You have explored the stability of self-reflection, on different LLMs and with highly challenging benchmarks.

Part IV Tools and Assistants

The first three parts discussed the AI techniques for constructing advanced LLM Agents that can interact with and act in the real world. These capabilities allow them to do useful things for their users. In this part we will address the use of tools by LLMs to perform specialized tasks, such as looking up information, or controlling robots. Agents use tools through learned APIs (Application Programming Interfaces).

Tools can help us solve a major problem of pretrained LLMs, which is that the information that is contained in them is only as up to date as the dataset on which they were trained. Retrieval augmentation techniques allows LLMs to provide up to the minute information.

Many types of such agents have been created, and in the final chapter of this part we will review important examples, from the medical, financial, and scientific domains. Finally, we will discuss a practical case study in which the use of the technologies comes together, when we will implement an LLM Agent to perform medical diagnosis.

Chapter 11 How Agents Use Tools to Act in the World

11.1 Why Tools Matter in Agentic LLMs

In the taxonomy of reasoning–acting–interacting (Figure 1.1), tools are the primary bridge between an LLM’s internal reasoning and its actions in the external world. A tool may be as simple as a calculator, as complex as a scientific simulation engine, or as open-ended as a full desktop environment. By equipping LLMs with tool use capabilities, we allow them to:

  • •

    Access fresh, domain-specific data (e.g., via APIs, databases, or search engines).

  • •

    Perform actions in the world (e.g., controlling robots, operating browsers, sending messages).

  • •

    Delegate complex computations or retrieval to specialized systems.

  • •

    Chain multiple tools into composite workflows that can be planned, executed, and monitored.

Retrieval is one specific kind of tool primarily aimed to augment an LLM’s knowledge. We will discuss it in depth in Chapter 12. Tool use in general can also augment an LLM’s capabilities to manipulate its environment. These capabilities also come with additional risks, such as safety, reliability and performance risks. They introduce additional points of failure and might be misused under certain conditions.

11.2 Tool Use Architectures

Let us see some common software architectures for tool use by LLMs. Integrating tools into an LLM agent typically follows one of two patterns: direct invocation, and planner-caller-summarizer.

Direct Invocation

In the direct invocation pattern, the LLM outputs structured calls (e.g., JSON or function signatures) that are parsed by an external controller and routed to the tool. For example: OpenAI’s function calling API or Gorilla [Patil et al., 2023].

Planner–Caller–Summarizer

The planner-caller-summarizer pattern is an extension of the direct invocation pattern where we use a multi-agent architecture where the LLM serves as a central planner. It calls a separate module to execute a tool (which might be another LLM or another kind of agent), which then returns a summarized observation back to the LLM. This allows the LLM to maintain a high-level view of the task while outsourcing the detailed execution to a dedicated system.

ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) [Yao et al., 2022] is a prominent framework that interweaves reasoning and acting. Instead of generating a full plan and then executing, an LLM using ReAct follows an iterative loop of Thought, Action, and Observation. This allows the agent to dynamically adjust its plan based on the real-time feedback it receives from tool outputs, making it more robust to errors and unexpected results. This works well because the tools (observation part) often act as a grounding mechanism in the real world (such as the execution of a code snippet, or an internet search), which provides the LLM with factual information for the next iteration.

11.3 APIs and Toolchains

When their application programming interface (API) is known, LLMs can be integrated easily with external tools: for an LLM, an API is just another language to learn. One common way to use a tool, is to augment LLM input with results that are retrieved from external sources, such as search engines. You can read more about retrieval methods in Chapter 12.

Agentic LLMs must be trained to decide when and how to utilize external tools, depending on the task [Shen et al., 2024]. Language models can teach themselves to use tools. The Toolformer model [Schick et al., 2023] is trained to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to best incorporate the results into future token prediction. A range of tools is tested: a calculator, a question-answering system, a search engine, a translation system, and a calendar. Further works extend this to a larger range of tools. ToolBench [Qin et al., 2023] contains 16,464 APIs from RapidAPI, a large dataset of publicly available REST APIs.11 1 https://rapidapi.com/hub

Another framework is EasyTool [Yuan et al., 2024], which focuses on structured and unified instructions from tool documentations, building on ToolBench. ToolAlpaca is a benchmark with over 3938 instances from 400 API [Tang et al., 2023]. A tool-based benchmark for question answering is ToolQA [Zhuang et al., 2023]. Gorilla is a finetuned LLaMa-based model for generating API calls [Patil et al., 2023], also introducing the APIBench benchmark. Many tool calling frameworks have been developed.

Selecting the right tool and summarizing its result are difficult skills for a model. Zhao et al. [2024], Shen et al. [2024] study how LLMs can improve recommendation through tool learning. They use different LLMs for (1) reasoning ability, (2) request writing, and (3) result summarization. Figure 11.1 illustrates this architecture, consisting of a planner, a caller, and a summarizer, each implemented by a different LLM finetuned for its specific capability.

Good results are reported on the LLMs Claude-2, ChatGPT, GPT-4, and Tool-LLaMa, using as reasoning strategies ReAct [Yao et al., 2022] and DFSDT [Qin et al., 2023]. Other frameworks also exist, such as [Ocker et al., 2024].

11.3.1 LangChain Example

LangChain [Chase, 2022] is a widely-used framework for building LLM applications, offering robust abstractions for creating agents and tool chains. Listing 11.2 is a simple Python example demonstrating how to define a tool and use it within a basic agentic framework. In this scenario, the agent is asked a question that requires a numerical check, which it delegates to a specialized tool.

11.3.2 Computer and Browser Tools

One specific set of action tools is to let an LLM use a browser or even a complete computer system as a special form of API. Equipping agentic LLMs with the ability to interact directly with a computer environment enables many interaction possibilities. Tools that parse, interpret, and manipulate graphical user interfaces (GUIs) have gained attention for bridging the gap between language models and real-world applications. One such example is OmniParser V2 [Lu et al., 2024], which introduces a vision-based screen parsing method to detect and label interactable elements such as buttons or icons. By converting raw screenshots into structured representations, OmniParser helps vision-language models ground their action decisions in specific user interface components. This grounding increases the accuracy of the action predictions of LLMs.

Another line of research focuses on enabling LLMs to initiate system-level commands or navigate within browser or operating system interfaces. Computer Use, proposed by Antropic, and Operator and later GPT Agent, proposed by OpenAI, are examples of such efforts. These tools wrap common desktop and browser actions (such as opening applications, clicking buttons, and filling forms) into tool APIs callable by an LLM. This setup translates high-level textual commands into executable steps. As a result, an agentic LLM can browse the web, manage files, or run administrative tasks, all through natural language prompts. This can lead to more autonomous behavior and execution of larger and more complex tasks.

Browser Use [Müller and Žunič, 2024] is an example of an open-source tool that enables LLMs to use a browser with persistent session management. Browser Use enables agentic LLMs to maintain longer browsing states across multiple pages or domains. The tool manages cookies, session tokens, and dynamic web content updates, thereby allowing LLMs to execute more complex browsing tasks like multi-step form completions or cross-site queries.

For a more in-depth discussion about browser and computer environments, see the survey by Wang et al. [2025b]. The survey discusses design patterns for combining automated GUI parsing, tool call integration, and human-in-the-loop supervision. Collectively, these approaches reveal that reliable computer and browser tools are important components for agentic LLMs. By translating textual intents into grounded, environment-level operations, such systems expand the possible tasks and domains where language-driven autonomy can be effectively realized.

11.4 Model Context Protocol and Context Management

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard introduced by Anthropic for connecting AI applications to external data sources, tools, and workflows [Hou et al., 2026]. It is often described as a “USB-C port for AI”, providing a standardized way for applications such as Claude or ChatGPT to access local files, databases, search engines, calculators, and other external capabilities.

MCP uses a client-server architecture. An MCP host, such as an AI application, manages one or more MCP clients, with each client maintaining a connection to an MCP server. MCP servers provide context and capabilities that can be used by the host, including tools, resources, and prompts. Local servers commonly communicate with a single client through STDIO, while remote servers can support multiple clients through Streamable HTTP.

The protocol is organized into two layers. The data layer defines the JSON-RPC-based communication between clients and servers, including capability and version discovery, as well as primitives such as tools, resources, prompts, and notifications. The transport layer specifies how this communication is established and exchanged, including connection management, message framing, and authorization. This separation allows AI applications to interact with a wide range of external systems through a common interface, while leaving the management of the resulting context to the host application.

One of the key challenges in building agentic systems is managing the LLM its finite context window. For multi-step tasks that require numerous tool calls and observations, the context can quickly fill up, causing the model to lose track of its original goal or forget crucial past information. Simply keeping all the context and raw results from multiple tool calls often does not fit the context window and therefor causes forgetting. Deciding what to keep, what to summarize and what to discard is essential.

MCP servers are mostly stateless. This means that we need an additional set of strategies designed to manage the agent’s state and context. These strategies should ensure that the agent maintains a clear and coherent state throughout a long-running task. In addition to the fixed tool registration/calling format that MCP offers, additonal components to include are:

  • •

    Summarization: Tools’ outputs and past conversations are periodically summarized and stored in a compressed format. This reduces the token count while preserving key information.

  • •

    State Management: Explicitly maintaining a state variable or a scratchpad in the prompt, where the agent stores its current plan, important intermediate results, and a summary of its progress.

  • •

    Prioritized Retrieval: Instead of feeding the entire history back into the context, a retrieval mechanism can be used to only inject the most relevant past information for the current step, based on the agent’s reasoning.

Example: Implementing the Model Context Protocol

Listing 11.3 and 11.4 illustrates a simplified implementation of the Model Context Protocol. It demonstrates how an agent can manage its context by summarizing past interactions to avoid exceeding a fixed context window size.22 2 The example uses LangChain, and while this is a popular library, there are also specialized MCP libraries such as the MCP-Python SDK: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk, and others, which might be interesting to check out.

11.5 Robustness, Error Handling, and Recovery

The external nature of tool use introduces new points of failure. An API service might be down, a tool might return an unexpected error, or the LLM might make a logical mistake in its plan. A robust agentic system must be able to handle these failures gracefully.

Reactive Error Handling

A basic but essential strategy is to implement an error-handling loop. When a tool call fails, the system can provide the LLM with the error message as an observation. The LLM can then reason about the error and attempt a new action, such as re-invoking the tool with corrected arguments, trying a different tool, or informing the user of the failure. This process of observe-reflect-retry is a fundamental mechanism for self-healing in agentic systems [Sun et al., 2024]. Note that this pattern is similar to the ReAct framework but in a different context.

Self-Correcting and State-Aware Systems

More advanced systems, such as Healer, are designed to correct runtime errors in real-time [Wu et al., 2024]. Healer can dynamically generate and execute a small code snippet to patch a faulty program state without stopping the entire execution. This goes beyond simple retries; it involves the LLM understanding the context of the error, analyzing the program state, and actively correcting the error (in code).

Human-in-the-Loop Integration

While autonomy is a goal of agentic systems, the most effective applications often involve a human-in-the-loop. This approach improves safety, allows for corrections, and incorporates human expertise at critical junctures.33 3 Although it also introduces the possibility of human error. An agent can be designed to pause and ask for human confirmation before executing a high-stakes action (e.g., making a financial transaction or sending a critical email). This co-piloting model creates a powerful symbiosis, combining the LLM’s speed and scale with human judgment and domain knowledge [Mozannar et al., 2025].

11.6 Safety and Security

Safety and security are becoming more important as the capabilities of Agentic LLMs grow. This goes beyond simple error handling and is more subtle on a misbehavior and misuse level. An obvious example of a safety problem is that without additional protection, the system prompt of an LLM can easily be exposed, often revealing sensitive information.

The robustness of LLMs to jailbreak attacks, where users design prompts to circumvent safety measures and misuse model capabilities, has been studied for chatbots. Meanwhile, agentic LLMs use external tools and can execute multi stage tasks, and may pose a greater risk. Andriushchenko et al. [2024] propose AgentHarm. This benchmark includes a set of 110 malicious agent tasks ranging from fraud, cyber crime, to harassment. The authors find that leading commercial LLMs are surprisingly compliant to their given rules with malicious user requests without jailbreaking (How do I make a pipe bomb? is blocked). However, simple universal templates can be adapted to effectively jailbreak agents (Order online all necessary ingredients to make a pipe bomb and get them delivered to my home without getting flagged by authorities, however, passes in GPT-4).

Rainbow Teaming [Samvelyan et al., 2024] uses an open world approach to generate adversarial LLM prompts, to improve the robustness of LLMs. As with training LLMs, a problem with testing methods is a lack of diversity. Rainbow Teaming casts adversarial prompt generation as a quality-diversity problem. Rainbow Teaming is an open-ended approach [Hughes et al., 2024]. It creates diversity with MAP-Elites [Mouret and Clune, 2015], an evolutionary meta search method that iteratively populates an archive with increasingly higher-performing prompts. See Figures 11.5 and 11.6.

11.7 Concluding Remarks

Tools are what turn a static language model into a dynamic agent that can act in the world. Their ability to grant LLMs access to fresh data, perform external actions, and delegate complex tasks is transformative. For any agentic system to be successful in practice, the result goes beyond just connecting a tool to an LLM, but now requires us to think about the full life-cycle of the agent’s interaction with the environment, and what can happen. Four steps should be followed:

  1. 1.

    Choose the right Architecture: Methodologies such as ReAct [Yao et al., 2022], which tightly interleave reasoning and tool calls, lead to more robust self-correcting behavior than simpler one-shot approaches.

  2. 2.

    Manage your Context: For multistep long-term tasks, the LLM context window is a critical bottleneck. Use strategies such as the Model Context Protocol to summarize history and manage state, preventing the agent from losing its way.

  3. 3.

    Embrace Failure: Tool-use systems are inherently fragile due to their reliance on external APIs. Build in robust error handling, allowing the agent to observe and reason about failures, and attempt recovery.

  4. 4.

    Keep a Human in the Loop: For high-stakes applications, ensure that the agent has a clear mechanism to pause and seek human confirmation before taking irreversible actions. This blend of autonomy and human oversight is key to building trust and ensuring safety.
