Chapter 12 Search and Retrieval in Agentic LLMs

12.1 Retrieval in General

Before examining how agentic LLMs consult external knowledge, it is worth situating retrieval within its own, much older, disciplinary history. Information retrieval (IR) is a mature field of computer and information science that predates neural networks by decades. Many of the ideas that power modern retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pipelines are direct descendants of classical information retrieval research. The standard reference works of the field, Salton and McGill [1983] and later Manning et al. [2008], still provide the conceptual vocabulary such as: indexing, term weighting, ranking and relevance, that this chapter builds on.

12.1.1 Bag of Words

Early information retrieval systems represented documents and queries as bags of words and asked a deceptively simple question: which terms make a document a good match for a query? Spärck Jones [1972] gave this question a statistical answer with the notion of inverse document frequency (IDF), observing that terms occurring in few documents are more discriminating than terms that occur almost everywhere. Weighting terms by how frequently they occur in a document (term frequency, TF) and how rare they are across the collection (IDF) yields the TF-IDF family of weighting schemes, still one of the most widely deployed representations in production search systems.

Term frequency counts how often a term tt occurs in a document dd:

TF⁡(t,d)=ft,d∑t′∈dft′,d\mathrm{TF}(t,d)=\frac{f_{t,d}}{\sum_{t^{\prime}\in d}f_{t^{\prime},d}} (12.1)

where ft,df_{t,d} is the raw count of tt in dd. Inverse document frequency, following Spärck Jones [1972], down-weights terms that occur in many documents:

IDF(t,D)=log|D||{d∈D:t∈d}|\mathrm{IDF}(t,D)=\log\frac{|D|}{|\{d\in D:t\in d\}|} (12.2)

where DD is the document collection. Combining the two gives the classic TF-IDF weight of term tt in document dd:

TF​-​IDF​(t,d,D)=TF⁡(t,d)×IDF⁡(t,D)\mathrm{TF\text{-}IDF}(t,d,D)=\mathrm{TF}(t,d)\times\mathrm{IDF}(t,D) (12.3)
12.1.2 Vector Space Models

Salton et al. [1975] formalized this idea into the vector space model, representing every document and query as a vector in a high-dimensional term space and ranking documents by their cosine similarity to the query vector. The vector space model established a pattern that persists directly into today’s dense retrievers (Section 12.3): reduce documents and queries to points in a shared geometric space, and let distance or similarity stand in for relevance.

More formally, in the vector space model, each document dd (and query qq) is represented as a vector of term weights, d→=(w1,d,w2,d,…,wn,d)\vec{d}=(w_{1,d},w_{2,d},\dots,w_{n,d}), typically using TF-IDF weights (Eq. 12.3). Relevance is then approximated by the cosine similarity between query and document vectors:

sim⁡(q→,d→)=cos⁡(θ)=q→⋅d→∥q→∥​∥d→∥\mathrm{sim}(\vec{q},\vec{d})=\cos(\theta)=\frac{\vec{q}\cdot\vec{d}}{\lVert\vec{q}\rVert\,\lVert\vec{d}\rVert} (12.4)

Documents are ranked by decreasing sim⁡(q→,d→)\mathrm{sim}(\vec{q},\vec{d}). This same operation, cosine similarity between two learned vectors, reappears in dense retrieval (Section 12.3), the only difference being how the vectors are obtained. Where the vector space model used raw term co-occurrence, modern dense retrievers such as dense passage retrieval (DPR) [Karpukhin et al., 2020] use learned neural embeddings, but the underlying geometric intuition is unchanged.

12.1.3 Latent and Sparse Representations

Two further developments bridge classical and modern retrieval. First, Robertson and Zaragoza [2009] developed the probabilistic relevance framework, which treats retrieval as a problem of estimating the probability that a document is relevant to a query given its term statistics. This framework produced BM25 Robertson et al. [1994], a term-weighting and ranking function which ranks document dd for query qq as:

BM25⁡(q,d)=∑t∈qIDF⁡(t,D)⋅ft,d​(k1+1)ft,d+k1​(1−b+b​|d|avgdl)\mathrm{BM25}(q,d)=\sum_{t\in q}\mathrm{IDF}(t,D)\cdot\frac{f_{t,d}\,(k_{1}+1)}{f_{t,d}+k_{1}\left(1-b+b\,\dfrac{|d|}{\mathrm{avgdl}}\right)} (12.5)

where |d||d| is the length of document dd, avgdl\mathrm{avgdl} is the average document length in the collection, and k1k_{1} and bb are free parameters that control term-frequency saturation and length normalization, respectively (typical values: k1∈[1.2,2.0]k_{1}\in[1.2,2.0], b=0.75b=0.75). BM25 remains the sparse-retrieval baseline referenced throughout the hybrid retrieval discussions in Section 12.3.

Second, Deerwester et al. [1990] introduced latent semantic analysis (LSA), which applies singular value decomposition to the term-document matrix to uncover latent topics and match documents by meaning rather than by exact term overlap. LSA was the first widely used technique to address the vocabulary mismatch problem, the same problem that motivates dense and semantic retrieval today.

LSA operates on the term-document matrix X∈ℝm×nX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, where mm is the vocabulary size and nn the number of documents. Its entries are typically TF-IDF weights (Eq. 12.3). Applying truncated singular value decomposition,

X≈Uk​Σk​Vk⊤X\approx U_{k}\Sigma_{k}V_{k}^{\top} (12.6)

retains only the kk largest singular values in Σk\Sigma_{k}, producing a rank-kk approximation of XX. Documents and terms are then represented in this reduced kk-dimensional latent space, where semantically related terms and documents lie close together even without exact term overlap.

The final bridge from classical IR to the neural retrieval methods used throughout this chapter is the emergence of learned, dense vector representations of words. Mikolov et al. [2013] showed that simple neural network architectures, trained to predict a word from its context, produce continuous word embeddings that capture rich syntactic and semantic regularities. This work, together with the encoder architectures that followed, supplied the representational building blocks on which dense retrieval, DPR-style bi-encoders, and ultimately retrieval-augmented generation are built.

Retrieval, in other words, is a decades-old discipline concerned with a single enduring question: given a query, which pieces of a large collection are actually relevant to it? What has changed with the arrival of LLMs is not the question but the stakes: models now consult retrieved evidence not merely to rank documents for a human reader, but to condition their own generation. We will now discuss why that shift matters.

12.2 Why Retrieval Matters for Agentic LLMs

Building on this foundation, large language models introduce a new reason to care about retrieval. LLMs are frozen snapshots of world knowledge. The LLM’s parameters can not contain information that was generated after the corpus was fixed. LLMs struggle when tasks require timely, proprietary, or long–tail information that was absent at pretraining time. Retrieval augmentation mitigates these limits by consulting external sources at inference time and conditioning generation on the retrieved evidence.

Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) methods have been developed to integrate data from external knowledge bases with the pretrained knowledge stored in the parameters of language models. Most RAG approaches work at inference time, although some can work during finetuning or even pretraining. Most RAG approaches work on unstructured (textual) data sources. These text documents are indexed to increase efficient access, and they can be organized and a knowledge graph can be created. Finally, database-type query optimization is often performed, where queries can be expanded or complex queries can be split into sub-queries [Cong et al., 2024].

This simple idea, popularized by early systems such as REALM [Guu et al., 2020], DPR [Karpukhin et al., 2020], and RAG [Lewis et al., 2020], has grown into a rich design space spanning indexing, query planning, re-ranking, citation and attribution, and continuous data refresh. Recent surveys synthesize the landscape and evaluation practices [Gao and others, 2023, Huang and others, 2024, Yu and others, 2024, Sharma and others, 2025, Peng and others, 2024].

When to retrieve.

Retrieval is most beneficial when: (1) the task is knowledge-intensive (definitions, entities, numbers, references), (2) the domain shifts rapidly (news, prices, docs), (3) transparency is required (with citations), or (4) models must respect strict source-of-truth constraints (compliance portals, internal wikis). In agentic settings, retrieval can be interleaved with tool use and planning (see Chapter 11).

12.3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipeline

A practical RAG system typically implements the following seven stages:

  1. 1.

    Indexing: The indexing phase is the first step. This step involves: Taking all raw source material, such as HTML pages, PDFs, tables, or code, and converting it into clean, consistent text. Keep important structure as metadata (headings, anchors, timestamps, authorship). Break content into chunks with meaningful boundaries (e.g., sentences or sections) and small overlaps so context isn’t lost. Create two types of searchable representations: sparse ones, like BM25 (a classic term-matching method) or SPLADE  [Formal et al., 2021] (a more modern variant that expands terms), which are good for exact keyword matches; and dense ones, which are embeddings that capture meaning for semantic matches. Storing both lets the system find exact matches (IDs, numbers) and semantic matches (paraphrases, synonyms) in the same search.

  2. 2.

    Query Construction: Turn the user’s question into one or more precise search queries. This can involve rewriting the question for clarity, breaking complex questions into sub-questions (multi-hop), adding related terms (query expansion), or even generating a hypothetical answer to use as a search target (HyDE) [Gao et al., 2023]. For structured data sources, generate specific queries such as SQL or graph lookups. The aim is to make the search engine understand exactly what to look for.

  3. 3.

    Candidate Retrieval: Use the constructed queries to pull in potentially relevant chunks from the index. Dense retrievers (e.g., DPR [Karpukhin et al., 2020], Contriever [Izacard et al., 2022]) match by meaning; sparse methods (BM25, SPLADE) match by exact terms; hybrids combine both. To search quickly at scale, use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes like HNSW [Malkov and Yashunin, 2020] or IVF-PQ [Jégou et al., 2011]. For code or images, use specialized encoders. This step is about casting a wide net without losing focus.

  4. 4.

    Re-ranking: Take the pool of retrieved candidates and reorder them by relevance using more accurate but slower models, like cross-encoders (BERT, MiniLM). Late-interaction models such as ColBERTv2 [Santhanam et al., 2022] balance quality and speed. This ensures that top results are the ones most likely to answer the question.

  5. 5.

    Context Assembly: Remove duplicates, ensure coverage of different aspects of the query (diversity), and prefer recent or domain-relevant sources. Bundle the selected passages, along with their metadata (source, URL, date), into a context package to feed into the LLM. This gives the model a curated, trustworthy information set.

  6. 6.

    Grounded Generation: Ask the LLM to generate the answer using the provided context, with citations for each claim. If evidence is insufficient, the model should abstain or ask for clarification. Some systems, such as Self-RAG [Asai et al., 2023], decide on the fly whether to retrieve more information. The focus is on answers that are both correct and well-supported.

  7. 7.

    Attribution and Logging: Show the sources alongside the answer so readers can verify claims. Log the entire process including queries, retrieved documents and versions, for debugging, evaluation, and compliance. This makes the system transparent and auditable.

A straightforward RAG system follows the seven‑step pipeline outlined above. Listing 12.1 shows Python‑style pseudo-code for this process. The function takes a user question, rewrites it into one or more search queries, retrieves and re‑ranks candidate passages, assembles a context window and finally generates an answer while tracking which passages were used. We will go into more details below.

12.4 Adaptive Retrieval Methods

Traditional RAG systems retrieve a fixed number of passages regardless of whether any retrieval is actually needed. This always–on strategy simplifies engineering but can hurt both efficiency and accuracy. Recent research explores adaptive or gated retrieval strategies that teach the model to decide when to search and how much evidence to consult. These methods align with the self‑reflection ideas introduced in Section 6.2.4: rather than blindly ingest retrieved text, the language model introspects about its own confidence and triggers retrieval only when it recognizes a knowledge gap.

Concretely, Asai et al. [2023] propose Self‑RAG, which trains a single model to generate answers, request retrieval, and critique its own outputs using special reflection tokens. When the model’s draft answer is uncertain, it emits a <RETRIEVE> token to call the search tool and incorporates the retrieved passages in the next step. Experiments show that this learned gating improves factuality over static RAG while avoiding unnecessary calls.

A more lightweight approach is Self‑Ask [Press et al., 2022], where the model decomposes a complex question into simpler sub‑questions, issues them to a search tool, and uses the answers to compose a final response. Self‑Ask can be combined with planning agents, enabling models to interleave reasoning, tool calls, and retrieval. Graph Toolformer [Zhang, 2023] extends this idea by training a policy to insert search queries into a program graph. At inference time the LLM dynamically decides whether to retrieve from a text index, a knowledge graph, or a database, based on the current state of reasoning.

Beyond these specific examples, adaptive retrieval can be implemented in several ways:

  • •

    Confidence‑based Gating: The model estimates its uncertainty (e.g., from entropy or calibration metrics) and triggers retrieval when confidence falls below a threshold.

  • •

    Iterative Retrieval: Rather than pulling all evidence at once, the system retrieves a few passages, reasons about them, and then decides whether additional rounds of search are needed. This approach is useful for multi-hop questions.

  • •

    Query Planning: An agent decomposes the user query into sub‑tasks, dispatches them to different tools (search, database, calculator), and integrates the results. Retrievers are called only when the plan requires external knowledge.

  • •

    Learning to Retrieve: Reinforcement learning or supervised finetuning can teach the model to emit <RETRIEVE> tokens at appropriate times. Self‑RAG is one instantiation; other methods explore training retrieval policies end‑to‑end with the generator.

Adaptive retrieval reduces latency and cost by avoiding unnecessary searches, and it often improves answer quality by focusing attention on missing knowledge. Designing effective gating policies, however, requires careful evaluation (see Section 12.7) and may demand additional supervision during training.

12.4.1 Adaptive Retrieval via Self‑RAG and Self-Ask

The Self‑RAG framework of Asai et al. [2023] teaches the model to request retrieval on demand by emitting a special <RETRIEVE> token during generation. The pseudo-code in Listing 12.2 sketches how such a loop operates. The model maintains a growing context and alternates between generating output tokens and pulling in new evidence when needed.

Self‑Ask [Press et al., 2022] on the other hand is not dependent on the language model. 12.4.3 Query Rewriting and Expansion

Effective retrieval often starts with transforming the original question into a form that the index can match. Large language models can act as query re-writers by paraphrasing, expanding acronyms, adding synonyms or even producing a hypothetical answer to use as a pseudo‑query (the HyDE technique).11 1 HyDE stands for Hypothetical Document Embeddings and generates a plausible answer which is then embedded and used to retrieve supporting passages [Gao et al., 2023]. Listing 12.5 sketches a simple function that calls an LLM to produce multiple rewrites and expansions and then merges the results into a set of search queries.

In practice, the rewrite_question function might call an API such as OpenAI’s gpt-5 to generate paraphrases and hypothetical answers, then use a thesaurus or entity‑linking tool to add aliases. Query expansion improves recall but can also introduce noise.

12.5 Beyond Text: Graphs, Code, Tabular Data and Multi-Modal

While most RAG systems operate over unstructured text, many agentic applications require reasoning over structured data, source code, or images. Extending retrieval beyond plain text opens up new opportunities but also introduces modeling challenges.

Graph‑RAG

A knowledge graph encodes entities as nodes and relations as edges. Building a lightweight graph over the corpus allows the retriever to follow links (e.g., works for, located in) rather than relying solely on bag‑of‑words similarity. The GraphRAG survey formalizes a three‑step workflow: graph‑based indexing, graph‑guided retrieval, and graph‑enhanced generation [Peng and others, 2024]. Indexing extracts entities and relations from text, canonicalizes them and builds neighborhood structures. Retrieval then expands the query through the graph to find related nodes and associated passages; this supports global reasoning and disambiguation. Finally, the generation model can use the graph structure to organize facts into a coherent narrative and avoid contradictions.

12.5.1 Graph‑based retrieval example

GraphRAG systems represent knowledge as a graph of entities and relations and use graph traversals to retrieve relevant nodes [Peng and others, 2024]. A lightweight implementation can be built with the networkx library. In the example in Listing 12.6 we construct a small knowledge graph and implement two simple retrieval primitives: (1) get the immediate neighborhood of an entity, and (2) find the shortest path between two entities. These operations can support multi‑hop reasoning.

In a full GraphRAG system the graph nodes would store pointers to the original text passages, and the retrieval procedure would return both the sequence of nodes and the associated passages to the LLM. Graph‑guided retrieval can reduce hallucinations by grounding reasoning in explicit edges and by encouraging consistency between related facts.

Code‑RAG

Source code has a rich syntax-structure. The semantics of source code differs from natural language. For code retrieval to be effective, it should index at the function or module level, including signatures, docstrings, abstract syntax trees (ASTs) and dependency graphs. Models such as CodeBERT [Feng et al., 2020] learn joint embeddings for code and natural language; they support tasks like natural‑language code search, code summarization, and documentation generation. In Code‑RAG, the retriever can fetch relevant functions, APIs and test cases, and the re-ranker can use code‑aware cross‑encoders or graph neural networks to prioritize exact matches. Retrieved code snippets, comments and dependency metadata are then provided to the LLM, which can answer questions, suggest fixes, or generate new code while citing the source files. Evaluation should consider correctness of the code, type safety and adherence to dependencies.

12.5.2 Code retrieval example using ASTs and embeddings

Retrieving source code requires understanding its syntax and semantics. An easy approach is to embed code snippets and natural language queries with a pretrained model such as CodeBERT [Feng et al., 2020]. Another complementary approach is to parse the code into an abstract syntax tree (AST) and search its structure. The example in Listing 12.7 demonstrates both: we embed functions with CodeBERT for semantic search and use Python’s ast module to extract function definitions and docstrings for indexing.

This example indexes the functions in an imported module and performs a cosine similarity search between the query and the encoded source code. In practice one might combine code embeddings with lexical features (identifiers, comments) and incorporate AST‑based matching to handle structural queries (e.g., find all functions that call a specific API). Code‑aware retrieval is essential for agentic systems that need to read, execute or modify existing code during tool use.

12.5.3 Multi-modal and heterogeneous sources
Tabular and other heterogeneous documents

Existing RAG approaches face critical limitations when applied to heterogeneous documents, comprising both textual and tabular components [Yu et al., 2025]. A primary challenge is Structural Information Loss. When tabular data is linearized or chunked for text-based RAG, its inherent relational structure, the interdependence of rows and columns, is compromised. This loss of structure impedes the LLM’s ability to perform accurate multi-hop heterogeneous reasoning. This indicates that merely converting non-textual data to text is insufficient. To address these challenges, hybrid frameworks such as TableRAG [Yu et al., 2025] have been proposed, that unify textual understanding and complex manipulations over tabular data.

TableRAG employs SQL programming and execution to treat table-related queries as indivisible reasoning units, thereby enhancing both computational efficiency and reasoning fidelity. Similarly, MixRAG [Zhang et al., 2025] has been shown to significantly improve retrieval performance for heterogeneous document RAG, which demands joint retrieval and reasoning across textual and hierarchical tabular data.

The success of these approaches demonstrates that a purely neural (embedding-based) RAG approach is insufficient for structured data. The integration of symbolic reasoning (e.g., SQL) alongside neural retrieval is a critical design pattern for heterogeneous RAG, reflecting a broader trend in Agentic LLMs towards neuro-symbolic integration for enhanced data understanding and fidelity.

Multi-modal RAG

Many knowledge bases contain tables, figures, diagrams, audio and video. A straightforward approach is to extract any textual content using OCR and treat the remainder as plain text. A richer approach stores embeddings for images or other modalities (e.g., CLIP or ViT representations) and pairs them with captions and context. Queries can be encoded jointly across modalities, allowing the system to retrieve relevant figures or equations that accompany the text. For example, a research agent might retrieve a plot and its caption to answer a data‑analysis question, or an educational agent might fetch diagrams from a textbook.

Multi-modal RAG remains an active research area. Challenges include cross‑modal alignment and efficient indexing of high‑dimensional embeddings. Furthermore, non‑textual evidence should be properly grounded in the generated answer.

12.5.4 Multi-modal retrieval example

Agentic systems sometimes need to retrieve images, diagrams or audio clips in addition to text. Multi-modal models such as CLIP or Contrastive Language‑Audio Pretraining (CLAP) embed both natural language and other modalities into a shared space. The high‑level pseudo-code in Listing 12.8 outlines how to use CLIP to find images relevant to a textual query:

The multimodal retrieval returns the filenames of the most similar images. In a RAG setting the retrieved images could be fed through a vision encoder to extract captions or objects, which are then incorporated into the context for the language model. Multimodal agents can thus ground their outputs in both textual and visual evidence.

12.6 Agentic RAG: Beyond Simple Retrieval

While traditional RAG systems augment LLMs with external knowledge, they are often passive, relying on a static, pre-defined pipeline. A significant and recent advancement is the concept of Agentic RAG, which integrates autonomous AI agents directly into the retrieval-augmented generation pipeline [Singh et al., 2025]. This paradigm shift moves RAG from a mere tool to an active, intelligent, and agent-driven process. Agentic RAG systems are characterized by their ability to dynamically manage retrieval strategies, iteratively refine contextual understanding, and adapt workflows to meet complex task requirements.

Agentic RAG represents a more sophisticated form of a retrieval loop, where the LLM agent itself is responsible for orchestrating the retrieval process. This differs from simpler RAG methods by embracing a continuous feedback loop that is fundamental to advanced agentic systems. Rather than a single-shot query transformation, the agent can actively refine its queries based on intermediate results and ongoing interaction. This approach addresses the limitations of conventional RAG systems, which are often constrained by static workflows and lack the adaptability required for multistep reasoning and complex task management [Singh et al., 2025].

12.6.1 Key Components of Agentic RAG

Agentic RAG frameworks typically incorporate several key components that enable their dynamic behavior:

  • •

    Dynamic Query Generation: The agent formulates queries based on its current understanding of the task and the retrieved context, allowing for more precise and effective searches. This can include query expansion, decomposition, or rewriting in response to initial retrieval failures.

  • •

    Iterative Refinement: The agent evaluates the quality of the retrieved information and, if necessary, initiates a new retrieval cycle with a refined query. This iterative process ensures that the final response is grounded in the most relevant and accurate information.

  • •

    Autonomous Tool Use: The agent can select and use a variety of tools, including different retrieval models (e.g., dense vs. sparse), ranking algorithms, and external APIs, to optimize its retrieval strategy. See Chapter 11 for additional information on how an agent can use tools.

  • •

    Self-Correction and Reflection: The agent can assess its own output for accuracy and completeness. If it detects a hallucination or an unsupported claim, it can trigger a new retrieval and reasoning process to correct the error.

The rise of Agentic RAG indicates a shift in the role of RAG in LLM systems. Retrieval shifts from a passive data lookup to an active, intelligent capability that is integral to the agent’s cognitive functions, allowing for more sophisticated, adaptive interactions with external knowledge sources. This shift is crucial for developing robust and reliable LLM agents capable of handling complex, real-world tasks.

12.6.2 Real-Time and Streaming RAG

While traditional RAG systems are effective for static data, they are often not designed for applications that require continuous, real-time information. This section looks into the architectural considerations and challenges of RAG systems that operate on continuously updating, high-throughput data streams. Examples of such streams are found in news feeds, social media, or financial markets. For streaming data, simply querying an updated static index no longer suffices. Retrieval now involves dynamic index management and continuous knowledge assimilation.

In traditional RAG systems, designed for static data, preprocessing is slow, and unsuitable for real-time analysis [Zhu, 2025, Sankaradas et al., 2025]. How should we maintain data freshness and semantic coverage under memory budgets and high data ingestion rates? Methods such as StreamingRAG [Sankaradas et al., 2025] try to overcome these issues with knowledge graphs that evolve dynamically in real-time.

LLM agents for dynamic domains such as medicine, logistics and finance, must have access to real-time, continuously updated information. Static RAG would yield obsolete or inaccurate information in such fast-changing environments. In many agentic applications real-time RAG is necessary for advanced, timely, and reliable information.

12.7 Evaluation

Evaluating a retrieval‑augmented system is more difficult than evaluating a stand‑alone language model because both the retriever and the generator contribute to the final answer. Good evaluation should separate these components and also judge their joint behavior.

Retrieval metrics

For a given query, we compare the retrieved passages to a set of gold documents. Standard metrics include:

  1. 1.

    recall@k (Eq. 12.7) and precision@k (Eq. 12.8), the fraction of relevant documents retrieved among the top kk

  2. 2.

    mean reciprocal rank (Eq. 12.9) and mean average precision, which capture ranking quality

  3. 3.

    normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) (Eq. 12.10), which weights higher ranks more heavily

BEIR presents a heterogeneous benchmark of 18 datasets covering tasks like question answering, fact checking and entity retrieval; their experiments show that late‑interaction and re‑ranking models improve zero‑shot performance but at increased cost [Thakur et al., 2021].

KILT evaluates knowledge‑intensive tasks under a unified Wikipedia snapshot and measures both task performance and provenance, encouraging models to cite the passages they used [Petroni et al., 2021].

Recall​@​k=|{relevant documents}∩{top-​k​ retrieved}||{relevant documents}|\mathrm{Recall@}k=\frac{|\{\text{relevant documents}\}\cap\{\text{top-}k\text{ retrieved}\}|}{|\{\text{relevant documents}\}|} (12.7)
Precision​@​k=|{relevant documents}∩{top-​k​ retrieved}|k\mathrm{Precision@}k=\frac{|\{\text{relevant documents}\}\cap\{\text{top-}k\text{ retrieved}\}|}{k} (12.8)
MRR=1|Q|​∑i=1|Q|1ranki\mathrm{MRR}=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{i=1}^{|Q|}\frac{1}{\mathrm{rank}_{i}} (12.9)

where ranki\mathrm{rank}_{i} is the position of the first relevant document for query ii.

nDCG​@​k=DCG​@​kIDCG​@​k\mathrm{nDCG@}k=\frac{\mathrm{DCG@}k}{\mathrm{IDCG@}k} (12.10)

with

DCG​@​k=∑i=1k2reli−1log2⁡(i+1)\mathrm{DCG@}k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{2^{\mathrm{rel}_{i}}-1}{\log_{2}(i+1)}

and reli\mathrm{rel}_{i} the graded relevance of the document at rank ii.

Generation metrics

Once context is assembled, we must assess the quality of the generated answer. Automatic metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore are of limited use because there is often no single ground‑truth answer. More appropriate are faithfulness and helpfulness. Faithfulness is often measured via entailment models. It works as follows for generated output yy and retrieved context xx (Eq. 12.11): check whether every claim is supported by the cited passages, for example via natural language inference models or quote checking.

Faithfulness=# outputs entailed by context# total outputs\mathrm{Faithfulness}=\frac{\text{\# outputs entailed by context}}{\text{\# total outputs}} (12.11)

Helpfulness (or utility) indicates whether the answer satisfies the user’s information need. To measure this, often human evaluation or specialized LLM‑based evaluators are needed. In interactive settings latency and cost are also important.

Helpfulness is based on human or model scoring:

Helpfulness=∑i=1Nscore​(yi,queryi)N\mathrm{Helpfulness}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\text{score}(y_{i},\text{query}_{i})}{N} (12.12)

where score is a Likert-scale or pairwise preference judgment.

Joint evaluation and new metrics

A key challenge is to evaluate retrieval and generation separately. For example, a system may retrieve irrelevant documents but still guess the right answer, or retrieve perfect evidence but fail to use it. Recent work therefore proposes unified evaluation frameworks. The Auepora process recommends reporting separate retrieval and generation scores and then to combine them into a holistic measure [Yu and others, 2024]. RAGAS and similar toolkits provide automated pipelines that compute context recall, answer correctness, and citation accuracy using small models. When we evaluate adaptive methods (Section 12.4), we also need to measure the trigger decisions: how often does the model retrieve when it should, and how often does it skip retrieval unnecessarily?

Attribution and freshness

In many applications the model must cite its sources and avoid outdated information. Claims can be aligned with evidence by attribution tests. Such tests use natural language inference and ensure URL–answer consistency. Freshness metrics measure whether the answer reflects the most recent valid sources. This metric can also quantify version drift.

Attribution and freshness are especially important for time‑sensitive domains like finance or medicine.

A good system design is based on careful evaluation. When we find high retrieval recall but low faithfulness, then better re‑ranking is needed. Similarly, high faithfulness but poor helpfulness may indicate insufficient context coverage. To support error analysis and auditing, evaluations should be accompanied by transparent logging of queries, retrieved passages and model outputs.

12.8 Concluding Remarks

Retrieval is an essential element of any agentic LLM system that needs to provide up-to-date information. Large language models are static snapshots of knowledge; RAG helps them stay up to date, transparent and grounded. Effective RAG requires careful engineering across indexing, query planning, retrieval, re‑ranking, context assembly and grounded generation, along with adaptive techniques that let the model decide when and how to search. We have also seen how retrieval can be extended beyond plain text to graphs, code and multimodal assets. For building trustworthy systems, rigorous evaluation is essential.

Operational considerations

In production systems the retriever is a living service, not a one‑off script, and it should be maintained carefully. Crawlers, webhooks and document pipelines should continuously ingest new data. Be careful to track versions and deprecations, and maintain per‑entity timelines to prefer recent facts. Your system should apply access control lists at retrieval time and redact personally identifiable information during indexing. Latency and cost matter: cache embeddings and top-kk results, reuse retrieval across conversational turns, compress context with extractive summarization, tune kk and chunk sizes per domain, and re‑rank only the top candidates.

Practical suggestions

When you create a RAG system, start with a hybrid approach: combine a strong dense retriever with BM25 or SPLADE and re-rank the top hundred hits with a cross‑encoder before sending six to twelve passages to the LLM. Be careful to chunk your corpus thoughtfully, for example using 300–500 token windows with 10–15 % overlap and preserved headings and tables, also attach timestamps or other metadata. For query writing, craft your queries carefully. Rewrite complex questions, decompose multi‑hop queries, expand entity aliases and enforce domain filters. For transparency, always require citations. If, however, the evidence is weak, ask follow‑up questions, or else abstain.

Finally, use evidence-based system design, measure what you build. You should track retrieval recall, groundedness, timeliness and cost. A further suggestion is to experiment with re-rankers. For debugging, you should log system traces.

Integration into agentic AI

Retrieval is an integral element of agentic LLMs, it is used in planning, self-reflection, and while acting in the real world (see Chapter 13). Agentic pipelines can call the retriever dynamically based on the model’s confidence or plan, as in Self‑RAG and Graph Toolformer. They can query different data sources such as text, graphs, code and images, and leverage the strengths of each. The line between the model and its memory therefore blurs: RAG becomes part of the agent’s cognitive loop.

Further Reading

For in‑depth exploration, consult the surveys on RAG, evaluation and graph‑based methods [Gao and others, 2023, Huang and others, 2024, Yu and others, 2024, Sharma and others, 2025, Peng and others, 2024]. Foundational works include REALM, DPR and the original RAG formulation [Guu et al., 2020, Karpukhin et al., 2020, Lewis et al., 2020]. The GraphRAG, evaluation and agentic RAG communities are evolving rapidly; following their latest papers and benchmarks is the best way to stay current.

Chapter 13 From Tools to Assistants: Real-World Applications

13.1 Agentic LLMs as Assistants

LLMs have moved from text generators to active assistants. They combine reasoning, retrieval, and tool use to perform actions in the real world. Assistants are the practical (software) form of agentic LLMs: systems that interact, plan, and learn from feedback. Assistants are where reasoning meets reality: they turn language models into collaborative actors in the world.

An assistant links perception, reasoning, and action. Through APIs and external tools, it can converse, execute tasks, and adapt to a specific context. These systems not only support users but also create valuable human-AI interaction data that we can then use for further developments and training the next generation of models.

This chapter reviews the main types of assistants. We start with conversational systems and their evolution toward multi-modal, tool-aware interfaces. Next, we discuss domain-specific assistants in medicine, finance, and trading. Finally, we look at scientific assistants for reasoning and discovery.

13.2 Conversational Assistants

The first application domain is in general conversational situations, such as helping with meetings by taking meeting minutes, acting as meeting chair or general administrative assistant.

In this type of application, the LLM basically serves to make the interaction between human and computer more natural and streamlined [Neszlényi et al., 2024, Oluwagbade, 2024]. For example, the AssistantGPT system [Neszlényi et al., 2024] is a general purpose administrative assistant, designed for deployment in an educational or corporate setting. Furthermore, it supports remote work environments such as Teams and Slack. AssistantGPT supports a diverse range of operations, including web searches, API interactions via OpenAPI, voice conversations, and command execution through the shell. The system consists of an LLM with access to various tools such as a planner, and memory (see Figure 13.1).

These conversation and meeting assistants have been shown to improve agile software development team meetings [Cabrero-Daniel et al., 2024]. They created favorable results for preparation and live assistance during Scrum meetings, although some testers remarked that LLM interventions felt unnatural and inflexible.

Other examples include LLM agents in a collaborative learning classroom setting where the LLM agents improved overall collaboration between participants [Wei et al., 2024b]. Another study [Bastola et al., 2023] reports improved work efficiency in a collaborative task scheduling experiment including conversational assistants.

A slightly different type of assistant is the thinking assistant. This assistant tries to improve human reflective thinking for difficult decisions, by asking instead of answering [Park and Kulkarni, 2023]. Similar initiatives have recently appeared from the large LLM vendors, such as Study mode in OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini applications.

Conversational assistants have mostly evolved from regular pretrained LLMs, sometimes finetuned for a particular domain. Some approaches use a specialized multi-LLMs approach, specializing LLMs for different sub-tasks, or orchestrating a single LLM with different prompt sequences focusing on different sub-tasks.

13.3 Shopping Assistant

In this section we examine how language-based assistants can be applied in the e-commerce domain. Our goal is to highlight the principal components, architectural choices and domain-specific challenges in this domain.

What does a shopping assistant do?

A shopping assistant is a conversational system built on an LLM that helps users navigate online shopping tasks. It can help in understanding product needs, comparing alternatives, recommending items and completing purchases. Such a system typically complements the underlying LLM with domain-specific modules, including retrieval of up-to-date product information, API access to product-catalogs, integration with recommender engines and reasoning (e.g., via chain of thought) over user requirements, attributes and constraints.

Key ingredients

Because general-purpose LLMs lack built-in awareness of e-commerce concepts (brands, categories, product hierarchies, user purchase behavior), building a capable assistant requires several augmentations:

  • •

    Retrieval Augmentation: dynamically fetch product metadata, pricing, availability from external sources.

  • •

    Tool / API Invocation: the assistant may call search, filter, ranking tools to interact with product databases.

  • •

    Domain Finetuning or Instruction Tuning: adapt the LLM to the shopping context (branded language, attribute reasoning, user intents).

  • •

    Structured Reasoning: add chain of thought prompting or explicit reasoning steps. This helps the model compare products, evaluate trade-offs (e.g., price vs features) and align with user preferences.

Benchmarking shopping-assistants

To study how well models cope with shopping-specific tasks, researchers have developed benchmarks. For example, the Multi-task Online Shopping Benchmark dataset (ShopMMLU) [Jin et al., 2024] defines 57 tasks grouped into four skills: concept understanding, knowledge reasoning, user-behavior alignment and multi-linguality. It draws on real-world e-commerce data (Amazon product catalogs, sessions and reviews) and evaluates how well an LLM can handle aspects like brand-model recognition, reasoning about product compatibility, session-based recommendation tasks, and multilingual queries. Another example is the LLaSA system (large language and E-commerce shopping assistant) [Zhang et al., 2024a] which is trained via an instruction dataset (65,000 samples) dubbed EshopInstruct. After instruction-tuning on shopping tasks, LLaSA competes on the ShopBench benchmark and achieves strong results, showing that adaptation significantly improves performance in this domain.

Practical Recommendations

The following principles are important for building shopping assistants:

  • •

    A capable assistant merges natural-language understanding and domain reasoning. It should know what noise-canceling headphones under 200 euro with ¿ 20 h battery means, and be able to translate this into product attributes and user constraints.

  • •

    Domain-specific data matters: off-the-shelf LLMs work to some degree, but fine-tuning or instruction-tuning on shopping tasks significantly lifts performance. LLaSA [Zhang et al., 2024a] shows this in practice.

  • •

    Evaluation must reflect the domain. Accuracy in understanding product attributes or generating queries is less relevant than whether the assistant can align with user behavior, handle multi-step sessions and support multilingual users.

  • •

    Tool and retrieval integration is important. The assistant must act as an interface to product systems, not just as a pure language model. This introduces additional complexity (API design, latency, freshness of data and handling integration errors).

  • •

    Consider ethics and trust. In shopping, recommendations carry commercial, privacy and bias implications. These issues should be assessed before deploying such a system in production, through questions such as: which brands are shown, is user history handled correctly, and how transparent is the reasoning.

Challenges and open questions

Even with recent progress, shopping assistants face several non-trivial challenges. First, handling long interaction trajectories (browsing, refining queries, switching intents) is still difficult for LLM agents. Second, updating product knowledge in real-time (new models, price changes, availability) remains a major engineering pain-point. Third, explaining and justifying recommendations to users (why this product vs another) is under-explored in LLM-based assistants. Finally, cross-lingual behavior and multilingual product queries increase complexity (shopping contexts span languages and regions).

13.4 Flight Operations Assistant

Language-based assistants are also applied in aviation operations, a domain that extends beyond consumer booking and moves into planning and decision support.

Booking and travel-planning

One of the simpler applications is a conversational booking assistant, similar to the shopping assistants in the previous section. For example, Manasa et al. [2024] present a system built on LLaMa 2 with RAG to interactively help users book flights. The assistant is fine-tuned on flight-booking data, and connects to current flight information via retrieval. User testing achieved strong marks for capturing user preferences and guiding the booking process efficiently.

Notice how this use-case remains relatively shallow in operational complexity. The assistant deals with structured user intents (I want to fly from A to B on date D), retrieval of up-to-date product data, preference elicitation and generation of responses. It does not (yet) deeply engage with, say, dynamic air-traffic constraints or safety margins.

Operational decision support

Moving to more demanding settings, LLM-based assistants are being proposed for actual flight operations. We discuss two examples.

In a study by Zhou et al. [2024], the arrival-slot-allocation problem (i.e., determining in which sequence arriving aircraft should land) is formulated as a language modeling task. The authors encode the scheduling inputs and outputs as tokens and fine-tune an LLM to generate conflict-free landing sequences. Their experiments show that the model can reduce conflict rate and total delay time even for airports where traditional methods struggle.

Another operational problem is planning under environmental hazards. Tabrizian et al. [2024] use chain of thought to support routing or flight plan generation under wind-hazard constraints. Here, the assistant’s task is no longer simply book a flight but it has to reason about constraints (wind, routing, aircraft performance) and propose operationally feasible plans.

Key recommendations

These studies illustrate several important aspects of agentic systems with LLMs:

  • •

    Tool/Backend Integration: in operational assistants, the LLM must not only converse but also interface with flight-databases, weather feeds, routing engines and slot‐allocation systems. This means implementing tool invocation, retrieval pipelines and decision logic.

  • •

    Reasoning under Constraints: these assistants must handle combinatorial or scheduling constraints, generate plans, and deal with real‐time uncertainties (such as weather, runway availability). The arrival-slot example is a good example, where the LLM must reason about dynamic sequencing.

  • •

    Domain-specific Data and Finetuning: the standard pretrained LLM lacks priors about aviation operations. The systems above are finetuned or prompted specifically for the domain. A dataset of domain-tasks, prompts, expected outputs are evaluation metrics tailored to the domain are necessary.

  • •

    From Conversational Agent to Autonomous Planner: while booking assistants remain user-driven (the user asks, the assistant helps), operational assistants increasingly take on planning roles. The assistant should handle requests such as here are constraints, propose a schedule or route. This change raises issues of trust, verification and explainability.

  • •

    Evaluation in Real Contexts: the evaluation of operational systems often involves more than does the assistant answer the user?, but also measure aspects such as conflict rate, delay time, and sequence efficiency. For example, the arrival-slot LLM study measured total delay and conflict rate.

13.5 Medical Assistant

Medicine is one of the most active application domains for LLM-based assistants [Thirunavukarasu et al., 2023, Clusmann et al., 2023, Mehandru et al., 2024]. Recent studies report that LLMs can outperform trained physicians on diagnostic tasks [Goh et al., 2024] and exceed human medical scribes in clinical note generation [Yuan et al., 2024]. Other evaluations confirm these strengths, while also identifying systematic weaknesses in specific clinical scenarios [Panagoulias et al., 2024].

Agentic architectures are increasingly used to address regulatory, ethical, and usability requirements. Sudarshan et al. [2024] present an agentic workflow for generating patient-friendly medical reports that comply with the 21st Century Cures Act. Their system uses reflexion (Section 6.2.4, [Shinn et al., 2024]) to iteratively improve clarity and correctness before information is released to patients.

Other studies explore the use of LLM agents for broader clinical support. Qiu et al. [2024] identify applications ranging from clinical workflow automation to multi-agent diagnostic support, although concerns remain regarding accuracy, completeness, and hallucinations. A scoping review by Ullah et al. [2024] emphasizes that medical domain knowledge and ethical constraints are essential when training and fine-tuning such systems.

To mitigate common failure modes, Das et al. [2024] propose an agentic retrieval-based architecture in which the LLM acts as a planner rather than a direct answer generator. The agent coordinates specialized tools to retrieve and synthesize evidence from trusted medical sources, reducing hallucinations and lost-in-the-middle errors.

High-risk application domain

Medicine is a high-risk application domain, where incorrect or biased outputs can have direct consequences for patient safety. As a result, medical AI systems are subject to strict regulatory frameworks, including the EU AI Act, which classifies many medical uses of AI as high-risk. Transparency, fairness, and accountability therefore play a central role, both in clinical practice and in academic research on medical LLMs. These concerns motivate increased interest in methods that go beyond post-hoc explanations and aim to understand model behavior at a deeper level. We return to this topic in the chapter on mechanistic interpretability (Chapter 21), where techniques for analyzing and controlling internal model representations are discussed.

Medical education

In medical education, agentic systems are used to simulate realistic training environments. Wei et al. [2024a] introduce a multi-agent copilot that supports case-based learning and clinical reasoning practice (Figure 13.2). For systematic evaluation of medical retrieval-augmented generation, a dedicated benchmark is provided by Qiao et al. [2024].

13.6 Trading Assistant

A further specialized domain is financial trading. Already many (non-LLM) algorithms are used in financial organizations for trading decisions. The interest in agentic LLMs in the financial world is large [Ding et al., 2024].

InvestorBench is a benchmark for financial trading systems [Li et al., 2024]. FinAgent is a tool-augmented multimodal agent for financial trading [Zhang et al., 2024b]. It contains a market intelligence module, which is able to extract insights from multi-modal datasets of asset prices, visual representations, news and expert analyses. The system can also perform query retrieval and performs reflection in a low-level module for technical analysis and in a high-level module to analyze past trading decisions.

FinRobot is an agentic LLM for financial analysis, to assist human traders. [Yang et al., 2024a]. FinRobot can provide document analysis and generation and market forecasts for individual stocks. FinMem is an agentic LLM framework devised for financial decision-making [Yu et al., 2024]. It features a layered memory system and adjustable character design for the trading agent. FinMem is inspired by the generative agents framework by Park et al. [2023] (see Section 17.2.1 and Case Study 4).

So far, most financial market machine learning has focused on single agent systems. An approach called TradingAgents uses a multi agent system to replicate real-world trading firms’ collaborative dynamics [Xiao et al., 2024]. TradingAgents simulates LLM-powered agents in specialized roles such as fundamental analysts, sentiment analysts, technical analysts and traders with varied risk profiles. The outcome of the system is a buy or sell advice to a human manager. A simulation showed that it outperformed baseline models.

Evaluation

Financial trading is a challenging field of research. The competitive interests in financial trading are high, and there is a natural tendency to keep strong research findings private, which creates a tension with the principles of openness and transparency of scientific research.

Furthermore, despite the abundance of available numerical data in the field, there are relatively few benchmarking studies that compare different agentic LLM approaches on the same data. A recent benchmarking study found methodological flaws in some financial LLM studies, such as selecting short evaluation periods with positive market trends or leakage of test in training data [Li et al., 2026].

13.7 Automated Scientific Discovery

The workflow of scientific experimentation is relatively standardized in certain fields of science. For example, in machine learning, (1) ideas are generated, (2) a hypothesis is formulated, (3) an experiment is designed, (4) datasets are acquired, (5) experiments are performed, (6) results are interpreted and (7) a report is produced. This standard workflow has attracted researchers to experiment with agentic LLMs for performing scientific research, see Eger et al. [2025] for a survey.

Google and OpenAI have both released Deep Research agents. These agents can perform multi-step research tasks, such as synthesizing online information. They are built with a reasoning LLM and use retrieval augmentation for finding information sources. The systems are able to create scientific research papers that look impressive, but are often not error-free.

AI Scientist [Lu et al., 2024] is a framework to automate the process of scientific discovery, from idea generation to paper writing, including a review process. Users must specify a topic and provide an experimentation template and indicate datasets. The authors report experiments in three areas of machine learning: diffusion modeling, transformer-based language modeling, and learning dynamics, with promising results. To improve idea generation and reviewing, the agent accesses open sources. Current limitations include limited experiments, incorrect implementation if ideas, and visual errors when the paper is produced. On the other hand, rarely are entire results hallucinated. Nevertheless, results of the AI scientist are recommended to be taken as hints of promising ideas, worthy of a follow up study [Lu et al., 2024].

Building on top of the AI scientist idea, the Agent Laboratory was proposed [Schmidgall et al., 2025], an open-source framework that employs specialized LLM-based agents to accelerate the full research cycle. Unlike the AI Scientist, Agent Laboratory is explicitly designed as a co-pilot for human researchers, complementing rather than replacing human ideation. The framework consists of three main phases: literature review, experimentation, and report writing. Each phase is executed by dedicated agents, such as the PhD, Postdoc, and Professor agents, coordinated through a structured pipeline. The system integrates two specialized components: mle-solver, responsible for autonomously generating, testing, and refining machine learning code, and paper-solver, which produces a complete research report in LaTeX format based on the experimental results. Both solvers employ iterative refinement, self-evaluation, and reward-based scoring to improve code and report quality across cycles.

Evaluation results demonstrate that Agent Laboratory can autonomously generate complete research projects, including executable code and publication-ready reports, at a fraction of the computational cost of comparable systems (approximately $2.33 per paper using the gpt-4o backend). Human-in-the-loop or co-pilot mode further improves research quality and usability, with participants reporting high satisfaction and continued use intentions. Nonetheless, human oversight remains essential, as automated self-evaluations tend to overestimate research quality compared to human reviewers.

13.8 Coding Assistants and General Advances

SWE-Agent (short for software engineering agent) [Yang et al., 2024b] aims to automate the process of software discovery, to help agents to autonomously use computers to solve software engineering tasks. SWE-agent introduces tools to create and edit code files, navigate through software repositories, and execute computer programs. Experiments on coding benchmarks such as HumanEvalFix achieve high success rates of over 80%. This success is attributed to the interactive design of the agent (see Figure 13.3).

MLGym [Nathani et al., 2025] follows the popular Gym reinforcement learning framework [Brockman et al., 2016]. Gym provides a standardized interface between environment and agent. Introduced in 2016, it accelerated the development of reinforcement learning algorithms, facilitating progress in the field. Taking further inspiration from SWE-agent (such as file editing capabilities) the MLGym work shows how the process of scientific discovery can be modeled as an interactive process. Applications are discussed in fields ranging from data science, game theory, computer vision, reinforcement learning, to natural language processing. Experiments are reported with commercial LLMs (OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Anthropic).

Most LLM-based assistants, including research and coding assistants, depend on pre-defined tools, limiting their autonomy and scalability. Toolmaker [Wölflein et al., 2025] addresses this limitation by enabling agents to create new tools directly from scientific papers and their code repositories. Given a task description and GitHub URL, it installs dependencies, configures a reproducible Docker environment, and implements a working Python tool through iterative self-correction and error diagnosis. The system was evaluated on TM-Bench (also introduced in Wölflein et al. [2025]), a benchmark of 15 real-world scientific tasks across medicine, biology, and AI. Toolmaker achieved 80% task success. Its closed-loop design allows agents not only to use but also to autonomously build new tools, marking a step toward self-extending research assistants and adaptive scientific workflows.

While systems such as Agent Laboratory and Toolmaker focus on the capabilities of individual agents, The Agent Company [Xu et al., 2024] provides a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate how LLM agents perform in realistic, work-like environments. It simulates a small software company where agents must complete professional tasks, ranging from software development and project management to finance and human resources, using standard digital tools like browsers, terminals, and communication platforms.

The benchmark includes 175 tasks designed to test multi-step reasoning, tool use, and collaboration with simulated colleagues powered by LLMs. Each task is divided into checkpoints that measure both full and partial completion. Experiments with twelve foundation models, including GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, and Llama, reveal that even the strongest current systems can autonomously complete only about 30% of tasks. Failures often come from weaknesses in communication, long-horizon planning, and navigation of complex user interfaces.

By introducing a reproducible, self-hosted environment that mirrors a modern workplace, The Agent Company offers a critical stress test for evaluating the maturity of agentic LLMs. It highlights both the rapid progress and the persistent limitations of current systems, underscoring that while digital work automation is within reach, truly autonomous collaboration remains a major research frontier.

13.9 Concluding Remarks

This chapter has shown how agentic LLMs have been used as assistants, interacting with the real world. Assistants move beyond passive question answering toward active collaboration in domains such as dialogue, flight operations, medicine, education and scientific research. They plan, retrieve information, invoke tools, reflect on outcomes and adapt their behavior over time. Agentic LLMs therefore shift the role of language models from isolated reasoning engines to participants in broader socio-technical systems.

Domain sensitivity and risk

Not all assistants operate under the same constraints. High-risk domains such as medicine and aviation demand strong guarantees on safety, robustness, transparency and fairness, and are shaped by regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act. In these settings, agentic designs increasingly rely on retrieval, planning, verification and human oversight rather than on end-to-end generation. Academic research mirrors these concerns, with growing emphasis on evaluation, bias analysis and interpretability as first-class design objectives rather than afterthoughts.

Practical advice

When building assistants, grounding (real-world evaluation) is important. Use architectures where agents retrieve evidence, justify actions and defer to humans under uncertainty (human in the loop). Treat tools as modular components with explicit contracts and failure modes. Log decisions, plans and intermediate states to enable debugging and auditing. In high-stakes domains, we suggest to design for graceful degradation; an agent asking for clarification or abstaining is preferable to confident error.

Outlook

The future of agentic assistants lies in tighter integration between reasoning, learning and control. Progress will require richer cognitive structure, continual adaptation from interaction and stronger guarantees around safety and ethics. These goals connect directly to advances in interpretability and transparency. In later chapters, particularly in mechanistic interpretability (Chapter 21), we return to techniques that aim to open the black box and better understand how agentic LLMs represent goals, plans and decisions internally.

Chapter 14 Case Study 3: Building a Multi-Agent Diagnosis Framework

14.1 Scenario Overview

This case study focuses on building and extending a simplified multi-agent hospital simulation using a shared context inspired by the Model Context Protocol (MCP, Chapter 11) [Hou et al., 2026]. The case study is designed to provide hands-on experience with agentic architectures in a high-risk domain, highlighting coordination, planning, evaluation, and safety considerations.

You will simulate a diagnostic workflow in a hospital setting. Patient cases are processed by agents that interact exclusively through a shared context:

  • •

    Planner agents decide which diagnostic pathway(s) should be followed.

  • •

    Executor agents apply trained ML classifiers to produce diagnoses.

  • •

    Shared context stores cases, tasks, intermediate decisions and results.

The simulation runs in discrete steps and logs how cases move through the system. As with the earlier case studies, the goal is not to build a clinically valid system. The goal is for you to understand how agentic architectures behave in a high-risk domain: how agents coordinate through shared state, how a language model performs when placed in a triage role, and where the limitations and safety concerns of such a system arise.11 1 This case study is partly based on a tutorial by Ayushman Pranav, Modeling Hospital Intelligence with MCP: A Multi-Agent Diagnostic Simulation, available at https://medium.com/@AyushmanPranav/modeling-hospital-intelligence-with-mcp-a-multi-agent-diagnostic-simulation-afeff0dd885d.

14.2 Environment Setup

As in the earlier case studies, we recommend working inside a dedicated virtual environment using Python 3.10 or higher (see Listing 14.1 for setup instructions).

14.3 Implementation Steps

14.3.1 Step 0: Training Diagnostic Models

You are provided with a script, 0_train_models.py, that trains simple classifiers (random forests) on three public datasets:

  • •

    Diabetes — the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset.

  • •

    Breast cancer — the Wisconsin breast cancer dataset, available directly through sklearn.datasets.

  • •

    Heart disease — the UCI heart disease dataset.

Execute the provided training script and store the resulting models for later use; the executor agents in Steps 1 and 2 load these trained models as tools rather than retraining them on every run.

Deliverables

Trained model files (or a clear, reproducible script to regenerate them) for all three diseases.

14.3.2 Step 1: Understanding and Running the Baseline

The baseline implementation, 1_basic_mcp.py, uses three rule-based planner agents, each hard-coded to a specific disease. Before running anything, read the code carefully. It implements three components that recur throughout this case study:

  • •

    Shared context (MCP-like layer). A central data structure that stores incoming patient cases, assigned diagnostic tasks, and diagnostic results. All agents interact only through this shared context, never directly with one another, mirroring the shared-state coordination pattern discussed for the Model Context Protocol in Section 11.

  • •

    Planner agents. Each rule-based planner reads unassigned cases, decides (using a fixed rule) whether its disease domain applies, and creates a task in the shared context.

  • •

    Executor agents. Each executor reads tasks assigned to its specialty, runs the corresponding trained ML classifier from Step 0, produces a prediction, and writes the result back into the shared context.

Run the baseline simulation and observe how a single patient case flows through the system: from arrival, through planning and task creation, to execution and logging of the result.

Analysis questions

Assess how realistic this baseline setup is. How well is performance evaluated? What assumptions are implicit in the way patients and diagnoses are handled?

14.3.3 Step 2: Replacing the Rule-Based Planners with an LLM Agent

In the second part, 2_llm_mcp.py, the three rule-based planners are replaced by a single LLM-based planner agent. This is a substantially harder task for the planner: each patient case now combines features drawn from all three datasets into one record, and is converted into a textual description using the provided make_case_text function, which you are not permitted to modify. The LLM planner must read this combined, textual case description and decide, without hard-coded rules, which diagnostic pathway or pathways apply.

Your tasks are to:

  • •

    implement a function that calls a real LLM (e.g., via Ollama for a local model, or the OpenAI or Gemini APIs) to obtain the planner’s decision for a given case;

  • •

    implement the step() method of the LLMPlannerAgent, so that it selects one or more diagnostic pathways together with a primary diagnosis for each case;

  • •

    handle malformed or unparseable LLM outputs gracefully, rather than letting the simulation crash on a single bad response; and

  • •

    log every planner decision, together with the case it was made for, so that planner behavior can be analyzed after the run.

Because the planner now has to infer relevance from unstructured text rather than from a fixed rule, this step should give you direct experience with the reliability problems that arise when an LLM is placed in a decision-making role: parsing failures, inconsistent formatting, and disagreement between the LLM’s routing decision and the dataset’s ground-truth label.

Deliverables

A working LLMPlannerAgent, a short note on which LLM you used and how you accessed it (local vs. API), and the logged planner decisions for a full simulation run.

14.4 Evaluation

You must evaluate both components of the system, and keep the two evaluations separate:

  • •

    Model (executor) performance: assess executor predictions using confusion matrices and standard classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) for each disease.

  • •

    Planner performance: evaluate the LLM’s triage quality using precision and recall of routing decisions (did the case get sent to the right disease pathway or pathways?) and primary-diagnosis accuracy (did the planner correctly identify the main concern?).

In your report, clearly separate errors due to incorrect routing (a planner error) from errors due to incorrect model predictions (an executor error). A case can fail for either reason independently: a well-routed case can still be misclassified by the executor, and a correctly-classifiable case can be missed entirely because the planner never routed it to the right pathway. Reporting only an end-to-end accuracy number would hide this distinction and is not sufficient for this case study.

14.5 Reflection Questions

The following questions are intended to guide a short written report on your implementation. You do not need to write a narrative essay; concise, direct answers are sufficient, and you should be prepared to elaborate on your reasoning verbally.

A. Baseline architecture
  • •

    Describe, in at most five sentences, the flow of a single patient case through the baseline system.

  • •

    Each baseline case is sampled from a dataset and therefore belongs to exactly one disease domain by construction. What does this imply about how the rule-based planner “decides,” and is this a realistic model of triage?

  • •

    The classifiers in Step 0 are trained and evaluated on the same data distribution used to generate simulation cases. Why is this methodologically problematic, and what would a fairer evaluation protocol look like?

B. LLM planner design
  • •

    Which LLM did you use, and how did you access it (local model, API)? Briefly justify the choice.

  • •

    The make_case_text function presents a patient as a combination of features drawn from three separate, unrelated datasets. Why is this medically unrealistic, and does that matter for the purposes of this exercise?

  • •

    Describe one concrete design choice in your step() implementation—for example, how you handle parsing failures, abstentions, or cases routed to multiple diseases—and explain why you made it.

C. Results
  • •

    Report triage precision and recall for each disease, along with confusion matrices for the executor models. What do these numbers tell you about how well the overall system works?

  • •

    The LLM planner can route a single case to multiple diseases simultaneously. Give one example scenario where this is beneficial, and one where it could be harmful.

D. Reflection
  • •

    Identify one safety risk that is specific to using an LLM as a planner in a medical triage context, and describe how it could be mitigated.

  • •

    Is it fair to evaluate triage performance by comparing the LLM’s routing decisions against the ground-truth labels of the original, single-disease datasets? Explain any reservations you have.

Optional Extensions

As an extra, you may extend the system by making patient sampling more realistic (e.g., mixed or comorbid cases sampled with more principled priors). You can also add another disease from the UCI repository, or introduce an evaluator or verifier agent that checks the planner’s decisions before they reach the executors. Another idea is simulating human-in-the-loop decision making, or incorporating uncertainty thresholds and abstention mechanisms so that the planner can decline to route a case when it is not confident. Finally, you can integrate retrieval from external knowledge sources (Chapter 12) so the planner can ground its routing decisions in clinical reference material rather than relying purely on parametric knowledge.

Notes

This assignment is educational and non-clinical. Do not claim medical validity for any system you build here. Emphasis is placed on clarity, reproducibility, and critical reflection rather than raw performance. A system that routes conservatively, abstains when uncertain, and is transparent about its limitations is, in this setting, a better outcome than one that maximizes accuracy while hiding its failure modes.

14.6 Concluding Remarks

This case study brought together several threads from earlier parts of the book: agent roles and coordination (Part III), tool use and the Model Context Protocol (Chapter 11), and the evaluation methodology needed to separate planning errors from execution errors in a compound agentic system. By first building a rule-based baseline and then replacing its planners with a single LLM-based planner, you have seen directly how much harder planning becomes once it depends on an LLM’s interpretation of unstructured, textual case descriptions rather than a fixed rule.

The medical framing was chosen deliberately: it is a domain where the cost of an overconfident, unexplainable error is high, and where questions of abstention, human oversight, and auditability are core design requirements. The same coordination pattern applies well beyond healthcare, to any agentic system where a language model is responsible for routing decisions that other, more specialized components then act on.
