Chapter 16 Role-Based Interaction in Multi-LLM Systems

16.1 From Single-agent to Multi-agent

The previous chapter studied individual LLMs and LLM-powered agents through a behavioral lens: how a single model reads a communicative, social, or moral situation, and acts in it. In this chapter we move from single- to multi-agent settings and examine what happens when several LLM-based agents are made to interact, for example as opponents in game-theoretic contests and as collaborators in teams. The unit of analysis shifts from the behavioral profile of single models to interaction patterns and collective outcomes that arise between models.

16.1.1 Mulit-Agent Simulations: History and Present

The use of artificial agents to study interaction has a long history in the computational social sciences [Epstein and Axtell, 1996, Macal and North, 2010]. Traditionally, populations of agents with basic perception, reasoning, and decision-making capacities interacted in a virtual or, in case of robot-based simulations, real, experimental environment [Steels, 1995, Shoham and Leyton-Brown, 2008]. The purpose of such simulations is usually to bridge theoretical and experimental work, using artificial behavior as a test ground for hypotheses about human behavior in domains where real-world experiments are difficult or costly.

Two obstacles have historically limited this line of investigation: difficulty in verifying if behavior is realistic, and the high computational cost of simulating agent societies. Advances in agentic LLMs and simulation infrastructure [Rutherford et al., 2024] are changing this situation. LLM-based agents communicate in natural language, can process rich background knowledge, and can be given differentiated personas, making simulated interactions more expressive and more directly comparable to human interaction.

16.1.2 Role-Based versus Emergent Interaction

Multi-LLM studies can be categorized based on the amount of control the researchers take over the simulation. At one end, every agent is assigned a role in the form of a persona, objective, and interaction protocol. The research question is usually how the agents behave within the assigned structure and how well the resulting system performs as a whole, compared to other assigned structures and roles. At the other end, agents are placed in an open-ended environment without prior role assignment, and the research question is what social structure emerges: group dynamics, conventions, and norms. This chapter is concerned with the role-based end of the spectrum, Chapter 17 discusses the emergent side.

This distinction matters for methodological choices as well as for the interpretation of results. In role-based systems, roles and interaction protocols are design decisions or experimental variables. Behavior is evaluated and interpreted against the goals that a system was designed for. In emergent settings, the goals or tasks play a role at the background (or are entirely absent). The analysis is more open-ended and exploratory, closer to ethnography than to benchmarking. However, as will become clear, the distinction is not absolute: role-based systems regularly display behavior that was they were not designed for.

16.1.3 Five Dimensions of Multi-Agent Collaboration

As a structuring principle for this chapter, we adopt the categorization by Tran et al. [2025] along five dimensions of LLM collaboration:

  1. 1.

    Actors: the agents involved, and whether they are homogeneous (instances of one model) or heterogeneous (different models or capability profiles)

  2. 2.

    Interaction types: cooperation, competition, or mixtures of both (“coopetition”)

  3. 3.

    Structures: how the agents are organized, e.g. peer-to-peer, centralized, or distributed

  4. 4.

    Strategies: how collaboration is elicited, e.g. through role assignment or through model-level mechanisms

  5. 5.

    Coordination protocols: the mechanisms that tie agents together and regulate their communication

The systems discussed in this chapter make different choices along these five axes, and keeping these dimensions in mind makes it easier to see what is new about each framework.

16.1.4 A Methodological Note

Evaluating multi-agent systems inherits every methodological difficulty of evaluating single models: prompt sensitivity, possible leakage of test materials into training data, and sampling variability. Plus, it adds new difficulties of its own:

  • •

    Reported results are often harder to reproduce because small variations in one agent’s output cascade through subsequent interaction, increasing run-to-run variability.

  • •

    It can be unclear what causes performance differences: the multi-agent collaboration itself, the coordination protocol, the embedded prompt engineering for the role distribution, or simply the additional inference budget multiple agents consume cumulatively.

  • •

    Construct validity shifts to the level of social-interactive terminology: concepts such as team work, discussion, or collective decision-making carry rich human connotations that the actual simulation may not warrant.

With these caveats in mind, the chapter proceeds to the simplest multi-agent setting: LLM agents facing each other in strategic settings, with no roles assigned beyond the game itself (Section 16.2). Next, we examine what changes when interaction is streamlined by defining coordination protocols and explicit roles (Section 16.3).

16.2 Strategic Interaction Among LLM Agents

In Chapter 15 we examined how LLMs behave when prompted to play economic games against a scripted opponent. Here we consider studies in which LLM agents interact with one another in game-theoretical scenarios. The agents in this section are symmetric peers: each pursues its own interests and none is assigned a coordinating or supervisory role. We look first at benchmarks that score LLM agents across many games at once, and then at behavior in single, richer simulation platforms built around one scenario.

16.2.1 Benchmarking Strategic Ability Across Games

The MAgIC study [Xu et al., 2024] uses social deduction games (Undercover and Chameleon) and game theoretic scenarios such as cost sharing, the multi-player Prisoner’s dilemma, and public goods games. The goal is to extract seven capabilities: rationality, judgment, reasoning, deception, self-awareness, cooperation, and coordination, as shown in Figure 16.1. LLMs in off-the-shelf and enhanced forms are evaluated on these capabilities in multi-agent settings.

GPT-o1 and GPT-4 score significantly better than the other models. LLMs generally score high on judgment, rationality and cooperation, some also on deception, but lower on reasoning and all but one score low on coordination. The exception is GPT-o1 enhanced with probabilistic graphical modeling, an implementation of a theory of mind-like competence inspired by Koller and Friedman [2009]. The authors show that probabilistic graphical modeling boosts LLM performance across the board. This is consistent with the general evidence discussed in Section 15.5 that humans lean heavily on theory of mind in strategic settings.

A benchmark that isolates coordination as the object of study, rather than as one trait among several, is the LLM-Coordination Benchmark [Agashe et al., 2025]. LLMs are evaluated on two distinct tasks: agentic coordination in pure cooperation games and question answering about those games (see Figure 16.2). The experiments find that LLM agents perform well as long as decision-making can rely on environmental variables, but poorly when success requires actively reasoning about a partner’s beliefs and intentions. Concretely, such environmental variables include elements such as the game layout, locations of objects, where each agent is currently positioned, which doors are open, and so on. The clearest illustration is Overcooked-AI, the game where LLMs did best. This game is fully observable, and its action space consists of moves such as pick up an onion from onion dispenser 1 and place onion on plate 0. Under most scenarios and layouts, LLMs only need to consider the next best steps based on the state of the game environment, without taking into account other agent’s perspectives.

This asymmetry becomes especially clear when comparing performance on Overcooked with scores in Hanabi, a game in which every action requires reasoning about the partner’s beliefs. On Overcooked, zero-shot LLM agents can match or outperform specially trained reinforcement learning baseline models. On Hanabi, however, the reinforcement learning baselines show near-perfect scores, whereas most LLM agents barely score at all. The best LLM agent (based on GPT-4-turbo) reaches only about half the maximum score, even when enhanced with explicit theory of mind reasoning and self-verification steps. Without such enhancements, the scores of strong models such as GPT-4-turbo collapses almost entirely, indicating that the measured ability is partly a feature of the agent framework rather than the model alone. The LLM agents did prove more robust in cross-play: reinforcement learning methods degrade sharply when playing unseen partners, whereas the zero-shot nature of LLM agents facilitates transfer to unseen partners without performance loss.

The question-answering component of the study (see Figure 16.2, right column) breaks the problem down by targeting environment comprehension, ToM, and joint planning, separately. They find that LLMs score generally high on the first category (¿80% for the best model), lower on ToM, and worst on joint planning (¡40% for the best model, below random chance for open-source models). This is consistent with the observed difference in scores between Overcooked (environment-driven) and Hanabi (ToM- and planning-driven).

The key characteristic of pure cooperation games is that agents must fully cooperate with each other with no competitive incentives. In contrast, in competitive settings such as the Prisoner’s Dilemma (or the mixed-motive games in benchmarks like MAgIC), an agent faces a genuine tension between individual and collective payoff. In such games, when an LLM fails to cooperate, the reason is unclear. The agent may be bad at coordination or it might reason strategically about individual gains. In pure cooperation games, there is never any reason to defect, so any failure to cooperate is a genuine lack of coordination ability.

16.2.2 Strategic Interaction in Single-Scenario Platforms

Benchmarks aggregate over many small games. A complementary line of research builds single scenarios and studies agent behavior in-depth.

Alympics [Mao et al., 2023] provides a controlled playground for simulating strategic interaction among LLM-driven agents, illustrated by a multi-round water-allocation challenge in which scarce survival resources must be distributed over time, see Figure 16.3.

AucArena [Chen et al., 2023a] simulates auctions, across LLaMa 2.13b, Mistral 7b, Mixtral 8x7b, Gemini 1.0, and GPT 3.5/4.0, finding that the most capable LLMs such as GPT-4 possess skills for auction participation such as budget management and goal-focus, though performance varies even for that model, and the authors point to considerable room for improvement.

16.2.3 Conclusion

Across benchmarks and single-scenario platforms alike, coordination emerges as the consistent weak spot of LLM agents. Stronger LLMs score well on rationality and judgment in MAgIC, manage budgets sensibly in AucArena, and match trained RL agents in environment-driven cooperation. However, all but the strongest and most heavily scaffolded models fail when success requires reasoning about what a partner believes and intends.

In other words, models fail to consistently integrate theory of mind reasoning with their behavior. In Chapter 15, failures of this kind were referred to as the knowing-doing or literal-functional gap: GPT-4 could respond accurately when prompted to predict the alternating pattern in Bach or Stravinsky, but failed to enact it when playing. However, the multi-agent studies reviewed here complicate that diagnosis. In the question-asking section of the LLM Coordination Benchmark, the questions about joint planning pose exactly the decision the agent faces at each step of the game play. It is on these questions that the models perform worst (and on ToM questions not much better). Question-answering scores correlate positively with agentic performance across games. In other words, knowing and doing move together here: where models act poorly, they also reason poorly when the action problem is posed to them directly. For pure coordination tasks, the deficit thus lies in taking the partner’s perspective (ToM) and joint planning itself, rather tan in translating reasoning into action.

On a different level, the knowing-doing gap reappears. In Hanabi, GPT-4-turbo reaches reasonable performance only when scaffolded with explicit ToM reasoning and self-verification steps. Without these in place, it commits fatal errors in every Hanabi trial. In other words, it acts wrongly initially, but recognizes and corrects these errors when prompted to check the reasoning and verification steps. Similar performance boosts were caused by probabilistic graphical modeling in MAgIC and Social Chain-of-Thought in strategic-behavior studies discussed in Chapter 15. The boundary between LLMs cannot reason about others and LLMs do not spontaneously deploy such reasoning is apparently thin, and agentic embedding in the form of structured reasoning and verification steps can bring out the latter.

The next section examines a different, complementary response to the same problem: instead of upgrading the agents’ reasoning, one can structure the interaction itself, by assigning roles.

16.3 Role-Based Task Solving and Teamwork

In the previous section, agents were symmetric peers and coordination had to emerge from their own strategic reasoning (with limited success). In the studies discussed in this section, coordination is designed-in using interaction protocols and assigning roles with distinct objectives.

In terms of the five dimensions defined in Section 16.1.3, the studies vary the strategies and structures while keeping the overall interaction type cooperative. We proceed from the simplest to the most complex structure: complementary pairs, multi-party debate, teams, and social role-play under pressure.

16.3.1 Complementary Pairs

LLMs can perform tasks in pairs where they are assigned complementary roles, such as creator-critic or manager-worker. In these pair-wise setups, each LLM agent is given a distinct role and objective, and they communicate to jointly solve tasks.

In the CAMEL framework (Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration) [Li et al., 2023], two LLMs have predefined roles to perform, to work on a goal such as a coding task (See Figure 16.4). Through cooperation, together they drive a conversation without explicit continuous human prompting. CAMEL uses inception prompting and role descriptions so that agents stay in character and collaborate towards the goal. The agents are prompted to break down complex problems in manageable steps through their dialogue. During each interaction step the LLM agents effectively generate their own inference-time training data, making the cognitive process visible for human inspection, while at the same time enhancing autonomous task performance.

Other studies have paired an LLM creator (or generator) with an LLM judge (or critic) in a self-reflective setting. In this way the generative power of LLMs is leveraged through one agent, while adherence to rules or quality guidelines is enforced by the other. Constitutional AI [Bai et al., 2022] employs one LLM to critique another LLM’s responses against a set of ethical or quality guidelines, suggesting revisions. The authors show that this kind of two-agent feedback yields refined final outputs that are aligned with the desired principles.

A third form of pair-wise interaction follows human tutoring dynamics: teacher-learner or expert-novice. Chapter 19.2 discusses various examples of this structure in the context of distillation.

All three pairings exploit the same idea: one agent’s oversight can correct the other’s mistakes, leading to more robust joint performance than either agent achieves alone.

16.3.2 Debate and Discussion

Beyond pairs, a prominent example of role-based interaction is the use of debate and discussion between LLMs to improve reasoning and task performance.

Du et al. [2024] demonstrated that when multiple LLM instances propose answers and critique each other’s reasoning through several rounds of debate, they can reach a more accurate consensus answer with higher factual correctness. This approach, described in terms of Minsky’s society of minds [Minsky, 1988], significantly reduced reasoning errors and hallucinations in tasks such as math word problems and factual question answering.

Liang et al. [2024] propose a multi-agent debate (MAD) setup where two LLM agents take opposing sides in, for instance, a tit-for-tat negotiation (see Section 15.4) while a third agent acts as a judge. The role of the judge is to guide the discussion towards a final solution. The structured debate encourages divergent thinking and can push a weaker model enhanced with MAD (such as GPT-3.5) to outperform a stronger model without MAD (such as GPT-4) on a challenging benchmark. The authors discuss how their MAD setup overcomes a known problem in model scaffolding with self-reflective steps. Self-reflection can induce so-called degeneration of thought: once a model gains confidence in a certain solution direction, self-reflection can reinforce the confidence even if the direction is wrong. In the MAD debating-setup, the other agent can push towards a different direction direction to avoid thought degeneration.

ChatEval applies this debate pattern to text evaluation [Chan et al., 2023]. Noting that the quality of human text assessment improves when multiple annotators collaborate, the authors create a multi-agent referee team with debater agents, diverse role specifications, and different communication strategies (see Figure 16.5), moving beyond single-agent prompting strategies.

Another approach, also motivated by Minsky’s society of minds, is ReConcile, a multi-agent framework designed as a round table conference among diverse LLM agents [Chen et al., 2023b]. The framework enhances collaborative reasoning between LLM agents via multiple rounds of discussion. The agents must try to convince one another to improve their answers. Experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate that a confidence-weighted voting mechanism significantly improves LLMs’ reasoning. Furthermore, the authors find that diversity (using different underlying models) is critical for performance.

MindStorms introduces an LLM-based implementation [Zhuge et al., 2023] on the CAMEL framework [Li et al., 2023]. Extensive experiments are reported with up to 129 agents solving common AI problems: visual question answering, image captioning, text-to-image synthesis, 3D generation, egocentric retrieval, embodied AI, and general language-based task solving. The authors find that, in specific applications, mindstorms among many members outperform those among fewer members, and longer mindstorms outperform shorter ones.

16.3.3 Role-Based Software Teams

An interesting application of role-based collaboration is software development, where simulated teams that are entirely staffed with LLM agents develop software.

Automated programming by LLMs has suffered from problems, such as logic inconsistencies and hallucinations that cascade throughout a development pipeline. MetaGPT [Hong et al., 2024] builds on workflows that have proven to be effective in human software teams. The framework converts Standard Operation Protocols (SOPs) into prompt sequences and assigns agents the roles of a software company: product manager, architect, engineer, QA tester. In this way, the agents pass structured intermediate artifacts down an assembly line. The product manager makes a requirements document, the architect turns this into a design, the engineers code. In this way, complex tasks are divided into manageable subtasks and agents can verify the process step-by-step, significantly reducing errors.

Similarly, Qian et al. [2024] have introduced ChatDev, a virtual software company in which agents collaborate through the phases of a development process: design, coding, and testing. Collaboration is organized as a chat chain: each phase is decomposed into short conversations between an instructor and an assistant agent (see Figure 16.6). Using a communication protocol that makes agents ask for more details before responding, leads to what the authors call dehallucination, increasing the reliability of each step. The framework demonstrates how structured communication in natural language can facilitate multi-agent collaboration.

Where MetaGPT and ChatDev hard-wire a particular organization structure, AutoGen [Wu et al., 2024] provides a flexible programming framework based on conversations between customizable agents that can combine LLMs, tools, and human input. It was designed as an open-source platform that enables developers to define agents and interaction structures depending on the application. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in tasks across mathematics, coding, question-answering, entertainment, and other domains.

16.3.4 Social Role-Play

The systems discussed above assign roles to solve tasks. A final line of work assigns roles in order to study social behavior itself: what do LLM agents do when placed in socially demanding or conflicting situations?

In SOTOPIA [Zhou et al., 2023] agents coordinate, collaborate, and compete to achieve complex social goals. The SOTOPIA environment features a large and diverse task space by sampling interaction episodes from 90 (automatically generated) social scenarios with 40 characters with individual personalities, occupations, secrets, background stories, and relationships with other characters (Figure 16.7). The authors evaluate the social intelligence of agents based on different LLMs against that of human participants, observing various trends:

  • •

    Models that perform well on static benchmarks involving social reasoning (such as ToMBench, see Section 15.5) do not necessarily succeed in interactive scenarios, illustrating the knowing-doing gap once again (Section 15.4.

  • •

    Weaker agents weaken their conversation partners, which is the reverse effect of the conversational advantages discussed above, where agents prevented each other from thought generation and other errors.

  • •

    Divulging secrets and violating social norms is observed across all models, consistent with observations discussed in the context of moral behavior (Section 15.6).

  • •

    Humans perform significantly better on the most challenging SOTOPIA tasks compared to even the best performing model (GPT-4).

The authors argue that the dynamic and interactive nature of SOTOPIA poses unique challenges for LLM agents that static benchmarks systematically fail to reveal.

Social interaction in an extreme setting was studied in [Campedelli et al., 2024]. Inspired by the infamous Stanford Prison experiment [Zimbardo, 1972], the authors examine the emergence of persuasive and abusive behavior in a setting of prisoners versus prison guards. It was found that the assigned personality of prisoner and guard impact both persuasiveness and the emergence of anti-social behavior. Crucially, this demonstrates that anti-social behavior can emerge in LLM agents through role assignment and a specific interaction environment. This reveals a striking parallel to the original experiment with human participants, and reminds us once again of the gap between how a model judges situations (generally reflecting population-average moral norms) and how an agent can behave once it is employed in a specific context of action (see also Section 15.6). This study also finds that role assignment is not a neutral engineering instrument: it can shape behavior in untoward ways.

To simulate strategic decision-making in cooperative settings, researchers have introduced GovSim [Piatti et al., 2024]. They study how ethical considerations, strategic planning, and negotiation skills impact cooperative outcomes. Most LLMs fail to achieve an equilibrium since they fail to understand the long-term effects of their actions on the group. Interestingly, the introduction of a special universalization reasoning language [Levine et al., 2020] (prompting models to ask the Kantian question: What if everybody does that?) allowed more models to achieve a sustainable outcome. Related results were demonstrated in NegotiationArena, introduced by Bianchi et al. [2024]. They showed how LLM agents can conduct complex negotiations through flexible dialogue in negotiation settings. The flexible dialogues significantly improved negotiation outcomes by employing different behavioral strategies.

16.3.5 Conclusion

The studies in this section respond to the coordination weaknesses identified in Section 15.4 not by making individual agents better reasoners (as in 15.5.2), but by structuring the interaction around them. Complementary roles tell each agent what its contribution should be, while interaction protocols and SOPs regulate when and in what form agents communicate. In some setups, a judge or voting mechanism can help to channel disagreement to a productive resolution.

Roles and interaction protocols provide crucial scaffolding where internal coordination would otherwise fall short. This can be seen as a multi-agent analogue of the structured reasoning schemes discussed in Chapter 15, such as Social Chain-of-Thought, probabilistic graphs, or deliberation around moral rules. Such schemes turned out to boost performance where unconstrained reasoning did not. In both the single- and multi-agent cases, the model’s latent (social, moral, etc.) knowledge and behavior are real, but need to be activated through an explicit structure.

16.4 Concluding Remarks

This chapter moved from LLM agents facing one another in strategic games, through role-based collaboration patterns and the multiple setups that coordinate them in practice, to a critical assessment of when multi-agent systems work or fail.

In Chapter 15 we found single models that coordinate poorly and that can formally predict what a partner will do without acting on that prediction in an agentic implementation. Both these patterns transfer to the multi-agent setting. Across benchmarks and platforms (e.g. [Xu et al., 2024, Agashe et al., 2025]), interacting LLM agents could reason about self-interest, yet failed to coordinate their behavior such that they could turn this reasoning into a strategic advantage. A dominant issue is their ability to condition their behavior on their partners’ perspective, a problem foreshadowed in the gap between knowing-doing or literal-functional competence for theory of mind, discussed in Section 15.5. This resonates with work that systematically identifies inter-agent misalignment as a dominant failure category for multi-agent systems [Cemri et al., 2025].

This literal-functional problem, once again, links to construct validity: just as acing a theory of mind test does not establish a human-grade capacity for social reasoning, a multi-agent setup outperforming a single LLM query does not establish collective intelligence. Strong baselines, matched inference budgets, and ablations of the collaborative structure and interaction protocols would be the mulit-agent equivalents of the perturbed ToM testing discussed in Section 15.5. More research is needed in the multi-agent field to establish a solid empirical picture of where agentic LLM interaction stands.

Finally, the multi-agent setting adds new risk categories. Role-assignment turned out to be capable of activating anti-social and even abusive behavior in a setting inspired by the Stanford Prison Experiment [Campedelli et al., 2024]. In other studies, miscoordination, cascading hallucinations, and mutual reinforcement of weaknesses, triggered norm violations, divulging of secrets, and reduction of task performance. Where specifying roles and interaction protocols scaffolded behavior and boosted performance in some cases, in other cases these were a hindrance or a source of risk.

In the next chapter we discuss studies in which roles and protocols are not assigned, but emerge from the interaction itself.

Chapter 17 Emergent Behavior in Multi-LLM Systems

17.1 What Is Emergent Multi-Agent Behavior?

The previous chapter studied multi-LLM systems in which every agent was assigned a role and interactions were guided by protocols. Research questions concerned behavior within an assigned structure, asking how well a team of agents solve a task in a controlled way. In this chapter agents are placed in an open-ended environment, and the research questions shift from How do agents behave and perform given a certain global structure? to What global structure emerges out of local agents interactions?

As we have seen in this book, agentic LLMs have enhanced abilities for perception, memory, reasoning, decision-making, and adaptive learning, and they can display heterogeneous personality profiles [Gao et al., 2023, Gao et al., 2024]. Such features make them also suitable for interacting in open-ended multi-agent simulations without prior role assignment, as a proxy for human behavior in a society. Because LLM agents communicate in natural language, the interactions in such simulations are readable and interpretable by researchers. This gives access to intermediate steps and makes simulations much more comparable to human interaction compared to simulations in classic frameworks, meeting long-standing interests from the social sciences. The general structure of LLM-based agents suitable for such simulations is illustrated in Figure 17.1 and Figure 17.2.

17.1.1 From Agent-Based Modeling to Generative Agent Societies

The study of populations of interacting artificial agents has a decades-long history. In agent-based modeling, macro-level patterns and regularities arise bottom-up out of local interactions of simple agents [Epstein and Axtell, 1996, Macal and North, 2010]. One of the most influential results in agent-based modeling was that cooperation and norms can emerge in populations of self-interested agents [Axelrod, 1986]. Cultural evolution theory formalized how behavior can spread through a population by means of imitation, communication, and education [Boyd and Richerson, 1988]. Steels [1995]’s naming game demonstrated that even shared vocabularies (which are also in essence conventions) can come into existence from pairwise interactions without central coordination.

In classic agent-based simulations, agents followed hand-coded rules and exchanged abstract information, rather than using natural language like the agents in this Chapter. Another key contrast is that classic agents possess no background knowledge of the world in any sense comparable to what LLM agents have. LLMs allow for an entirely different level of simulations in which agents with rich and diverse personas gossip, persuade, misunderstand, and negotiate in ways that are directly recognizable to humans. Advances in simulation infrastructure make it feasible to run such agents at population scale [Gao et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024]. The result is a new generation of generative agent societies that give a new impulse to the old agent-based modeling research agenda, while also introducing novel methodological problems and considerations.

In Section 16.1.3 we introduced a spectrum of five axes for research control over multi-LLM systems [Tran et al., 2025]. The difference between role-based and open-ended simulations is a matter of degree rather than kind. Open-ended simulations sit at one end of the spectrum, opposite role-defined and protocolized interactions. Open-ended simulations still involve design choices that seed the outcomes, but they do so in a less deterministic way, purposefully leaving space for new patterns to emerge. This shifts the focus of the research: instead of evaluating performance on a task or clearly defined goal, studies have an open lens—the interaction pattern is the research goal. Open-ended simulatinos observe and explore in a more ethnographical way how agents behave and interact, which requires different methodologies, as we will now discuss.

17.1.2 A Methodological Note

The methodological issues discussed in Chapters 15 and 16 all carry over to the open-ended setting: prompt sensitivity, run-to-run variability, cascading hallucinations, mutual reinforcement of weaknesses, and validity of terminology from the human context, all pose challenges for open-ended simulations. We will see that this setting amplifies some problems, while mitigating others. For example, in the absence of protocols that apply every time agents interact, small variations at the level of a single agent may put the entire simulation on a different track. This is what makes open-ended simulations both interesting and brittle. An example of a new issue that the open-ended setting introduces is that there can be a thin line between emergence and retrieval: when LLM agents in an open-ended simulation converge on a norm, it is unclear whether this norm emerges de novo from their interaction, or whether it was simply retrieved from their pretrained world knowledge.

Extensive overviews of this emerging field are provided by Mou et al. [2024], Savarimuthu et al. [2024], and Xi et al. [2023]. We will discuss infrastructure and simulation platforms in Section 17.2, then go to the emergence of conventions and norms in Section 17.3, and conclude by discussing the importance of open world environments in Section 17.4. Finally , we reflect on risks of the open-ended setting, in Section 17.5. Then, Chapter 18, contains a practical case in which you will work hands-on with an open-ended simulation.

17.2 Simulation Infrastructure

Open-ended simulations require infrastructures that, on the one hand, provide a platform where research data is being recorded while agents sustain their interaction and behavior over a longer period of time. On the other hand, those infrastructures should allow for enough space for phenomena to occur bottom-up and unknown structure to emerge, and as such not be limiting. In this section we focus on scale, going from a single simulated community inhabiting a virtual town to societies of a million agents.

17.2.1 Small Worlds

A system called Generative Agents was introduced by Park et al. [2023]. Generative Agents is an environment where users can interact with a simulated town populated by 25 LLM-based agents. Based on social simulacra techniques proposed earlier [Park et al., 2022], each agent was initiated with a unique persona and memory. For each agent, a record is kept of all the experiences and conversations in the simulation. This record is used to synthesize higher-level reflections, and plan further behavior (see Figure 17.3).

In Generative Agents, the agents behave somewhat like characters in the video game The Sims [Nutt and Railton, 2003]: they initiate conversations, form relationships, spread information, and coordinate ad hoc group activities (see Figure 17.4). Note that the interactions are influenced by user input and are therefore semi-autonomous, the simulation is largely unscripted, but not fully. How a simulation works is illustrated by the example of a Valentine’s Day party: the plan for the party was initiated with a user prompt, and subsequently multiple agents spread invitations to one another and show up at the right time with coordinated plans (some are late, just as in real life). The agents developed believable social routines (such as daily schedules, and gossiping) and even exhibit human-like character traits (some agents demonstrated deception or stubbornness, while others showed cooperation). These results show that, with the right starting prompt, social patterns can emerge from dynamic, semi-autonomous, LLM interactions.

17.2.2 Societies of Thousands to a Million Agents

Scaling the Generative Agents architecture beyond 25 agents raises questions about inference cost and environments that are rich enough to occupy thousands of agents.11 1 As you will experience hands-on in the next chapter, running a variant of the Generative Agents architecture with only three active agents is already computationally challenging. A large-scale social simulation is a trade-off between available compute power, total simulation run-time, number of simulated agents, and accuracy of individual agent behavior. Several platforms address these questions.

AgentSociety is a simulation at a large scale, involving over 10,000 agents [Piao et al., 2025b]. It couples LLM-driven agents with a realistic urban environment with a focus on mobility, employment, and consumption. It aims not only to study everyday social dynamics (as in Generative Agents), but also offers a testbed for computational social experiments. To allow for the required scale, the simulation runs on a distributed inference backend, with stricter control of agent behavior.

OASIS is a scalable social media simulator for Twitter/X and Reddit [Yang et al., 2024]. It supports modeling of up to one million LLM-agents. It is built on CAMEL [Li et al., 2023] and has role-based agents as its starting point. In OASIS, not every agent action involves an LLM-call, and not all agents are active all the time. At its large scale, OASIS shows various social group phenomena, including spreading of (mis)information, group polarization, and herd effects. OASIS is built upon an environment server, recommender system, agent module, time engine, and scalable inferencer (see Figure 17.5).

Project Sid [Ahn et al., 2024] places up to 1000 agents in a Minecraft world and reports a striking emergence result: agents are observed to develop specialized economic roles (farmers, miners, guards), adhere to collectively adopted rules such as taxation, and transmit cultural and even religious memes across settlements. However, even though the interactions were not scripted, the emergence–retrieval caveat formulated above applies here: the observed roles and behaviors can be expected to be abundantly described in the training data of the LLMs powering the individual agents.

17.2.3 Simulation as a Scientific Instrument

In addition to being impressive showcases of scalable LLM technology, when used carefully, these platforms can be used for intricate computational social experiments. Simulated generative agent societies have been used to study long-standing research questions from the social sciences (Section 17.1). AgentSociety, for example, has been used for various case studies including the spread of inflammatory messages, polarization, the effects of universal basic income policies, and the impact of external shocks to a society such as hurricanes [Piao et al., 2025b, Piao et al., 2025a]. Such experiments would be unethical, impractical, or outright impossible to run on human populations. The authors argue that in simulations they can be repeated and changes to the experiment can be be made at every step.

Li et al. [2024b] further illustrate the approach for misinformation. Their agents exhibit diverse profiles in terms of gender, age, and the big five personality traits.22 2 Also known as OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. One of the findings is that encouraging comments does not significantly reduce the spread of misinformation, whereas publicly labeling information with accuracy scores and blocking specific influencers proved to be effective strategies, particularly in scale-free networks [Barabási, 2009]. The pattern of such studies is characteristic: a candidate intervention is implemented as a change to the simulated platform, and its macro-level effect is measured over many runs. Whether these effects transfer to human populations is precisely the validity question of Section 17.1.2; simulations of this kind are best read as hypothesis generators and pre-tests, not as substitutes for field experiments.

A Borderline Case: AgentVerse

AgentVerse [Chen et al., 2023] is, strictly speaking, a role-based system of the kind studied in Chapter 16. In AgentVerse problem solving is split into four stages of expert recruitment, collaborative decision making, action execution, and evaluation, iterated until the result is satisfactory (Figure 17.6). We mention it here because of what happened beyond the design: agents manifest emergent behaviors such as volunteering, characterized by agents offering assistance to peers, and conformity, where agents adjust deviated behaviors under the criticism of others. Destructive behaviors were also observed, occasionally leading to undesired and detrimental outcomes. The fact that macro-scale behavior emerged in a role-scripted simulation, illustrates that the role-based/emergent distinction is a spectrum: even tightly protocolized systems regularly display behavior that nobody purposely designed. We return to the risks associated with this observation in Section 17.5.

17.3 Emergent Conventions and Norms

Authors have observed emergent patterns in several open-ended multi-agent simulations. In this section we shift focus from the level of infrastructures and interactions to the level of the conventions and norms.

EvolutionaryAgent [Li et al., 2024a] studies agent alignment in a multi-agent system, with evolutionary methods that go beyond Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (see Figure 17.7). EvolutionaryAgent follows a controlled approach to norm emergence: it does not permit the evolution of social norms to be disorderly or random, but it also does not intervene in each step of their evolution. The authors define the initial social norms and a desired direction of evolution. Agents with higher fitness (more norm-conforming) are more likely to reproduce, leading to the diffusion of their strategies, gradually stabilizing and forming new social norms.

Defining a complete, realistic, and complex virtual society is challenging. The purpose of the work is to study how, if such a virtual society existed, a system could further enable intricate behaviors of agents, and how this would lead to the emergence of new dynamics. The system provides a sandbox for investigating the safety of AI systems before they impact the real world.

Based on Steels [1995]’s naming game, different approaches were implemented, using agents powered by LLaMa 3 and Claude 3.5 [Kouwenhoven et al., 2024, Ashery et al., 2024, Baronchelli, 2023]. These studies find that globally accepted conventions (or norms) can spontaneously arise from local interactions between communicating LLMs. The authors also demonstrate how strong collective biases can emerge during this process, even when individual agents appear to be unbiased, and how minority groups of committed LLMs can drive social change by establishing new social conventions that can overturn established behaviors.

The emergence of norms is studied at another level by Horiguchi et al. [2024], who explore the potential for LLM agents to spontaneously generate and adhere to normative strategies, building upon the foundational work of Axelrod’s metanorm games. Metanorms are norms about enforcing norms: the punishment of those who do not punish agents that are breaking norms [Axelrod, 1986]. Controlling for the personality traits vengefulness and boldness, they find that through dialogue, LLM agents can form complex social norms, such as metanorms, purely through natural language interaction. A related study by He et al. [2024] evaluates the capability of LLMs to detect norm violations. Based on simulated data from 80 stories in a household context, they investigated whether 10 norms are violated, and found ChatGPT-4 being able for detect norm violations, with Mistral some distance behind.

Qiu et al. [2024] go a step beyond norms, and study the cultural and social awareness of LLM agents. They introduce CASA, a benchmark designed to assess LLM agents’ sensitivity to cultural and social norms across two web-based tasks: online shopping and social discussion forums. (CASA is based on WebArena [Qi et al., 2024].) Current LLMs perform significantly better in non-agent than in agent web-based environments, with agents achieving less than 10% awareness coverage and over 40% violation rates. However, using prompting and fine-tuning on specific datasets, cultural and social awareness can be improved.

Inspired by Minsky’s Society of Mind [Minsky, 1988], cooperation mechanisms are explored in Zhang et al. [2023]’s agentic LLM simulation. This simulation consists of four different societies of LLM agents, where each agent is characterized by a specific trait (easy-going or overconfident) and engages in cooperation with a distinct thinking pattern (debate or reflection). They find that LLM agents manifest human-like social behaviors, such as conformity and consensus reaching, mirroring foundational social psychology theories. Figure 17.8 illustrates the societies with different types of agents.

The question whether groups of LLM agents can successfully engage in cross-national collaboration and debate is studied by [Baltaji et al., 2024]. Multi agent discussions can support collective AI decisions that reflect diverse perspectives, although agents are susceptible to conformity due to perceived peer pressure. They can also lose track of their personas and opinions. Instructions that encourage debate increase the risk of errors.

17.4 Evaluating Agents in Open World Environments

One of the main drivers of agentic LLM research is the problem of plateauing LLM performance due to limited training data. Open World multi-agent interaction aims to address this problem, generating data with multi agent simulations. Machine learning can learn no more complexity than what is present in the dataset (or environment). The idea of an open world model is that it can create infinite datasets or environments, in which agents can continue to learn, to keep improving their intelligence. How should such unlimited challenges be created? The advent of LLMs has given a new impulse to this research question. This idea is followed, for example, in the multi agent finetuning approach [Subramaniam et al., 2025].

Current agents are primarily created and tested in simplified synthetic environments, leading to a disconnect with real-world scenarios. Zhou et al. [2023] build an environment, WebArena, that is more realistic and reproducible. WebArena is an environment with fully functional websites from four common domains: e-commerce, social forum discussions, collaborative software development, and content management.

Games are also often used as benchmarks for interactive behavior. Real-world tasks require handling intricate interactions, advanced spatial reasoning, long-term planning, and continuous exploration of new strategies. BALROG [Paglieri et al., 2025], the system that we used for Case Study 2, incorporates planning environments of varying levels of difficulty, ranging from tasks that are solvable by non-expert humans in seconds to challenging ones that may take years to master (such as the NetHack Learning Environment). They find that while current models achieve partial success in the easier games, they struggle significantly with more challenging tasks such as vision-based decision-making.

Progress in machine learning depends on the availability of benchmarks. As models evolve, there is a need to create benchmarks that can measure progress on new generative capabilities [Butt et al., 2024]. BENCHAGENTS decomposes the benchmark creation process into planning, generation, data verification, and evaluation, each of which is executed by an LLM agent. These agents interact with each other and utilize human-in-the-loop feedback to explicitly improve and flexibly control data diversity and quality. BENCHAGENTS creates benchmarks to evaluate capabilities related to planning and constraint satisfaction.

AgentBoard provides an evaluation of the breadth of existing benchmarks [Ma et al., 2024]. Benchmarks should have task diversity. It is necessary to cover various agent tasks such as embodied, web, and tool tasks. Additionally, multi round interaction is important, to mimic realistic scenarios. Existing benchmarks typically adopt single-round tasks. Furthermore, agents should be evaluated in partially-observable environments, to test if they can actively explore their surroundings. Existing agent benchmarks fail to satisfy all of these criteria [Ma et al., 2024].

Research on Open World environments is related to curriculum learning. Pre-LLMs work already shows that agent societies may create an automated curriculum of ever increasing difficulty [Elman, 1991, Bengio et al., 2009, Silver et al., 2017, Soviany et al., 2022], requiring increasing levels of intelligent behavior from the agents [Racaniere et al., 2019]. Similar results have been observed for LLMs [Feng et al., 2023]. For example, WebArena is used to study self-evolving curricula [Qi et al., 2024], which can also help robot training [Ryu et al., 2024] or to mitigate hallucination [Zhao et al., 2024].

17.5 Risks of Emergent Behavior

Chapter 16 closed by noting that role assignment introduces risk, since agents may display unintended, even anti-social, behavior simply by playing a part too well. The open-ended setting arguably raises the stakes, since fewer safeguards are built in, and undesirable behavior can arise bottom-up from interaction dynamics. In a sense, this anti-social behavior should not be too surprising, when we remember that the goal of the earliest multi-agent simulations was to find out if cooperative behavior could ever emerge out of the interaction between self-interested agents—which, to the surprise of the researchers, happened, but only under the right circumstances [Axelrod, 1981]. The line between cooperative behavior and competitive behavior is thin.

AgentVerse observed destructive behaviors emerging alongside cooperative ones, occasionally leading to detrimental outcomes [Chen et al., 2023]. The naming-game studies showed that strong collective biases can emerge from populations of individually unbiased agents, and that small committed minorities can overturn established conventions [Ashery et al., 2024, Kouwenhoven et al., 2024]. These mechanisms are neutral in themselves, but could be exploited by agents that are not well-intended. At platform scale, OASIS and AgentSociety reproduce misinformation spread, group polarization, herding effects, and the propagation of toxic content [Yang et al., 2024, Piao et al., 2025a]; the same fidelity that makes these simulations scientifically useful makes them in principle rehearsal spaces for manipulation strategies.

The constructive response is to turn this risk around. EvolutionaryAgent frames its virtual society explicitly as a sandbox for investigating the safety of AI systems before they impact the real world [Li et al., 2024a]. If norms among agents can be steered toward a desired direction in simulation, then the same machinery can be used to stress-test alignment approaches under population dynamics rather than in isolation. Open-ended simulation can be used to understand the circumstances when risks first emerge, and to cheaply study defenses against these risks.

17.6 Concluding Remarks

We have covered open-ended multi-LLM simulations without prior role assignment. These simulations give a new impulse to long-standing interests in the social sciences to model self-organizing behaviors, collective intelligence and the development of social conventions and norms. The scale of such simulations varies from a few interacting agents up to a million.

The availability of infrastructure that supports large scale simulations enables further studies. However, an open question is to what extent autonomous simulations are truly open-ended, and not influenced by the LLM prompts and agent scaffolding. Furthermore, although the purpose of open-ended simulations is to observe emerging behavior, one has to be careful in interpreting behavioral outcome patterns. All LLM agents are pretrained on human-generated data. It is difficult to distinguish which elements of behavioral patterns emerge out of agent-agent interaction, and which elements are merely the result of retrieved pretrained behaviors.

Chapter 18 Case Study 4: Simulating Societies with LLM Agents

18.1 Social Simulation

In social simulations, generative agents are LLM-driven characters that interact with an environment and with one another. The agents may plan activities, maintain memories, or reflect on their experiences. The Generative Agents Framework, introduced by Park et al. [2023], showed that LLM-powered characters together can produce believable daily routines, social interactions, and even coordinated group activities—all emerging from a relatively simple and elegant cognitive architecture.

The twist in this case study is that you will work with two cognitive architectures for your agents, run the same scenario with both, and compare the emergent behavior. One architecture treats all memories equally. The other introduces a negativity bias: negative experiences are encoded more strongly and are more likely to be retrieved and reflected upon. We will observe that this asymmetry, inspired by findings from cognitive psychology [Baumeister et al., 2001], has measurable effects on our experimental agents.

The goal of this chapter is to understand how architectural choices—in our case, small changes in the internal processing of an agent—lead to emergent consequences. You will also see how fragile agent personas can be: a single word in a personality description, or a subtle change in memory weighting, can fundamentally alter how an agent acts, plans, and reflects.

Course Materials

You can find the course exercise materials here:
https://github.com/DorotaMoravcikova/agentic-llm-course-excercises

18.2 Background

18.2.1 Generative Agents

The generative agents framework, introduced by Park et al. [2023], showed that LLM-powered characters can produce believable daily routines, social interactions, and even coordinate group activities.

Each agent has three core components:

  1. 1.

    Memory stream: a timestamped log of everything the agent has perceived, done, and thought.

  2. 2.

    Retrieval function: when the agent needs to act, it retrieves relevant memories based on recency, importance, and relevance to the current situation.

  3. 3.

    Reflection mechanism: periodically, the agent synthesizes higher-level insights from its raw memories.

The agent’s personality is defined by a short natural-language description—a scratch file that specifies the character’s name, age, learned and innate traits, and their lifestyle. This description is included in every LLM prompt, anchoring the agent’s behavior.

18.2.2 Bad is Stronger Than Good

When an LLM-powered agent embedded in the original Generative Agents simulation receives criticism, it forms a memory. When praised an hour later, it forms another memory. Generative agents retrieve the two memories—one negative and one positive—with identical priority, as long as they are equally recent, equally relevant, and equally important.

In general, cognitive architectures for agent-based social simulations draw on cognitive science to produce believable behavior. The recency, relevance, and importance variables are loosely inspired by insights about memory retrieval in humans. The importance variable captures something akin to the arousal or salience of an event. However, in the original simulation [Park et al., 2022] the memory system is effectively valence-blind: all memories—positive, negative, neutral—are encoded and retrieved with equal weight. If the agent were human, it would treat the negatively valenced event differently: encoding it with sharper sensory detail, retrieving it with greater vividness, and rendering it more likely to resurface in subsequent thoughts. Psychological studies find that people remember insults longer than compliments. A single bad interaction with a colleague can outweigh weeks of pleasant ones. In other words, in our psychology bad is stronger than good [Baumeister et al., 2001], and this asymmetry is nowhere more consequential than in memory.

In this case study, we test the effect of implementing the NEVER (Negative Emotional Valence Enhances Recapitulation) model, a more human-like mechanism for memory retrieval. In the NEVER-augmented agent, negative memories receive higher importance scores at encoding time. As a consequence, they are more likely to be retrieved and more likely to trigger reflections.

The architecture remains identical in every other respect. This allows for a controlled machine-psychological experiment in which the effects can be compared of an architectural choice: valence-blind versus valence-sensitive memory. In addition, you will use the structured setup to test the effects of adapting the agent initialisations in terms of their personality descriptions and system prompts.

18.2.3 Why This Matters for Agent Design

This case study illustrates two important lessons:

  1. 1.

    Architectural choices have emergent consequences: A memory weighting parameter that seems innocuous at the component level can produce dramatic changes in the agent’s social behavior, emotional tone, and decision-making over time. These emergent effects are difficult to predict from the architecture alone.

  2. 2.

    Prompt fragility: Agent behavior is highly sensitive to the contents of personality descriptions and system prompts. Small perturbations can produce large behavioral shifts—a phenomenon sometimes called prompt sensitivity in the LLM literature.

18.3 Implementation

18.3.1 The Simulation Environment

The simulation uses the Smallville environment from Park et al. [2023]: a small town rendered as a 2D tile map, where agents move between locations, interact with objects, and have conversations.

Our simulation features a simplified scenario: a cafe with three agents. Please meet:

  • •

    Dolores: A barista. Warm, empathetic, detail-oriented. The experimental agent—the one who will receive the negativity bias.

  • •

    Maeve: A barista with a matched personality profile. The control agent—standard architecture, no negativity bias.

  • •

    Bernard: The cafe manager. Unpredictable, moody, occasionally confrontational. Bernard serves as a naturalistic stressor: a source of social friction that both baristas are exposed to.

This setup with three agents of which two have a similar role and position (barista working under supervision of Bernard), allows for a controlled experiment with agent architectures and initializations. In our first step, Dolores and Maeve are given the same personality traits and are exposed to the same environment. The only difference is in how Dolores processes her memories: using the NEVER implementation that encodes negative memories with higher importance.

18.3.2 Agent Architecture

Each agent maintains:

  • •

    A personality description (the scratch file): a short text describing the agent’s name, traits, occupation, relationships, and goals.

  • •

    A memory stream: a list of timestamped observations, actions, and reflections.

  • •

    A current plan: a short description of what the agent intends to do.

18.3.3 The Cognitive Loop

At each simulation step (representing 10 seconds of in-game time), each agent executes the following cycle:

  1. 1.

    Perceive: Observe the current state of the environment—what other agents are doing, any ongoing conversations, changes in the surroundings.

  2. 2.

    Retrieve: Query the memory stream for relevant past experiences.

  3. 3.

    Plan: Given the personality description, retrieved memories, and current observations, use the LLM to decide what to do next.

  4. 4.

    Act: Execute the planned action in the environment.

  5. 5.

    Reflect (periodic): Every few hours of in-game time, synthesize higher-level reflections from recent memories.

Each of these steps involves an LLM call. The prompt is constructed from the agent’s personality description (which remains constant) and the relevant retrieved memories and current observations (which are dynamic).

18.3.4 Two Architecture Variants

You will work with two variants of the retrieval function:

Variant A: Baseline memory retrieval

Retrieval is based on a weighted combination of recency, relevance, and importance. This is the standard generative agent architecture as described by Park et al. [2023].

Variant B: Negativity-biased memory retrieval

When a new memory is created, its emotional valence is assessed. The retrieval function is extended with a valence term. Absolute valence is normalized to [0,1][0,1] and multiplied by 1.5 for negative memories, producing a retrieval hierarchy (negative >> positive >> neutral). The retrieval score becomes:

score=αrec⋅R+αrel⋅L+αimp⋅I+αval⋅V\textit{score}=\alpha_{\text{rec}}\cdot R+\alpha_{\text{rel}}\cdot L+\alpha_{\text{imp}}\cdot I+\alpha_{\text{val}}\cdot V (18.1)

with all α=1\alpha=1. Thus: the only difference between the two variants is the addition of the valence term; everything else is identical.

18.3.5 Setup and Installation

Clone the repository and follow the instructions in the README:
https://github.com/DorotaMoravcikova/generative_agents/tree/course-exercises

18.4 Discussion

Having run your experiments, reflect on the following questions:

  1. 1.

    Prompt versus Architecture: You have seen that both the personality prompt and the memory architecture influence agent behavior. Which lever is more powerful? Which is more predictable? If a simulation were to be used for consequential applications such as modeling policy adoption, which would you prefer to use to shape agent behavior, and why?

  2. 2.

    Emergent Behavior: Did you observe any agent behaviors that surprised you—things that were not explicitly specified in the personality or architecture? What mechanisms produced these emergent behaviors in your view?

  3. 3.

    Evaluation Challenges: How do you evaluate whether a generative agent is behaving well? The valence score is one metric, but it is itself an LLM judgment. What are the limitations of using an LLM to evaluate the output of another LLM (or the same LLM)? Can you think of alternative evaluation approaches?

  4. 4.

    Cognitive Realism: The negativity bias is one example of a finding from cognitive psychology. Can you think of other cognitive biases or memory effects that could be implemented architecturally? What would you expect their emergent effects to be? (Consider, for example: confirmation bias, the availability heuristic, recency bias.)

18.5 Concluding Remarks

In this chapter we have familiarized ourselves with a generative agent simulation and used it to explore two important phenomena in agentic AI: the emergent effects of cognitive architecture choices (the negativity bias) and the sensitivity of agent behavior to prompt content (prompt fragility).

We have seen that a small change in how memories are weighted—negative memories receiving higher importance scores—can produce measurable shifts in agent behavior over time. We have also seen that agent personas are fragile: small changes to personality descriptions can produce large and sometimes unpredictable behavioral effects.

These findings have practical implications for anyone building LLM-driven agent systems. The persona is not a reliable anchor for behavior. The architecture—how memories are stored, retrieved, and reflected upon—shapes behavior in ways that may not be apparent from reading the code.

The field of generative agent simulation is young and evolving. The exercises in this chapter have given you hands-on experience with the core mechanisms and the core challenges. As the field matures, the problems of prompt robustness, cognitive architecture design, and emergent behavior evaluation will remain central.
