Part VI Advanced Topics

Agentic LLMs are new, and there is much research activity, on many topics. In this part we have selected four research areas where important developments are under way. These are: synthetic data generation, advanced architectures, mechanistic interpretability, and perspectives on the cognitive architectures of agents. There are certainly many more interesting research directions in agentic LLMs; we have selected these topics because they connect to important points that were raised earlier in the book.

Note that the purpose of the previous chapters was to explain matters as clearly as possible—suitable for a master’s course. The purpose of the next chapters is to cover more advanced material—suitable for a master’s thesis. Of course we still try to be clear, but the speed will be higher, and the depth will be deeper, with more references to research papers. We encourage you to look up these sources. If you are looking for inspiration for your own further research, we hope that these chapters will be of help.

Chapter 19 *Synthetic Data Generation for Training Agentic LLMs

19.1 The Importance of Data

The rapid scaling of LLMs has led to a significant demand for training and evaluation data. Some have coined training data the digital oil, reflecting the importance as primary ingredient for AI development. Furthermore, data is increasingly becoming a differentiating factor since other components of the pipeline, such as model architectures, are homogenizing [Kim et al., 2025a]. As models continue to scale, they require trillions of words of human-generated text scraped from the internet; however, there is only a limited amount of human-generated data available, which raises the question of whether training data could become the main bottleneck to scaling, see Figure 19.1 [Villalobos et al., 2024]. Moreover, as data requirements grow in scale, the acquisition of data becomes increasingly prohibitive in terms of cost and time, since most of the straightforward sources are becoming exhausted. Furthermore, issues with privacy, copyright, and bias cause the field to be looking beyond the curation of web-based human-generated data, and instead turn towards synthetic data generation [Liang et al., 2022].

LLMs increasingly generate the data that trains the next generation of LLMs themselves: models are prompted to produce instructions, dialogues, reasoning traces, and even entire training corpora that are then used to finetune, distill and evaluate other models [Long et al., 2024]. This self-reinforcing loop lowers the cost and effort of data collection compared to sourcing and annotating human-generated text, while also offering fine-grained control over style, difficulty, and coverage of the resulting datasets. By now, this approach has drawn significant industrial [Kapania et al., 2025] and academic interest [Viswanathan et al., 2025, Alismail and Lanquillon, 2025], spanning applications from general-purpose instruction tuning to the more specialized data needed to train agentic behaviors such as tool use, planning, and multi-step reasoning (illustrated in Figure 1.1 on page 1.1).

The growing reliance on model-generated data has also introduced a new term in the scaling laws (Chapter 4), one that accounts for the proportion of synthetic data present in a pre-training corpus. Recent work such as SYNTHLLM [Qin et al., 2025] illustrates why this matters: by automatically extracting high-level concepts from source documents and recombining them through a graph-based algorithm, it generates synthetic corpora diverse enough to follow a predictable, rectified scaling law across model sizes. In this version of the scaling laws, the gains taper off earlier (before other token budgets typically used in pretraining), and larger models reach their optimal performance on comparatively fewer tokens than smaller ones. This suggests that synthetic data can be tuned not just for volume, but also for the shape of the scaling curve it produces.

Beyond scaling behavior, generating data for agentic capabilities—tool use, planning, and multi-step reasoning—increasingly depends on coordinated multi-agent workflows rather than on a single generator model. Specialized agents can take on distinct roles (e.g., proposing tasks, executing them, critiquing the results), which tends to produce data that is of higher quality, more diverse, and structurally closer to what agentic training actually requires. Matrix [Wang et al., 2025a] is one example of this direction: a decentralized framework in which control and data flow are both represented as messages passed between agents through distributed queues, allowing the pipeline to scale horizontally without a central coordinator. Let us have a closer loop on the synthetic training pipeline.

19.2 Distillation Loop

Using synthetic data in the agentic LLM training pipeline follows the overall distillation loop, as shown in Figure 19.2. A generator (a strong model, or an orchestration of several agents) uses a small amount of seed or real data to generate a large pool of raw synthetic data. That pool is then curated (Section 19.4) before being used to train or distill a model. Crucially, the resulting model can itself become the generator for the next iteration. This closing of the self-reinforcing loop brings considerable risk to training stability and downstream performance (see also the discussion of stability in metalearning, Chapter 8).

Distillation is the special case of synthetic-data generation in which the generator is a stronger model whose capability we are trying to transfer. In knowledge distillation, a compact student model learns to copy a more capable teacher [Hinton et al., 2015, Hu et al., 2022]. It can do so by directly optimizing against the teacher’s output predictions, or it can do so by simply training on synthetic data emitted by a teacher. The goal of distillation is to get a more efficient version of the teacher, both at inference time and in terms of data cost, without sacrificing too much task performance. Distillation has been applied widely, including in agentic settings [Li et al., 2025a, Du et al., 2025, e.g.,]. Distillation can also be used to derive preference data for instruction tuning. Zephyr [Tunstall et al., 2024], for example, was trained with AI feedback, where outputs are generated and ranked by strong teacher models, aligning a small model with user intent at minimal data and training cost.

Four axes of distillation

Concrete distillation methods can be organized along four axes. (1) The signal: whether the student imitates teacher logits, full output sequences, or a scalar reward derived from the teacher. (2) The data source: whether the sequences being scored are generated by the teacher or sampled from the student. (3) The timing: whether that data is produced once up front (off-policy) or continuously as the student changes (on-policy). (4) The teacher identity: whether the teacher is a stronger separate model or the student itself.

We will now discuss these four axes of distillation.

19.2.1 Signal: The Distillation Objective

When we have white-box access to the teacher’s (qq) probabilities, the student pθp_{\theta} is trained to make the student’s next-token distribution match the teacher’s. In distillation, we often soften the distributions with a shared temperature τ\tau (so qτ​(⋅)∝exp⁡(z/τ)q^{\tau}(\cdot)\propto\exp(z/\tau) for logits zz). A generic distillation loss over a corpus of sequences is

ℒ(θ)=Ex[∑tD(qτ(⋅∣x<t)∥pθτ(⋅∣x<t))],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathrm{E}_{x}\left[\sum_{t}D\big(q^{\tau}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\,\|\,p^{\tau}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\big)\right], (19.1)

where the sum runs over token positions tt, DD is a divergence (most commonly the KL divergence), and the temperature τ>1\tau>1 flattens both distributions so that the student also learns from the teacher’s relative confidence. When only the teacher’s text is available (black-box distillation, the usual case when distilling from a proprietary API), we no longer observe qq but only some tokens that we sample from it. The soft target qτ(⋅∣x<t)q^{\tau}(\cdot\mid x_{<t}) then collapses to a one-hot vector on the sampled token, the divergence DD becomes the token-level cross-entropy, and Equation 19.1 reduces to ordinary supervised fine-tuning on the teacher’s generations. In Section 19.3 we discuss the Self-Instruct technique [Wang et al., 2023b]. This methods perform distillation from the data side, and is therefore a black-box approach.

19.2.2 Data Source: Teacher-Student Paradigm

In distillation, the intuitive assumption is that a bigger, stronger teacher is always better. However, there are exceptions [Xu et al., 2025a, Li et al., 2025b]. A capable teacher may produce traces that are too long, too complex, or stylistically mismatched for a small student to absorb. This phenomenon is known as the small model learnability gap. Figure 19.3 illustrates a situation where small students learn more from the shorter reasoning of a weaker teacher than from the elaborate chains of thought of a frontier model. The practical implication is that the teacher should be chosen relative to the current capabilities of the student rather than maximized in isolation [Zhang et al., 2026a].

19.2.3 Timing: Off-policy versus On-policy Distillation

The third axis concerns timing. The most common recipe in distillation is off-policy distillation. Here we sample a fixed dataset of completions from the teacher and then fine-tune the student on them (as in the black-box case above). This is a simple and parallelizable approach, but it suffers from a train/inference mismatch. The student is only once shown teacher-generated token sequences at training time, yet at deployment time it must continue its own, possibly flawed, sequences, which may be different than the ones it has been trained on. This exposure bias compounds over long agentic trajectories.

On-policy distillation addresses this by sampling sequences from the student itself and having the teacher score them, all within the loop. Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) trains the student on its self-generated output sequences using teacher feedback on those sequences [Agarwal et al., 2024]. The student is corrected exactly on the distribution of the states that it actually visits.

This on-policy view makes the connection to reinforcement learning through imitation learning explicit. The per-token teacher divergence in Equation 19.1 acts as a dense, token-level reward. Distillation is turned into a form of reinforcement learning where the teacher, rather than a sparse outcome checker, supplies the reward signal [Lu and Lab, 2025]. Hybrid schemes push this idea further by selectively imitating the teacher only where it helps during a reinforcement learning phase [Zhang et al., 2026b].

19.2.4 Teacher Identity: Self-Distillation and Self-Improvement

The teacher and student model do not have to be different. When the teacher and student model are the same, distillation becomes self-improvement: the model generates candidate solutions, keeps the ones that pass a check, and trains on them. STaR [Zelikman et al., 2022a] bootstraps reasoning in this way, iteratively generating rationales, retaining those that reach the correct answer, and finetuning on them.

Another approach is Self-Play Finetuning (SPIN) [Chen et al., 2024]. In this method the model distinguishes its own generations from reference data across iterations, improving alignment without any external teacher. Perhaps surprisingly, even repeated self-distillation, with no new data source, can yield measurable gains, up to a point [Pareek et al., 2024].

Self-improvement is most powerful when candidate outputs can be verified cheaply. In such cases, an external signal can still be incorporated effectively. This is the case for problems defined in code and math, as solutions are easy to execute and check. CURE, for example, is a reinforcement learning framework whose reward co-evolves a model’s coding and unit-test-generation abilities from their interaction outcomes. There is no ground-truth code as supervision. Since code is easy to execute and check, the coder and the test-writer act as mutually adapting agents, enabling long-horizon optimization on hard problems. The same principle underlies self-challenging and self-evolving agents, which propose their own increasingly difficult tasks and update their generation policy over time [Zhou et al., 2025, Huang et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025b].

19.3 Simulating Human-generated Content

The move away from naturally occurring human-generated text, either directly obtained or scraped from the web, is perhaps best seen in the evolution from curated human-generated instruction data towards datasets where synthetic generation plays a more central role. We will now discuss these methods, where datasets are, in their core, still based on human-generated data.

As an example of a resource where humans still underpin most of the data, Natural Instructions [Mishra et al., 2022], contains 61 distinct tasks, their human-authored instructions, and 193k task instances (input-output pairs). The instructions were gathered from instruction documents for existing NLP datasets, all mapped to a unified schema. Experiments with LLMs indicate that models benefit from observing the instructions alongside examples, although these models have remained far behind an estimated performance upper bound.

Subsequent work focuses on increasing the number of unique tasks and task types [Wang et al., 2022], varying the length of the instructions [Bach et al., 2022], or including particularly difficult tasks [Srivastava et al., 2023]. Importantly, all these meta-datasets (datasets of datasets) are still ultimately built from human benchmarks: every sample they contain is authored by a person. Therefore, there is a practical limit to how much of this data can be freely found online.

Because these approaches rely on large amounts of human supervision in the form of crowd-sourced datasets, recent work focuses on generating synthetic data that fills the same role. Here, we see the creation of datasets such as Unnatural Instructions [Honovich et al., 2023], which contain creative and diverse instructions collected with little human labor, instead relying on prompting various LLMs. Experiments indicate that training models on the somewhat noisy Unnatural Instructions dataset yields results comparable to those trained on high-quality, human-curated data, as shown in Figure 19.4. This result suggests that machine-generated data offers a cost-efficient alternative to human labor for expanding and diversifying training datasets.

The simulation of human-like text, code, and reasoning by generative models has unlocked new methodologies for both training and evaluating machine learning systems. By prompting strong models, researchers can generate highly diverse and complex datasets that mimic human content generation. For example, PersonaHub [Ge et al., 2025] steers a generation process with a large-scale collection of personas, using them to prompt LLMs towards a far greater diversity of synthetic data than unconditioned generation would produce.

Similar to self-improvement, training on synthetic data has shown much promise in domains where model outputs are relatively easy to verify, such as mathematics [Yang et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2023], programming [Haluptzok et al., 2023], and games [Wang et al., 2023a].

19.3.1 Generating Training Data

We will now focus on generating training data. The use of synthetic data for training has transitioned from a niche data augmentation technique to a core component of modern model alignment and reasoning pipelines. Techniques such as Self-Instruct [Wang et al., 2023b] have demonstrated that smaller, open-weight models can be instruction-tuned using data generated entirely by a stronger, proprietary model. The process, as shown in Figure 19.5, involves seeding an LLM with a small set of human-written instructions and prompting it to iteratively generate novel task descriptions, inputs, and outputs. The simulated human content allows models to acquire complex zero-shot capabilities without the need for large groups of human annotators.

Leveraging existing data

Other approaches combine curated human data with synthetic data, instead of replacing one with the other. Gunasekar et al. [2023] show that training on a mixture of human-written textbooks and synthetically generated text yields highly capable language models, suggesting that curated human data and machine-generated data are complements rather than substitutes. One challenge is that synthetically generated data tends to lack diversity and inherits errors and hallucinations, even when it is seeded with human-generated data. Subsequent improvements use a generation process that is based on ground truth documents [Lupidi et al., 2025, Yue et al., 2024].

A complementary way to amplify a limited seed set is backtranslation. This approach was originally introduced in machine translation to synthesize parallel data by translating sentences from a source language to a target language, and then back into a source language [Edunov et al., 2018]. The same principle can be repurposed for reasoning tasks: instead of only generating specific solutions for a single problem, we generate new problems that are consistent with an existing solution. MathGenie [Lu et al., 2024] applies this idea to mathematical reasoning by taking a seed set of question–solution pairs. It augments the solutions, and then back-translates them into new questions. Because each newly generated question is grounded in a verified solution, this approach expands both the size and the diversity of the training data while reducing errors and hallucinations.

Human-in-the-loop approaches

Fully automatic generation pipelines are not always sufficient. Models can struggle to generate specific scenarios or domain-relevant cases. The reason for these failures is usually that the generating LLM has specific blind spots, which can also make it difficult to generate genuinely informative data [Lippmann et al., 2024].

Such problems motivate human-in-the-loop approaches, in which people steer, filter, or revise machine-generated content rather than authoring it from scratch.

WANLI [Liu et al., 2022] pairs a language model that proposes challenging natural language inference examples with human annotators who filter and relabel them, combining the scalability of automatic generation with human quality control.

EvalAssist [Santillán Cooper et al., 2025] applies a similar principle to evaluation tooling, using synthetic data to support and accelerate human judgment. A related strategy is to prompt the language model to produce an initial seed text, which human raters then edit before the result is used to bootstrap a larger fully-synthetic dataset. In this way, the human effort is spent on correcting the model rather than on authoring every example.

19.3.2 Generating Evaluation Data

Beyond training, synthetic generation plays a critical role in evaluation. Traditional static benchmarks suffer from rapid data contamination, where test sets inadvertently leak into the pretraining corpora of modern LLMs. To mitigate this, dynamic evaluation frameworks [Kiela et al., 2021] increasingly rely on synthetic data generation to create bespoke, single-use test cases.

Furthermore, the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm [Zheng et al., 2024] simulates human evaluation by prompting a strong model to grade the outputs of other models, highly correlating the models with human preference and significantly reducing the latency of evaluation cycles.

Further creation of dedicated hard benchmarks for LLMs can once again be done with human-in-the-loop approaches, such as the MATH2 benchmark. For this benchmark, multiple LLMs are used to iteratively generate and adjust mathematical questions and solutions through multi-turn prompting. Human annotators then further expand on the questions and check the answers, again aided by LLMs in the process [Shah et al., 2024]. Other approaches to efficient generation of synthetic evaluation data shift the task for annotators from coming up with new samples, to editing samples to be harder for the LLM [Yuan et al., 2021].

Automated red teaming

One specific use case for machine-generated evaluation is through the safety-oriented evaluation by means of automated red teaming. In this approach, one LLM generates adversarial prompts to probe a target model for vulnerabilities before deployment [Ganguli et al., 2022]. By synthesizing many potentially malicious prompts, researchers can stress-test and harden models against toxic outputs, jailbreaks, and misalignments at a scale that human red teams cannot match [Perez et al., 2022]. Because the same generated prompts can subsequently be used to finetune the target model against those failures, red teaming sits at the boundary between synthetic evaluation and synthetic training data.

19.3.3 Generating Agentic Data

In agentic settings, data must be synthesized for an entire trajectory (and not just in single instruction-response pairs). As the agent is interacting with its environment, a full sequence of tool calls, observations, and decisions is produced [Kang et al., 2025]. This goes beyond data that trains or evaluates a regular LLM operating on a single input-output pair. Generating agentic data is a more complex problem than generating data to instruct the underlying LLM itself, even though the same generative models are typically used to produce it. Let us look at an example.

Example 2.

Consider synthesizing a single training trajectory for a tool-using agent, roughly following the two-phase recipe of APIGen-MT [Prabhakar et al., 2025].

First a task proposer invents a plausible user goal and a set of available tools, together with a ground-truth answer:

User: “What will the weather be in Leiden this weekend, and should I bring an umbrella?”  Tools: get_forecast(city, days).

An actor model then rolls out the interaction, emitting the intermediate tool call and consuming its (simulated) observation before answering:

get_forecast("Leiden", 2) →\rightarrow {sat: rain, sun: clear} →\rightarrow “Rain on Saturday, clear on Sunday—bring an umbrella for Saturday.”

Finally a verifier checks that the emitted call is well-formed, that its arguments match the request, and that the final answer is consistent with the observation. Only trajectories that pass verification are kept.

Note what had to be synthesized: not just a single input–output pair, but the goal, the tool schema, the call, the observation, and a checker that verifies the whole trace.

Methods for agentic generation usually involve entire orchestrations of agents for multi-turn conversations including human inputs and tool use [Wu et al., 2024]. APIGen-MT [Prabhakar et al., 2025] exemplifies this shift with a two-phase framework that generates verifiable and diverse multi-turn agent data. TOUCAN [Xu et al., 2025b] pursues a similar goal at a larger scale, simulating realistic tool calls to construct a large tool-agentic dataset. Beyond generating trajectories for a fixed skill, some work synthesizes data explicitly to transfer a new skill or behavior from a strong model to a weaker one, a process referred to as Generative Teaching [Crispino et al., 2024]. Furthermore, agentic synthetic data is not limited to text, analogous generation pipelines extend to images, tabular data, and other forms of interaction or behavioral data.

For the generation of agentic synthetic data, controlling the task complexity is a recurring challenge. Deep-research agents, for example, aim to solve complex question-answering tasks through long-horizon interactions with online tools, but the data typically used to train them lacks fine-grained control over difficulty and quality, yielding synthetic data that falls short of capturing sufficient complexity. Pandit et al. [2025] address this issue with a pipeline that synthesizes question-answer pairs that progressively increase task complexity until a frontier baseline web agent fails. This curriculum learning approach calibrates task-difficulty directly against agent capability rather than a fixed heuristic.

AReaL-SEA [Gao et al., 2026] addresses reliability from a complementary angle. Here, a multi-agent engine synthesizes tool-grounded dialogues in combination with executable per-instance checkers. Next, a closed-loop self-evolving process updates the prompts over time to improve reliability.

19.4 Data Curation

Once synthetic data has been generated, we need to check it for quality and curate it. Usually, this means filtering, scoring, and selecting samples so that only the examples that are useful are retained. Evaluating synthetic data usefulness can be approached in two complementary ways: extrinsically, by measuring its effect on a downstream task, or intrinsically, by examining properties of the generated data (or the generative process) directly.

In practice, curation is implemented as a multi-stage filtering pipeline in which criteria that we will discuss below are turned into concrete operators. Typical stages include semantic deduplication (removing near-duplicate examples via embedding similarity to preserve diversity), perplexity filtering (discarding incoherent or off-distribution text using a reference model), rule-based or format checks, and reward-model or judge scoring to retain only high-fidelity samples. The seminal Textbooks Are All You Need paper [Gunasekar et al., 2023] is a reminder that this curation step often matters as much as the volume of data: aggressive filtering for quality can outweigh sheer quantity. Without it, models readily learn the generative artifacts and statistical anomalies of their teachers.

19.4.1 Extrinsic evaluation

Extrinsic evaluation answers a simple question: does the synthetic data actually help on a downstream task? This topic is also referred to as utility. In practice, utility is measured by training or finetuning a model on the synthetic data (alone or mixed with real data) and evaluating it on a held-out, real-world test set. Extrinsic evaluation is the most direct measure of whether synthetic data is useful. For example, if the performance (e.g., in terms of perplexity) of a pretrained model increases when synthetic data is included, we can conclude that the data is useful. However, it is also the most expensive: it requires a full training run before any signal is available. If we make changes to the generation process or select a different set, we need to retrain and evaluate our model. This makes the extrinsic evaluation a poor fit for filtering or selecting individual examples during generation.

19.4.2 Intrinsic evaluation

Intrinsic evaluation instead looks at characteristics of the generations themselves, without the cost of a downstream training run. A number of quality aspects have been proposed for evaluating synthetic text [Ramesh et al., 2025]. Rather than evaluating at the output level, it is also possible to benchmark the language models of the generative process directly [Kim et al., 2025b]. This can give an earlier and cheaper signal than inspecting the generated data.

Data correctness

A generated example is only useful if its content is factually and logically sound. Since synthetic data often comes from other LLMs, it inherits the generating model’s failure modes. This includes hallucinated facts, inconsistent reasoning, or labels that do not match the content. These errors can subsequently propagate into models that are trained on them. Correctness is typically checked by comparing generations against human-generated labels [Long et al., 2024, Chim et al., 2025], performing verification (e.g., a rule-based checker or a separate judge model) [Chen et al., 2025a, Yang et al., 2025, Setlur et al., 2024], or through consistency checks across multiple generations for the same input [Zelikman et al., 2022b, Seegmiller et al., 2025].

Data diversity

A key problem in creating synthetic data is maintaining diversity. Logit suppression and temperature sampling can improve data diversity but come at a cost of data correctness [Chung et al., 2023]. Diversity is also difficult to measure: lexical heuristics (e.g., ROUGE) or neural heuristics (embedding-based similarity) are commonly used as proxies, but each captures only a fraction of the possible variation in the data.

MetaSynth addresses this problem by generating synthetic data that enhances diversity through meta-prompting, where a language model orchestrates multiple expert LLM agents to collaboratively generate data [Riaz et al., 2025].

Data contamination

A serious risk for synthetic data is contamination [Deng et al., 2024, Balloccu et al., 2024]. The generating LLM is pretrained on large, imperfectly filtered web datasets, and can memorize benchmarks and reproduce or closely paraphrase them when prompted to generate new training examples. After many steps, synthetically generated data converges to that of existing benchmarks. This inflates evaluation scores artificially, for example in the case of code generation benchmarks [Matton et al., 2024]. Solutions for this type of leakage should go beyond simple exact-match filters, and requires n-gram overlap search against known benchmarks, membership-inference-style probing [Puerto et al., 2025, Huang et al., 2026], or dynamic dataset construction pipelines [Chen et al., 2025b].

Fairness and biases

LLMs inherit and amplify social biases from their own training data. If we, in turn, use the LLMs to generate synthetic corpora, we risk further perpetuating stereotypical associations, skewed demographic representation, or unequal generation quality across social groups [Gallegos et al., 2024]. This is of particular concern for synthetic data because it is produced at scale and often consumed directly as training material for new LLMs.

Finally, intrinsic metrics are only proxies for usefulness. A dataset can score well on diversity or pass correctness checks while failing to improve, or even harm, extrinsic evaluation. Lexical and neural diversity heuristics measure surface-level variation and can fail to spot redundancy in ways that matter (e.g., repeated reasoning patterns) or overestimate diversity. Correctness checks further depend on the availability of a trusted reference, rule-based verifier, or judge model, which for open-ended or subjective generations may not exist, or may be unreliable. For these reasons, intrinsic evaluation is best treated as an additional check rather than a true replacement for extrinsic evaluation.

19.5 Risks

As should be clear by now, using synthetic data for training agentic LLMs is a solution that is not without problems. We will discuss several more risks associated with synthetic data, including model collapse, bias amplification, security and privacy vulnerabilities, and legal and ethical concerns.

19.5.1 Model Collapse

The defining risk of the loop in Figure 19.2 is that it feeds on its own output. Model collapse is the well-documented phenomenon where training successive model generations on recursively generated AI data causes the diversity of the original distribution to disappear [Shumailov et al., 2024]. Rare events and low-probability linguistic nuance are sampled less often, so each generation forgets a little more of the distribution’s long-tailed behavior until the model converges to a repetitive, high-probability model. Some experiments show that repeated training on purely synthetic data yields diminishing and eventually negative returns [Singh et al., 2024], and concentrating a corpus on a few synthetic sources, rather than many, increases the fragility of the resulting model [Schaffelder and Gatt, 2025]. Similarly, small students distilled from a teacher are prone to hallucination and often fail on long-tailed knowledge [Kandpal et al., 2023]. More subtly, imitating a teacher can produce a student that matches the teacher’s style while lagging on factuality, a gap which is usually only revealed by targeted capability benchmarks [Gudibande et al., 2023]. The standard mitigation is to keep anchoring the corpus with real human data rather than training on synthetic data alone.

19.5.2 Bias Amplification

Because generative models over-represent the majority modes of their training distribution, synthesizing data tends to cut off the diverse, long-tail perspectives found in natural human discourse [van der Meer et al., 2024]. A student trained on such data can therefore exhibit an amplified, caricatured version of the teacher’s social biases. The student model reproduces stereotypical associations, skewed demographic representation, or unequal generation quality across groups [Gallegos et al., 2024]. This concern is larger for synthetic data than for original model outputs because the data is produced at scale and consumed directly as training material, and each round of the loop compounds the previous round.

19.5.3 Security Risks

There are also security risks associated with synthetic training data. Relying on generated data introduces new attack vectors for maliciously polluting training data. If the teacher model or any stage of the generation pipeline is compromised, an adversary can mount a data-poisoning attack. Because synthetic corpora are typically too large to audit exhaustively, subtle back doors or malicious instruction–response pairs can be inserted, which remain dormant until triggered in the deployed student. Poisoning even a tiny fraction of a web-scale corpus has been shown to be practical and cheap [Carlini et al., 2024], and the risk is heightened when the “teacher” is an uncontrolled third-party model whose training data and alignment are opaque.

19.5.4 Privacy Preservation

Synthetic generation is frequently mentioned as a solution for data privacy. The idea is that synthetic data does not contain personally identifiable information (PII) [Dwork and Roth, 2014], yet is able to reflect the statistical properties of private data (such as medical records).

However, in this type of data there is a substantial risk of memorization. Without strict privacy guarantees during the generation phase, generative models can unintentionally reconstruct and therefore leak exact snippets of the sensitive human data on which they were originally trained [Carlini et al., 2021]. Privacy evaluations show that off-the-shelf privacy-preserving methods can fail [Ramesh et al., 2024].

Common privacy approaches rely on differential privacy [Dwork et al., 2006], a guarantee on the generative process that bounds how much the output distribution can change when a single individual’s record is added to or removed from the dataset. This bound is controlled by a privacy budget, where smaller values enforce stronger protection at the cost of greater utility loss [Yue et al., 2023].

19.5.5 Copyright and Terms of Use

Part of the appeal of synthetic data is that it sidesteps the unclear legal status of scraping internet-scale human text, which has already produced copyright litigation. The 2025 Bartz v. Anthropic settlement in the US is illustrative. A district court found LLM training itself exceedingly transformative and thus a candidate for fair use, however, liability still arose from how the underlying corpus was obtained, namely the ingestion of hundreds of thousands of pirated books, and Anthropic settled at roughly $3,000 per work (about $1.5 billion in total), with parallels in other legal cases such as Kadrey v. Meta. This shows that to an increasing degree the data underlying training is scrutinized for copyright and terms of use.

Synthetic data does not fully escape this issue. Distilling from a proprietary model raises a distinct issue: the terms of service of most commercial LLM APIs explicitly forbid using their outputs to train competing models. Data generated by a black-box teacher may therefore be legally problematic regardless of copyright. Such a tension surfaced publicly in 2025 amid accusations that competing systems had been trained on the outputs of frontier APIs. For practitioners, this means that the licence of the generator is as important to check as the licence of any human data it replaces.

19.6 Concluding Remarks

Synthetic data has moved from a niche augmentation method to a central ingredient of the LLM pipeline (Chapter 3), driven by the prospect that human text becomes a scaling bottleneck (Chapter 4). Strong models and multi-agent orchestrations can simulate instruction data, evaluation benchmarks, and, more recently, whole agentic trajectories of tool calls and decisions (Chapters 9 and 11).

Because raw generations are noisy, curation, extrinsic utility together with intrinsic checks on correctness, diversity, and contamination, are as important as generation itself. The various setups can be considered forms of knowledge distillation organized along the axes of signal, data source, timing (off- vs. on-policy), and teacher identity.

Reusing synthetic data from the same model for self-improvement has promises for enabling verifiable reasoning (Chapter 6). However, in all these pipelines we need to be careful about what data these models are consuming: without real-data anchoring and careful auditing, model collapse, bias amplification, security, privacy, and licensing risks all compound with every iteration.

Chapter 20 *Advanced Transformer and Agentic Architectures

20.1 Transformer Architectures

The success of large language models has spawned interesting new research avenues into transformer architectures. LLMs were good at language, but not at other problem types such as reasoning and planning. This caused researchers to explore the limits of the types of computations that transformers were able to do, and we will discuss some of the topics in the following sections. Specifically, they asked the questions whether transformers were Turing complete (Section 20.1.1)? The weak performance on planning problems prompted studies that trained transformers directly on decision traces, to see if that allowed them to be able to plan and backtrack (Section 20.1.2). Next, we will look at looped language models, where multiple models are connected directly at the level of the embeddings.

20.1.1 Transformers are Turing-complete

The difficulty of LLMs to manage state at inference time suggests that LLMs are limited in the type of computations that they can perform. In theoretical computer science the concept of Turing completeness indicates whether a certain model of computation is powerful enough to be able to perform any type of computation of a certain category (which includes being able to manage state values correctly). This concept was introduced in a famous paper by Alan Turing in 1936, in which he proved that a certain type of machine would be powerful enough to do so [Turing, 1936]. To be called Turing complete, a system must be able to simulate any other computational device and be able to process any problem that can be expressed in an algorithm (but perhaps take infinite time and memory to do so). It turns out that it is not too difficult to achieve Turing completeness; most general purpose programming languages are Turing complete.11 1 For example, the Python programming language is Turing complete, but simple regular expression matching, without backreferencing, is not.

The difficulty of LLMs—and of transformer-based models in general—to manage state would suggest that the transformer architecture may not be Turing complete. Interestingly, already in 2021 Pérez et al. [2021] have studied this question, and have proven that the transformer architecture is able to simulate a Turing machine, and is thus Turing complete.

This is an encouraging result, since it indicates that there is no fundamental reason why transformers would not be able to manage state correctly. It may well be a matter of finding the right prompt, or finding the right pretraining and finetuning dataset.

Unfortunately, the fact that something is theoretically possible, does not mean that achieving it will be easy, or that it can be done efficiently. For example, it might be that certain architectural extensions to the transformer architecture would enhance the ease with which efficient state management can be achieved. We will now discuss methods that have been developed so that LLMs can efficiently solve decision making and planning problems.

20.1.2 Pretraining Backtracking on Decision Traces

The finding that transformers are Turing-complete encourages research in planning and decision making. In this section we will discuss studies that pretrain a transformer architecture on decision traces, to good results. Note that this section is not about transformers that are trained on natural language—LLMs—but on transformers trained on decision traces.

First we discuss pretraining transformers directly on decision traces: sequences of state-action-reward triples, not language tokens. Several works study whether transformer networks can be trained to perform reinforcement learning—to learn from feedback, to perform learned policies, and to explore to learn better actions. Chen et al. [2021], Lee et al. [2023], Wang et al. [2024] showed that basic transformer architectures can indeed be pretrained and finetuned on decision traces from typical planning problems. When an empty (non-language trained) transformer is pretrained on decision traces, it can exhibit in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL). So far, this has been shown using toy problems such as Boyan’s chain and Cartpole (see Figure 20.1). Furthermore, in the games of Chess and Hex encouraging results were achieved by pretraining the decision transformer on minimax [Markeeva et al., 2024, Knuth and Moore, 1975] and MCTS [Browne et al., 2012] search traces [Schultz et al., 2024, Kempinski et al., 2025]. Transformers were able to learn to lookahead and search a few steps. Other works report encouraging results in the game of Othello [Li et al., 2023, Kempinski et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2025].

A further work that studies how transformer architectures can be trained to perform decisions is self backtracking [Yang et al., 2026a]. In this approach the model is again trained on decision traces. However, a new kind of token is introduced, <<backtrack>>, that prompts the model to perform explicit backtracking at inference time. The model is trained on a dataset of decisions, and when an error is encountered during training, the <<backtrack>> token is learned, to find an alternative solution. At inference time, then, this backtracking is performed. A mechanism that consists of expansion/backtracking/selection is executed by the model, so that alternative solutions for the state in question are examined.

The self backtracking approach reports good results on typical planning problems such as the 24-game and maze navigation, compared to standard baselines on small versions of DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3. Through the introduction of a new type of token and new backtracking-functionality in the model, this approach allows enhanced-transformer models to perform search, blurring the line between training and inference.

These are encouraging results, although it is still an open question to what extend the weakness of transformers in managing state has been solved. Performing inference-time ICRL on larger problems is an area of active research.

20.1.3 LoopedLLM and Recursive Multi-Agent Systems

Improving the expressive power of transformers brings them closer to a general purpose programming architecture. We will discuss two other developments: looped language models and recursive systems.

It is easy to connect LLM agents at the language level: just let them speak to each other in natural language, on which they are all trained. However, this necessitates many (de)tokenization steps, which take time and introduces differences between embeddings. Can we directly connect embeddings, bypassing the tokenizers, and do training and inference at that level?

Giannou et al. [2023] show how looped transformers (transformers whose input neurons are directly connected to transformer output neurons, either from the same or from another model) can emulate a basic calculator, a basic linear algebra library, and in-context learning algorithms that employ backpropagation. Looped transformers are a powerful architecture, see for example Yang et al. [2023], Saunshi et al. [2025], Zhu et al. [2025].

A further development of direct embedding-to-embedding connections is recursive multi-agent systems [Yang et al., 2026b]. This approach connects heterogeneous agents in a collaboration loop, enabling in-distribution latent thought generation and cross-agent latent state transfer. An inner-outer loop learning algorithm (metalearning, see Chapter 8) performs whole-system co-optimization through shared gradient-based credit assignment across recursion rounds. Experiments with four agents over benchmarks from mathematics, science, medicine, search, and code generation, showed stable multi-agent training. In comparison with other single/multi-agent and recursive baselines, accuracy is improved by a few percentage points, inference is twice as fast, and token usage is reduced by comparable ratio.

An innovation of RecursiveMAS is the introduction of a two-level recursive-link. Training a multi-agent system is difficult because gradients must flow through multiple models, and this process can become unstable. RecursiveMAS improves this process by freezing the parameters of the underlying LLMs and only training the lightweight RecursiveLink modules. The training occurs in two stages.

20.2 Agentic Architectures

In addition to new transformer architectures, the work on agentic LLMs has also led to advanced agentic architectures. First, we will look at in-context reinforcement learning, where we will see that LLMs are able to perform policy improvement when the prompt is given a history of state-action-reward triples. Second, we will look at self-modifying agents, and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this approach. Finally, we will look at meta agents.

20.2.1 In-Context Reinforcement Learning

Recall from Section 2.2.3 that the goal of reinforcement learning is to compute a policy that has an optimal action for each state [Sutton and Barto, 2018]. As the agent converges towards this policy, in each timestep, the agent learns these actions from feedback from its environment, the rewards. These rewards reinforce the confidence of the agent in the policy’s actions in each state (see Figure 20.2). The self-reflection approaches from the previous section borrow many ideas from reinforcement learning for the agentic harness. We will now discuss related methods that optimize prompts by in-context reinforcement learning, where the LLM performs prompt improvement.

Reinforcement-type learning mechanisms have been observed to emerge directly in LLMs, when environment histories were provided to the LLM by an external prompt optimizer: the LLM in certain self-reflection loops can perform policy-improvement. This phenomenon is called in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) [Song et al., 2025], see Figure 20.3.

Krishnamurthy et al. [2024] asked the question whether generic LLMs that are trained on language can explore in-context, and whether they can learn in-context from feedback. This question has since been answered positively by various studies [Demircan et al., 2024, Song et al., 2025, Moeini et al., 2025, Monea et al., 2024, Nie et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024].

In ICRL, an external harness iteratively calls the LLM, feeding it a sequence of action, state, and reward triples, in-context (Figure 20.3). The history of triples grows in each iteration. The LLM reacts by improving its implicit policy, providing increasingly good action choices in each iteration, thus we conclude that it performs the essence of reinforcement learning inside the LLM.

In ICRL, the agent-algorithm selects an action, to sample a step and get an answer (a state, reward pair) from the environment, see Figure 20.3. A Markov decision process, or MDP, is a process in which all relevant information to calculate the next state is contained in the previous state and the action taken. Therefore, the prompt for the policy-LLM contains all relevant information, it accumulates the history of (s,a,r)(s,a,r)-triples, which the LLM can use to improve the policy of the best action for each state.

For state, the history of answers is a natural choice, but, in general, how to best model LLM prompt improvement as an MDP is still an active area of research.

In ICRL the agent uses the LLM for the policy-function. The LLM can also be used (with a different prompt) to play the role of environment, as in a self-reflection harness.

In-context reinforcement learning occurs in a multi-round prompting harness, where, after the environment-LLM generates a response at the current round, a numerical reward is calculated by the LLM for the response that the LLM just calculated. At the next round, the agent-LLM is prompted again with the same task and a context that now consists of the previous responses and rewards. The quality of the agent-LLM’s response increases as the context becomes longer. Just like a reinforcement learning algorithm, the LLM is able to maximize the numeric reward, at inference time. Song et al. [2025] report how the ICRL approach was validated on the applications of tree of thoughts (Game of 24, creative writing, and ScienceWorld), outperforming self refine and reflexion.

How does the ICRL process work, inside the LLM? At inference time the LLM performs a forward pass through the transformer network, computing the inference token. This forward pass has been found to implicitly perform reinforcement learning [Wang et al., 2024]. In other words, in-weights learning is where the model has learned the right answer from its trained weights, at training time; in-context learning is where the model has learned the right answer at inference time from few-shot examples provided in its context; and in-context reinforcement learning is where the LLM has learned the right answer using (apparent) reinforcement learning on a growing sequence of the state-action-reward triples that it produced itself through inference. Thus, the reinforcing algorithm, optimizing the policy, is done implicitly by the LLM forward pass (inference step) when a sequence of prompts or history is given in the context.

Note that the LLM can be used for the agent, as a policy optimizer, and for the environment, to calculate the next state and reward. To ensure that the agent is learning without accidentally benefiting from the environment’s knowledge, it is better to use a separate LLM. This, too, is an active area of research.

20.2.2 Self-Modifying Hyperagents

In this book, we have discussed self-reflective prompt improvers that are based on search algorithms and reinforcement learning. The code for these external algorithms is written by human researchers, and does not change as the agent is learning. The approach by which the prompt is improved is limited by these static algorithms.

LLMs excel at manipulating and judging computer code [Zhuge et al., 2024]. We could, in principle, easily ask them to generate code for an agentic prompt harness, or for an in-context reinforcement learning harness. We could even ask the LLM to run the code on a particular problem instance, and, based on the outcome of the experiment, ask for an improvement of the prompt-improver code. If the LLM is good at using experiment-results for writing prompt-improvement code, this approach could work better than standard approaches from the published literature.

Self-modifying code (computer programs that alter their own instructions while they are being executed) has a long history in computer science [Cai et al., 2007], as an alternative to conditional branching statements. Many computer languages support it, from assembly languages, to Lisp [Abelson and Sussman, 2022] and Python. It is a powerful method that can be used for performance improvement, for example in just-in-time compilation [Ansel et al., 2011]. However, programs become less predictable, which may cause problems in finding errors in the program, and raises security concerns. For this reason the use is sometimes discouraged when predictability of programs is important.

An advantage of self-modifying agents is open-endedness: they can continuously improve themselves, without fixed boundaries set by static algorithms [Schmidhuber, 2007]. A challenge is to do this safely [Zhang et al., 2026b]. In Darwin-Gödel-Machine-Hyperagents the authors integrate (1) an agent to solve the target task with (2) a meta agent to modify itself and the task agent, into a single (editable) program. Note that the meta-level modification procedure is itself editable, enabling self-modification. This allows, in principle, not only improving the task-solving behavior, but also the mechanism that generates future improvements [Zhang et al., 2026c]. The experiments, however, do not achieve full openness, as they use a fixed task distribution, as well as fixed parent selection and evaluation protocols.

As approaches become more open-ended, paradoxically, a challenge becomes to control the process of improvement, to ensure that it does not degenerate, but keeps improving [Cemri et al., 2025, Ecoffet et al., 2020]. In general, the problem of powerful metalearning approaches is to ensure stable learning processes. Powerful generation requires powerful evaluation—adaptation to fit the environment.

20.2.3 Meta Agents

The two-level optimization process of metalearning that we have seen in many self-reflection approaches, can be applied as an explicit design principle in harness design for agents. Recently, several such architectures have been published. In these designs, the inner learning loop is formed by the harness and the LLM, and the outer learning loop improves the configuration of this inner harness. The inner harness configuration typically performs prompt management, memory management, tool use, and security and control, and can be represented as language or code. The outer loop analyzes execution traces of the inner loop, to improve the configuration or code of the inner harness. We will briefly describe some of these approaches.

Self improving coding agent [Robeyns et al., 2025] is based on the idea of self-modifying agents. They demonstrate that an agent system, equipped with basic coding tools, can autonomously edit itself. Their approach improves performance on software engineering benchmark tasks, achieving substantial performance gains from 17 to 53 percent.

Meta harness [Lee et al., 2026] also achieves good results, using external memory and text optimization. Figure 20.4 illustrates how meta harness works. (1) A filesystem has all prior candidates’ source code, execution traces, and scores; the agent reads this, and generates code for a new harness. (2) The proposed harness is evaluated on evaluation tasks. (3) All proposed code, reasoning traces, and evaluation scores are stored in the filesystem in a new directory, and the loop repeats.

Self harness [Zhang et al., 2026a] and Agentic Harness Engineering [Lin et al., 2026] further explore harness design, achieving substantial improvements on software engineering tasks. Recursive self-evolving agents [Nguyen et al., 2026] focuses on the selection aspect of self-improving agents.

Another use case is described by Luo et al. [2026]. They use a meta harness to design a harness for turning a scientific paper into a conference-poster. This work thus has contributions on two levels: a method for making a meta-harness, and a concrete harness for designing posters—which the authors, obviously, use on their own paper.

The Shepherd system [Yu et al., 2026] provides a functional meta agent programming environment.22 2 https://shepherd-agents.ai Shepherd defines LLM agents as Python functions, allowing an agent’s execution traces to be monitored, rolled-back, forked, modified, and resumed. Early experiments show significant performance improvements on three different benchmarks, as illustrated in Figure 20.5.

A comprehensive survey with more approaches on self-improving agent designs is Ren et al. [2026]. Their taxonomy explicitly recognizes the two-level architecture.

20.3 Concluding Remarks

In this chapter we have discussed some advanced architectures, at the level of the transformers, and at the level of the agents. Both are highly active fields of research.
