Chapter 21 *Mechanistic Interpretability for LLM Agents

21.1 Opening the LLM

How do LLMs work inside? Opening up the black box of large neural architectures is an important topic of research. We wish to understand how the billions of neurons embed representations, how they reason and how they come to conclusions. The field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) provides many different methods to do so [Minh et al., 2022, Rios et al., 2020, Van Stein et al., 2022, Selvaraju et al., 2017, Ali et al., 2022].

Static XAI methods from the classical machine learning community have been quite successful [Molnar, 2020]. Methods exist to relate how input pictures map to output classes, for example using feature maps [Ren et al., 2016, Kohonen, 1982, Redmon et al., 2016]. Counterfactual analysis [Karimi et al., 2020, Huang et al., 2024], LIME [Ribeiro et al., 2016] and SHAP [Lundberg and Lee, 2017], among others, help understand how inputs map to outputs for structured data. These methods belong to the behavioral and attributional class of explainability algorithms, where the model is seen as a black-box (Figure 21.1). Attribution methods such as SHAP and LIME approximate the contributions of different input features to the final output. Behavioral analysis such as achieved by using counterfactual methods provide insight into which features matter (but not perse how much they matter).

Moving beyond surface-level input-output correlations, concept-based interpretability seeks to identify whether specific, human-understandable information is encoded within the model’s internal states. This is primarily investigated through linear probing, where a simple supervised classifier is trained on frozen hidden activations to detect the presence of particular semantic concepts—such as parts of speech, sentiment, or factual entities [Alain and Bengio, 2016, Belinkov, 2022]. While attribution methods highlight which parts of the input are influential, probing allows researchers to verify what knowledge the model represents at different layers (Figure 21.1). However, a known limitation of probing is the causal gap: discovering that a concept is represented in a layer does not necessarily mean the model uses that information for its final prediction.

More recently, dynamic methods have been developed to uncover patterns under the hood of large transformer models. These belong to the sub-domain of mechanistic interpretability (MI). The goal of MI is to uncover the mechanisms by which the model dynamically comes to conclusions [Nanda et al., 2023, Bereska and Gavves, 2024, Ferrando et al., 2024, Rai et al., 2024]. In other words, MI seeks a low-level, causal explanation of a model’s behavior in terms of its internal activations and connections, analogous to decompiling a program’s binary into readable code. Methods such as sparse autoencoders [Cunningham et al., 2023, Makelov et al., 2024], neural lenses [Black et al., 2022] and circuit discovery [Conmy et al., 2023] are being used to successfully enhance insight into how LLMs work, for example, in chess [Davis and Sukthankar, 2024].

XAI and MI in particular are active areas of research that will allow us to better understand how LLMs reason and come to conclusions [Sharkey et al., 2025]. Once a better understanding is reached, LLMs can be improved accordingly, for example, to reduce hallucinations.

This chapter will dive deeper into the many facets of MI.

21.2 Hallucination and Faithfulness in Model Reasoning

A significant barrier to the deployment of LLMs in high-stakes environments is the phenomenon of hallucination: the generation of syntactically plausible but factually incorrect content. From an interpretability perspective, the challenge lies in distinguishing whether a model’s output is the result of a robust internal computation or a post-hoc justification. This distinction is formalized as the study of faithfulness, the degree to which a model’s stated reasoning (e.g., in chain of thought prompting) is causally responsible for its final output.

Mechanistic interpretability (MI) provides the tools necessary to move beyond behavioral metrics of accuracy and toward a causal understanding of model failure modes. For instance, research using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has identified specific honesty or knowledge-retrieval circuits [Lindsey et al., 2025]. In these studies, researchers identified latent features that activate when a model encounters unfamiliar entities; a failure in the inhibitory logic of these circuits, where the model proceeds to generate tokens despite low activation in the relevant knowledge feature, directly results in fabricated answers.

Furthermore, MI allows us to investigate the causal necessity of intermediate reasoning steps. While a model may produce a convincing chain of thought (CoT), it remains possible that the model has already calculated the final answer via a separate internal shortcut and is merely generating the CoT as a stochastic parrot.

To test this, Chen et al. [2026] utilized causal mediation analysis combined with SAEs to intervene on the latent thought process during arithmetic tasks. By injecting the latent activations from a CoT-enabled run into a standard zero-shot run, they demonstrated that in sufficiently large models, these intermediate thoughts significantly boosted solution confidence. This provides empirical evidence that for larger architectures, the CoT is not merely cosmetic but represents a faithful causal link in the model’s reasoning chain.

Conversely, the absence of such causal links in smaller models suggests that faithful reasoning may be an emergent property of scale, appearing only when the model possesses sufficient parameters to represent complex, multi-step algorithms. Developing robust metrics to quantify this faithfulness is a critical frontier in AI safety; by peeking into the model’s activations, we can potentially develop hallucination detectors that trigger when a model’s internal confidence features do not align with its external verbosity.

21.3 The Residual Stream and Iterative Refinement

Before exploring specific MI methods it is necessary to establish a formal mental model of the transformer architecture. Unlike classical feed-forward networks where each layer replaces the representation of the previous one, modern transformers operate on a residual stream [Elhage et al., 2021].

Formally, let hℓ∈ℝdm​o​d​e​lh_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}} be the state of the hidden representation after layer ℓ\ell. The Transformer architecture is defined by the recurrence:

hℓ=hℓ−1+ℱℓ​(hℓ−1)h_{\ell}=h_{\ell-1}+\mathcal{F}_{\ell}(h_{\ell-1}) (21.1)

where ℱℓ\mathcal{F}_{\ell} represents the computation performed by the ℓ\ell-th layer (comprising multi-head attention and feed-forward blocks).

This structure implies that the final representation hLh_{L} is a cumulative sum of the initial embedding xe​m​b​e​dx_{embed} and the contributions (Δ​h\Delta h) from every subsequent layer:

hL=xe​m​b​e​d+∑ℓ=1LΔ​hℓh_{L}=x_{embed}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\Delta h_{\ell} (21.2)

In this view, the residual stream acts as a high-dimensional communication channel. Individual layers do not transform the entire state; rather, they read information from the stream, perform a local computation and write their results back into the stream via vector addition. This additive nature ensures that information can persist across many layers, and more importantly, it justifies the linear decomposition of the model’s final output.

21.4 Polysemanticity and Superposition

A primary bottleneck in reverse-engineering neural networks is polysemanticity (Figure 21.2): the empirical observation that individual neurons frequently activate for multiple, semantically unrelated concepts. This phenomenon is deeply linked to superposition, a regime where a model represents nn features in mm dimensions, where n>mn>m. Under the linear representation hypothesis, models exploit the high-dimensional geometry of activation space to store features as almost-orthogonal vectors. While this allows for efficient information compression, it results in a basis mismatch where the fixed neuron basis does not align with the true feature basis.

A formalization was provided by Elhage et al. [2022], who demonstrated using toy models that superposition is a mathematically principled strategy for models to maximize information density when features are sparse. They identified phase transitions in feature encoding: as the sparsity of a concept increases, the model can pack more features into the same number of dimensions, albeit at the cost of interference or noise between those features.

To resolve this entanglement, researchers have turned to dictionary learning, most notably via sparse autoencoders (SAEs). The objective is to learn a linear transformation that maps the tangled neuron activations into a much higher-dimensional, sparse latent space. Bricken et al. [2023] successfully applied this to small-scale transformers, demonstrating that the resulting SAE features are significantly more monosemantic and human-interpretable than the original neurons. This suggested that models are not inherently uninterpretable, but rather that we have been looking at them through the wrong coordinate system.

Subsequent work has explored whether architectural modifications can mitigate the emergence of polysemanticity. For instance, Liu et al. [2023] and others have investigated how different activation functions or regularization penalties (e.g., L1L_{1} sparsity) can pressure the model into adopting a more aligned, interpretable internal basis. Despite these advances, polysemanticity remains a pervasive challenge in state-of-the-art models. The current consensus in MI is that interpreting a model requires moving beyond the “neuron-as-a-unit” paradigm and instead identifying the underlying sparse feature basis in which the model’s causal logic is actually computed.

21.5 The Logit Lens

A fundamental intuition in mechanistic interpretability is that a transformer model does not compute its output in a single leap at the final layer. Instead, it iteratively refines a representation within the residual stream. The logit lens11 1 First introduced in the following blog post: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/AcKRB8wDpdaN6v6ru/interpreting-gpt-the-logit-lens. An updated implementation is provided by [Wang, 2025]. provides a window into this process by decoding the hidden states of intermediate layers directly into the output vocabulary space.

21.5.1 Formal Mechanism

Consider a transformer with LL layers. Let x0x_{0} be the initial embedding of a token, and hℓh_{\ell} be the state of the residual stream after layer ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}. In a standard forward pass, the final hidden state hLh_{L} is converted into logits yy via the layer norm (LN) and the unembedding matrix WU∈ℝdm​o​d​e​l×|V|W_{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times|V|}:

y=Softmax​(LN​(hL)​WU)y=\text{Softmax}(\text{LN}(h_{L})W_{U}) (21.3)

The logit lens generalizes this by applying the same unembedding transformation to intermediate states hℓh_{\ell}:

y^ℓ=Softmax​(LN​(hℓ)​WU)\hat{y}_{\ell}=\text{Softmax}(\text{LN}(h_{\ell})W_{U}) (21.4)

where y^ℓ\hat{y}_{\ell} represents the model’s tentative probability distribution at layer ℓ\ell. By visualizing these distributions across all layers, researchers can observe the evolution of belief as the model moves from vague semantic clusters to specific token predictions.

Direct Logit Attribution

While the logit lens provides an aggregate view of the residual stream hℓh_{\ell}, we often wish to isolate the contribution of a single layer or head. Because the final logit yy is a linear function of the cumulative sum of layer outputs, we can compute the direct logit attribution (DLA) of layer ℓ\ell by projecting its specific output Δ​hℓ\Delta h_{\ell} directly into the vocabulary space:

DLA​(ℓ)=LN​(Δ​hℓ)​WU\text{DLA}(\ell)=\text{LN}(\Delta h_{\ell})W_{U} (21.5)

DLA allows researchers to determine which specific components are writing the correct answer into the stream, rather than just identifying where the answer becomes visible. In the study of factual recall, DLA often reveals that a single knowledge-producing layer provides the vast majority of the probability boost for the correct token.

21.5.2 From the Logit Lens to the Tuned Lens

While the initial logit lens is highly informative for the final third of a network, it often yields gibberish or high-entropy distributions in early layers. This occurs because the residual stream at layer 2, for example, is not yet formatted for the output distribution; it may be storing low-level positional information that is mathematically orthogonal to the unembedding matrix WUW_{U}.

To bridge this gap, Belrose et al. [2023] introduced the tuned lens. Instead of using the static WUW_{U}, the tuned lens trains a layer-specific affine transformation ϕℓ\phi_{\ell} to map hℓh_{\ell} to the logit space:

yt​u​n​e​d,ℓ=Softmax​(ϕℓ​(hℓ))y_{tuned,\ell}=\text{Softmax}(\phi_{\ell}(h_{\ell})) (21.6)

The transformation ϕℓ\phi_{\ell} is trained to minimize the KL-divergence between yt​u​n​e​d,ℓy_{tuned,\ell} and the model’s actual final output yy. This effectively translates the internal language of early layers into the output vocabulary, revealing that factual information often emerges much earlier in the network than the naive logit lens would suggest.

21.5.3 Applications and Interpretations

Lenses serve as a critical diagnostic tool for identifying early exit candidates and locating specific knowledge neurons. For instance, if the logit for a specific fact (e.g., Paris) jumps from the 100th to the 1st rank at layer 14, it suggests that the attention heads or MLP sub-layers in layer 14 are responsible for the factual retrieval.

Variants such as the attention lens [Sakarvadia et al., 2023] apply similar logic to the outputs of individual attention heads, allowing us to see what each head contributes to the prediction in isolation. Collectively, these tools shift our view of the transformer from a sequential pipeline to a cumulative iterative refiner of latent information.

21.6 Circuit Analysis

A central objective of MI is the identification of circuits: minimal subgraphs of a model’s computation graph that are both necessary and sufficient to implement a specific high-level function. Unlike behavioral analysis, circuit discovery seeks to explain how information is transformed step-by-step, from input embeddings to the final logit.

21.6.1 The Prototypical Circuit: Induction Heads

The discovery of the induction head represents a landmark in transformer interpretability [Olsson et al., 2022]. Induction heads are a specialized circuit consisting of at least two attention heads that implement a prefix-matching algorithm. Formally, given a sequence [A]​[B]​…​[A][A][B]\dots[A], an induction head at the current position [A][A] attends to the previous occurrence of [A][A] and copies the subsequent token [B][B] into the residual stream (Figure 21.5).

The Mechanism of Composition

To understand how the two heads in an induction circuit communicate, we must define the three types of attention composition [Elhage et al., 2021]:

  • •

    V-Composition: The output (Value) of a previous head is used as the input to a subsequent head.

  • •

    Q-Composition / K-Composition: The output of a previous head affects where a subsequent head looks by writing into the Query or Key vectors of a token.

An induction head typically relies on K-Composition: a previous token head in an early layer writes information about the preceding token into the residual stream. The induction head in a later layer then uses this information in its Key vector to match the current prefix, allowing it to attend to the correct historical token [B][B].

Olsson et al. [2022] observed that these heads emerge during a specific phase transition in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in the model’s in-context learning capabilities. This was one of the first instances where a complex capability was traced to a specific, discrete algorithm implemented across multiple layers.

21.6.2 Methodologies for Circuit Discovery

Manually identifying circuits is labor-intensive. The study of the indirect object identification (IOI) task by Wang et al. [2022] remains the standard for manual tracing. By utilizing path patching, they identified a network of 26 attention heads (classified into roles such as Name Movers, S-Inhibition Heads, and Duplicate Token Detectors) that collectively perform coreference resolution. Coreference resolution refers to the process of identifying when different tokens in a text refer to the same underlying entity. For example, in the IOI task, the model must determine that a later mention of a name (the indirect object) refers back to a specific person introduced earlier in the sentence, a computation implemented by a specialized sub-network of attention heads.

However, scaling these findings to frontier models requires automated circuit discovery (ACD).

  • •

    ACD: Conmy et al. [2023] introduced an algorithm that performs recursive ablation to prune edges in the computation graph, preserving only those whose removal significantly degrades model performance on a specific task.

  • •

    Sparse Feature Circuits: Moving beyond neurons, more recent frameworks integrate sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to trace circuits in feature space rather than neuron space [Marks et al., 2024]. By treating SAE features as the nodes and the weights between them as edges, researchers can build attribution graphs that visualize the flow of human-understandable concepts (e.g., refusal, translation, or grammar checking).

Evaluation: Faithfulness, Completeness, and Minimality

It is vital to distinguish between a suggested circuit and a causal circuit. A circuit is considered faithful if the model’s performance is preserved when all components outside the circuit are ablated. It is complete if it captures all pathways the model uses to solve the task.

As models scale, we find that algorithms are often represented redundantly or in a distributed manner across the residual stream. Therefore, circuit tracing is not merely a search for a single wire, but an attempt to map the causal mediation of information through the high-dimensional latent space of the model.

21.7 Activation Patching and Causal Interventions

While observational tools such as the logit lens or probing can identify correlations between internal states and outputs, activation patching (also termed causal tracing or interchange interventions) allows researchers to make definitive causal claims. This technique is a practical application of causal mediation analysis [Vig et al., 2020], designed to isolate the effect of a specific model component on a downstream behavior (Figure 21.6).

Formal Framework

The procedure involves two distinct forward passes:

  1. 1.

    Clean Run (xc​l​e​a​nx_{clean}): An input that produces the target behavior (e.g., The Eiffel Tower is in Paris).

  2. 2.

    Corrupted/Counterfactual Run (xc​o​r​rx_{corr}): A modified input where the target behavior disappears (e.g., The Colosseum is in Rome or adding Gaussian noise to the embedding of Eiffel Tower).

Let zi,ℓz_{i,\ell} be the activation of component ii at layer ℓ\ell. In activation patching, we compute a patched run by replacing the activation zi,ℓc​o​r​rz^{corr}_{i,\ell} with zi,ℓc​l​e​a​nz^{clean}_{i,\ell} during the corrupted forward pass. We then measure the probability recovery:

Effect=P⁡(yt​a​r​g​e​t|patched)−P⁡(yt​a​r​g​e​t|corr)P⁡(yt​a​r​g​e​t|clean)−P⁡(yt​a​r​g​e​t|corr)\text{Effect}=\frac{P(y_{target}|\text{patched})-P(y_{target}|\text{corr})}{P(y_{target}|\text{clean})-P(y_{target}|\text{corr})} (21.7)

An Effect score near 1.0 indicates that the patched component is a sufficient causal mediator for the information being studied.

Locating Knowledge and Circuits

Activation patching has led to significant architectural insights. Meng et al. [2022] utilized massive patching sweeps to demonstrate that factual associations are often localized within specific MLP blocks in the middle layers of a model. They found that patching these knowledge neurons could force a model to output a specific fact even when the input context was corrupted.

Beyond localization, patching is the primary tool for path patching, which identifies interactions between components. In the indirect object identification study mentioned before, Wang et al. [2022] patched specific attention heads to trace how information flows from duplicate token detectors to name movers. This reveals the computational graph of the model, moving beyond simple localization to understand the internal algorithm.

Scalability and Attribution Patching

A major challenge of activation patching is its computational cost, as a full sweep requires a forward pass for every component in the model. To mitigate this, researchers use attribution patching [Syed et al., 2024], which uses gradients to linearly approximate the effect of a patch. This allows for rapid hypothesis generation, where the most promising causal candidates are later validated with exact (but slower) activation patching. This surgery-like precision makes patching an indispensable part of the MI toolkit for moving from speculative interpretation to rigorous causal proof.

21.8 Sparse Autoencoders: Dictionary Learning for Feature Discovery

As discussed in the context of superposition, neural networks often represent more features than they have dimensions (n>dn>d). To resolve this tangled representation, we utilize sparse autoencoders (SAEs), a form of unsupervised dictionary learning designed to project activations into a higher-dimensional sparse latent space where features are approximately monosemantic.

Formal Architecture and Training Objective

An SAE consists of an encoder that maps a model activation x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} to a high-dimensional hidden state c∈ℝNc\in\mathbb{R}^{N} (where N≫dN\gg d), and a decoder that attempts to reconstruct the original activation (Figure 21.7).

The encoder is typically defined as:

c=ReLU​(We​n​c​(x−bd​e​c)+be​n​c)c=\text{ReLU}(W_{enc}(x-b_{dec})+b_{enc}) (21.8)

And the reconstruction is given by:

x^=Wd​e​c​c+bd​e​c\hat{x}=W_{dec}c+b_{dec} (21.9)

To ensure the model learns a sparse dictionary rather than a simple identity mapping, we optimize a loss function combining reconstruction fidelity with a sparsity-inducing penalty:

ℒ=‖x−x^‖2+λ​‖c‖1\mathcal{L}=\|x-\hat{x}\|^{2}+\lambda\|c\|_{1} (21.10)

where λ\lambda controls the trade-off between reconstruction accuracy and feature sparsity. Recent advancements, such as JumpReLU SAEs [Rajamanoharan et al., 2024], utilize a thresholded activation function to achieve near-binary on-off feature behavior, which more closely aligns with the theoretical ideal of discrete semantic features.

21.8.1 Monosemanticity and Shadow Models

The efficacy of SAEs has been validated across various scales. Cunningham et al. [2023] demonstrated that SAEs could recover latent features in GPT-2 representing specific grammatical concepts (e.g., numerical context), while Gao et al. [2024] successfully scaled this to billion-parameter models, identifying features for programming languages and sentiment.

A profound implication of this work is the ability to construct a shadow model: by replacing a model’s polysemantic MLP layers with a sparse feature-based approximation, we can preserve model performance while rendering the internal computation legible. Bricken et al. [2023] showed that these SAE features are significantly more monosemantic than the original neurons, effectively untangling the superposed states into a basis that humans can reason about.

In the context of circuit tracing, researchers have moved beyond simple autoencoders to transcoders [Dunefsky et al., 2024]. While a standard SAE reconstructs a single layer’s activations (x→x^x\rightarrow\hat{x}), a transcoder is trained to map activations from layer ℓ\ell to the output of layer ℓ\ell (e.g., x→MLP​(x)x\rightarrow\text{MLP}(x)). This forces the latent features cc to represent the actual computational transformation performed by the layer, providing a direct map of how information is processed rather than just how it is stored.

Evaluation and Open Challenges

Evaluating SAEs requires metrics that balance faithfulness (how much performance is lost when using features?) and interpretability (can humans or automated LLM-probes reliably describe the feature?). Despite the success of SAEs, challenges such as feature splitting, where a single semantic concept is divided across multiple redundant features, and the difficulty of interpreting very rare features remain active areas of research.

21.9 Concluding Remarks

21.9.1 Outlook and Emerging Directions

Mechanistic interpretability has transitioned from a niche curiosity to a rigorous discipline that seeks to bridge the gap between statistical performance and scientific understanding. As the field matures, several frontier directions are defining the research agenda for the next decade.

The most pressing challenge remains the interpretability labor bottleneck. While manual circuit discovery on GPT-2 was a breakthrough, the sheer number of features in frontier models like GPT-4 or Claude 3 necessitates automated workflows. Automated interpretability [Bills et al., 2023] utilizes LLMs to generate and test hypotheses about the semantic meaning of millions of latent features discovered via SAEs. This recursive loop—using a model to interpret its own predecessors—is likely the only path toward the complete transparency of trillion-parameter systems.

To move beyond just-so stories, the field is adopting more rigorous validation frameworks. Causal scrubbing [Chan et al., 2022] represents the current state-of-the-art for hypothesis testing. By systematically replacing components of a proposed circuit with their expected values under a specific hypothesis and measuring the performance drop, researchers can quantitatively measure the faithfulness of their explanations. This moves MI closer to a formal verification science, where one can prove that a model uses a specific algorithm.

Mechanistic interpretability is increasingly viewed as a prerequisite for robust AI alignment. By identifying the circuits responsible for deceptive alignment or situational awareness, researchers hope to build safety buffers that detect if a model is merely producing a user-pleasing answer while internally calculating a different, potentially harmful outcome. Furthermore, understanding the training dynamics, such as the grokking phenomenon where a model suddenly moves from memorization to generalization [Nanda et al., 2023], allows us to intervene during the training process to steer models toward more interpretable and safe representations.

While this chapter focused on language models, the principles of MI are being rapidly extended to other domains, for example to time-series transformers [Kalnāre et al., 2026]. Time-series transformers present unique challenges, as the tokens lack discrete human semantics, requiring the development of new dictionary learning techniques for continuous signals. Similarly, interpreting vision transformers and multi-agent reinforcement learning systems will require a synthesis of spatial, temporal and social interpretability lenses.

21.9.2 Further Reading

The journey from post-hoc behavioral observation to mechanistic circuit diagrams represents a paradigm shift in AI research. We are no longer satisfied with models that merely work; we demand to know how they work. By combining the microscope of sparse autoencoders with the scalpel of activation (and attention) patching, the community is building a comprehensive map of the transformer’s mind, one circuit at a time.
